TL;DR: Mortgage rates continue to climb under pressure from inflation.

Mortgage rates keep rising as markets anticipate a near-certain Fed rate hike next month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.34% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is seven basis points higher than yesterday and 34 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.84% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3030. With Democrats to Control Congress, Is It Better to Buy Bitcoin or an Index Fund?

Investors tend to have a number of misconceptions about what happens when Congress changes political hands.

By Alex Carchidi – Nov 18, 2026 at 7:45AM EST

Control of Congress just changed poltical hands in a big way, and, much as with all major changes, it's no surprise that it's making some investors a bit uneasy. Many holders of Bitcoin (BTC -1.68%) openly worry that the new Democratic majority will have a grudge against crypto due to the Trump administration's embrace of it. At the same time, index fund owners, even for the funds tracking the entire market like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.08%), are concerned about high valuations, persistent inflation, and artificial intelligence (AI), and those worries are amplified by widespread (and overstated) impressions that Democratic congresses tend to be bad for asset prices.

So, in light of the congressional switchover and the many uncertainties in the market right now, does it make more sense to buy Bitcoin, or an index fund?

First, let's establish some basic facts. A party gaining control of both houses of Congress is not something that's strongly associated with the market tanking or flying afterward.

From 1955 to 2023, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.02%) delivered a total return of 8.6% annually in years when a Republican president was balanced by a Democratic Congress (and one of those years, during the 2008 financial crisis, skews those results to the downside significantly). Patience and consistency were still the most important traits that investors needed to have to build their portfolios during those periods.

For Bitcoin, the last time Democrats held control of both congressional chambers, through all of 2021 and 2022, it fell 48%. But don't read too much into that; during the same time, the crypto industry was being rocked by the spectacular collapse of the FTX exchange, and Bitcoin was in one of its bear markets after a strong upward trend in the prior years.

Still, Senator Elizabeth Warren, a loud critic of the cryptocurrency industry, is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee when the new Congress is seated in 2027. She's also one of the senators that detractors traditionally single out as being noxious to stock and crypto prices. A closer inspection reveals that Warren's recent crypto scrutiny has focused on allegedly corrupt practices of some crypto businesses, like those associated with the Trump family and the Trump administration. Similarly, Warren has been in politics for a long time, and the stock market has still on average increased annually during her tenure.

So, it's my assessment that many of the politics-related concerns about Bitcoin and the U.S. stock market are heavily overstated despite being modestly grounded in reality.

Politics aside, there are other reasons that investors propose for being a bit squeamish about buying either Bitcoin or an index fund.

The lofty valuation of the market is a big and real concern. One valuation metric, the Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio, divides the S&P 500's price by its average inflation-adjusted earnings during the prior decade, and it was near 40 on Nov. 17, whereas its long-run mean is 17.5. High valuations tend to predict lower future returns until either earnings catch up or share prices go down; Vanguard's forecast as of Sept. 30 is for  U.S. stocks to return 4.8% to 6.8% per year during the next decade, suggesting a lower-than-average annual return.

Bitcoin is having somewhat of the opposite problem. With its price at $63,360 as of Nov. 17, it's almost 50% below its peak set in October 2025. Its price now is just a bit higher than it was five years ago. That can make it hard to stomach making a purchase.

If you must pick between buying Bitcoin and shares of an index fund, pick the index fund.

An index fund tracking the S&P 500 holds shares of roughly 500 large companies, so its value rests on corporate profits even if valuations shrink. Furthermore, a committee at index provider S&P Dow Jones Indices periodically swaps out companies that no longer meet its criteria, and companies whose market value is growing carry more weight in the index. In contrast, Bitcoin has no cash flow, so its price depends on new buyers willing to pay the market price, and it's obviously harder to attract them when its price isn't climbing steadily.

Of course, most people needn't choose only one of these assets. Anyone buying Bitcoin should already own plenty of index fund shares, and Bitcoin is also something that should be a limited part of most diversified portfolios already.

#3029. Have $1,000? This Beaten-Down Biotech Has 4 Phase 3 Obesity Trials Underway.

Even a small share of the massive market for weight loss drugs could lead to a significant increase in this company's share price.

By Lee Samaha – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Viking Therapeutics ›

Phase 3 trials are always interesting because of their proximity to approval and ultimate commercialization of drugs, and particularly so when it involves one with a huge total addressable market (TAM) such as obesity. In addition, the drug in question here, Viking Therapeutics' VK2735, is in a class that already includes one blockbuster drug: Eli Lilly's (LLY -0.89%) tirzepatide (Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for obesity with type 2 diabetes), which is approved. All these developments make Viking Therapeutics an attractive stock for investors. Here's why.

The four phase 3 trials comprise two ongoing 78-week trials of VK2735 in subcutaneous form (obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes; results due in 2027) and two recently started 68-week trials in oral form (results more likely in 2028) for the same indications.

The trials are part of management's strategy to potentially offer VK2735 across a range of dosing options, including a dual formulation option in which initial weight loss from subcutaneous dosing could be followed by maintenance dosing with a more convenient oral form.

Investors have high hopes for the glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist, on the back of the success of Eli Lilly's GLP-1/GIP agonist, tirzepatide, and the phase 2 data from the VK2735 trials, which indicate it could achieve a steeper rate of weight loss than tirzepatide. I use cautionary language, as any comparison between two independent trials (let alone a phase 2 and a phase 3) should be accompanied by qualifications.

That said, VK2735 has demonstrated an impressive ability to produce rapid weight loss, as confirmed in a recent small 33-week maintenance study, in which an initial 21-week subcutaneous dose was followed by a subcutaneous maintenance dose over 12 weeks. An exploratory cohort in this trial reported 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks.

The success of this maintenance trial, the first part of a two-part trial, encouraged management to raise a net $547.8 million in a well-received stock offering at $35 and convertible senior notes.

As good as the maintenance trial was, investors should note the second part of the trial (ongoing) is arguably more important, as it involves an initial 21-week subcutaneous dose followed by oral dosing over 12 weeks. The point is that phase 2 of oral VK2735 had questionable tolerability (a 20% discontinuation rate due to adverse events in the treated group), and Viking will have to demonstrate better tolerability in the maintenance trial and the phase 3 oral trials.

I previously outlined the math showing how a $10,000 investment in Viking Therapeutics could grow to $47,800 in 2030; it follows that a $1,000 investment could grow to $4,780.

That's the bullish case scenario, but investors always need to consider the risk that the phase 3 trials will fail to meet their primary endpoints or could deliver efficacy or tolerability data that negatively impacts the commercial appeal of the drug, not least because it's a highly competitive market with Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and others developing rival drugs.

The strongest case for the stock isn't that VK2735 will become a blockbuster drug, but rather that even if it captures only a relatively small share of the market, it will be enough to drive a significant increase in the share price of the $3.5 billion market-cap company.

It could do so provided its phase 3 trials deliver on the weight loss generated in the phase 2 trials and, ideally, some improved tolerability data in the maintenance study, which is due to report results next year. Investors will need to be patient, as the oral trial results (crucial to the dual formulation strategy) aren't likely to be available until 2028. The long-term potential is obvious, and Viking Therapeutics could always be acquired by a larger company seeking a late-stage obesity drug candidate.

#3023. Nvidia Is in Turmoil, But Earnings Are Still Rocketing Higher. Is the Stock a Buy?

Jensen Huang resigned last week following allegations of affairs.

By Adria Cimino – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:05AM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -0.36%) just continued to do something that it's done quarter after quarter in recent years: The tech powerhouse reported earnings that beat analysts' estimates and spoke of soaring demand for its high-powered artificial intelligence (AI) chips. So Nvidia has once again demonstrated that the potential slowdown some investors feared hasn't materialized.

That's fantastic news, but this comes at a time of turmoil for Nvidia. Jensen Huang, who founded the company and led its successes for more than 30 years, stepped down last week. This followed allegations of affairs, including one with a person U.S. intelligence says is a Chinese spy. Nvidia's board named longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while a search for a permanent leader takes place.

Against this backdrop of uncertainty yet tremendous earnings growth, is the stock a buy? Let's find out.

So, first, a quick summary of the Nvidia story over the past few years. The company got in early on AI, designing its chips to suit this area well before others. This gave Nvidia a head start from a technology perspective and the time to build valuable relationships with customers. All of this resulted in earnings soaring once the AI boom gathered momentum -- and Nvidia's stock price followed as investors were eager to bet on this high-potential space.

Jensen Huang took center stage through it all due to his leading role in Nvidia's successes and his significant presence in the AI community. He was viewed as a driving force at the company and within the industry as a whole. So his departure clearly introduced an element of uncertainty.

That said, the technology built under Huang's leadership and the plan set out for the coming years haven't disappeared. Nvidia has a solid foundation, as we can see through the fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings numbers. Revenue soared 103% to $115 billion, beating analysts' estimates of about $109 billion, and net income of more than $65 billion surpassed estimates by about $5 billion.

The period was an important one for Nvidia as it rolled out its most advanced platform yet, Vera Rubin, and the ongoing solid demand for this system bodes well for the quarters to come. In this, its first quarter, Rubin generated almost $20 billion in revenue, for Nvidia's fastest product ramp ever, Kress said during the earnings call.

Nvidia's compute continues to be fully used across customers, a testament to demand and the popularity of the company's chips. And based on data center readiness, the durability of demand, and customer access to capital, Nvidia raised its outlook for growth in the coming full year to 75% from its earlier estimate of 70%.

All of this is reassuring for investors who might have worried about a potential flagging of demand.

Meanwhile, Nvidia shares look dirt cheap, trading at a little over 16x forward earnings estimates.

Still, it's important to remember that Huang's absence, as well as uncertainty about who will be the next leader at Nvidia, could weigh on the stock in the weeks to come. Sentiment, rather than earnings figures and market position, may guide the stock price. Huang also must testify before Congress following allegations of his relationship with a possible spy. Any information gathered could lead to more government scrutiny concerning Nvidia or even greater regulation.

Of course, that is one possibility. Considering the stock already dropped 35% from early last month through Nov. 17, it might be ripe for a rebound. Investors could jump to get in on this opportunity, pushing the stock higher over the next few weeks.

That said, until Nvidia names a permanent CEO and that person lays out a clear roadmap for the future, a certain amount of risk remains. Should you buy? If you're a cautious investor, you might prefer to wait on the sidelines for now, but if you don't mind a bit of risk, the positive points I mentioned above may outweigh the negatives, and now might be a great moment to pick up a few Nvidia shares.

#3022. More Subscribers Won’t Save Your Business: The Trap Of Vanity Growth

Vasudeva Akula, VOZIQ AI cofounder and head of data science. Helps recurring revenue businesses improve customer retention using ML.

For years, customer acquisition has been treated as a straightforward equation: Generate demand, identify prospects most likely to convert, optimize sales and measure success through conversion rates, customer acquisition cost and new customers added. These metrics are still important, but especially for subscription businesses, they leave leaders in the dark about whether the business wins today are contributing to tomorrow’s growth.

Compare these two leads: One is highly likely to convert but switches to a competitor before the acquisition cost is recovered. Another has a lower conversion propensity but stays loyal for years. Businesses that optimize acquisition only for conversion can become more efficient at winning customers without becoming better at building a valuable customer base. This gap between acquisition and long-term value becomes more consequential as subscription businesses try to improve their growth trajectory against headwinds.

In this article, I’ll discuss this disconnect and provide three actionable steps that are proven to bridge the gap between acquisition and long-term value.

A lead-scoring model can become increasingly accurate at predicting purchases without identifying which customers will generate lasting value. When success is measured at the point of sale, a customer who stays for years and one who leaves within months can both count as successful acquisitions. Without customer outcomes informing acquisition decisions, businesses can improve conversion performance without improving the long-term economics of their customer base.​

Retention and service teams see which customers leave early, which remain for years and which generate sustained value. Acquisition teams, meanwhile, work with prospect characteristics and conversion data.

When these datasets are disconnected, customer outcomes don’t consistently influence future targeting. The same weaknesses can persist across successive acquisition cohorts, even when historical evidence could help identify prospects more likely to become valuable customers.

Closing the feedback loop means using retention outcomes to identify the characteristics associated with valuable, long-lasting customer relationships, then applying those insights to future prospect evaluation and lead scoring. As new cohorts mature, their outcomes provide further evidence to refine future acquisition decisions.

Increasing acquisition alone may therefore fail to deliver sustainable growth. Reducing avoidable departures and expanding existing relationships can also contribute to growth. The outcome depends on how effectively the business acquires customers, sustains relationships and increases their value together.​

Conversion rates and customer acquisition cost remain important, but leaders should evaluate them alongside outcomes. How many acquired customers remain after 90 days or one year? How much value do they generate relative to acquisition and service costs? Which acquisition sources produce stronger long-term outcomes?

These measures help distinguish acquisition volume from acquisition quality and reveal whether better conversion translates into stronger customer economics.

Customer outcomes should inform future targeting and lead scoring. If particular customer characteristics or acquisition sources are associated with stronger long-term outcomes, that evidence should influence where the business invests its acquisition resources.

Predictive customer lifetime value (PCLV) can help estimate the economic value a customer is expected to generate over time. Used alongside conversion propensity, acquisition costs and observed outcomes, it helps businesses evaluate both the likelihood of winning a customer and the potential value of that relationship. The goal isn’t to replace conversion metrics with a single prediction but to make acquisition decisions using a more complete view of customer economics and refine them as actual outcomes become available.

Each of the “get,” “keep” and “grow” life cycle stages require different strategies, but their effectiveness depends on how they inform one another. “Keep” helps identify which customers stay and generate lasting value. “Get” uses those insights to find prospects with similar characteristics, while “grow” focuses on expanding the value of established relationships.

When these levers share a common view of customer value, acquisition is informed by actual customer outcomes, and growth decisions become more closely connected to long-term economics.​

Acquiring more customers alone won’t improve the quality of growth. Long-term growth and a competitive edge will come from learning from each customer relationship and using that knowledge to acquire the right customers. And sustainable growth depends on whether those customers create lasting value and whether the business uses what it learns to make better decisions.

#3021. Intel vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Intel is betting big on external foundry customers, while Taiwan Semiconductor's margins sit above 50%. Which chipmaker deserves your capital heading into the next cycle?

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:08AM EST

The chip industry is undergoing a massive shift as artificial intelligence and local manufacturing take center stage. Choosing between Intel (INTC -0.40%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +0.76%) requires weighing a turnaround story against a market leader.

Intel focuses on designing its own processors while opening its factories to external customers. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing serves as a pure-play foundry, producing high-end chips for nearly every major player among semiconductor stocks. Both companies are central to the global tech supply chain but offer very different risk and reward profiles.

Intel designs and manufactures a wide range of processors, accelerators, and software solutions for the modern computing world. Under its latest strategy, the company is combining its internal chip design with a massive expansion of its foundry services to manufacture chips for other businesses. Its customer base is diverse, including distributors, original equipment manufacturers, and cloud service providers across sectors like healthcare, finance, and telecommunications.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached approximately $59.9 billion, representing revenue growth of nearly 12.1% compared to the previous period. However, the company faced significant headwinds, reporting a net loss of roughly $12 billion during this time frame. This result highlights the high costs associated with its ongoing efforts to regain a leading position in the semiconductor market.

As of Intel's December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.4, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio is approximately 2, indicating the ability to cover short-term financial obligations with assets that can be converted to cash within a year. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was approximately negative $4.9 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 25.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as a pure-play foundry, focusing exclusively on manufacturing semiconductors designed by its customers. It serves the most demanding segments of the market, including smartphones and high-performance artificial intelligence applications, from its base in Taiwan and facilities worldwide. By acting as a manufacturer for others, the company avoids competing directly with its clients while maintaining a critical role in the global tech supply chain.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $150.2 billion, an increase of approximately 36.1%. This growth translated into net income of close to $76.8 billion, resulting in a robust net margin of roughly 51.1%. These figures demonstrate the strong demand for the advanced manufacturing nodes that the company provides to its diverse customer base.

As of TSM's December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was roughly 2.5, reflecting a healthy cushion for meeting short-term liabilities. The company maintains a conservative debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.2, showing that its total debt is low relative to its equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $30.1 billion, providing substantial capital to reinvest in the next generation of chip technology.

Intel faces intense competition from companies like NVIDIA (NVDA -0.36%) and AMD (AMD +2.09%), as well as hyperscalers who are increasingly designing their own custom silicon. The company is also navigating legal challenges, including shareholder lawsuits filed in November 2026 alleging concealment of manufacturing and inventory issues. High capital intensity and the operational risks of its turnaround strategy remain significant hurdles as it builds out new leading-edge factories while relying on sole-source suppliers like ASML (ASML +0.48%) for critical tools.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is exposed to risks associated with the high concentration of its manufacturing facilities in a single geographic region. This concentration creates sensitivity to geopolitical tensions and potential supply chain disruptions that could impact its global operations. Additionally, the company must continually invest billions in new technology nodes to stay ahead of rivals, which entails significant capital risk if demand for high-end chips from major customers like Apple (AAPL +0.85%) or NVIDIA fluctuates.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing looks cheaper on a forward P/E basis, while Intel has a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

A large part of the reason Intel reported that $12 billion loss is because it's in the midst of a turnaround. It's pivoting toward providing chip manufacturing services for third parties. In order to do so, the chipmaker is having to shell out a lot of money to build fabrication plants. Intel even suspended its dividend a few years ago in pursuit of this new strategy. That spending will likely continue, as turning around a ship of Intel's size is neither a fast nor an easy endeavor.

Now, let's see how each stock has performed over the past 10 years:

Intel's stock is miles behind Taiwan Semiconductor's, and worse yet, it hasn't even kept pace with the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%), trailing it by over 180 percentage points.

Taiwan Semiconductor dominates the foundry market and maintains a strong net margin despite operating in a capital-intensive business. It also pays a modest dividend.

I think there are too many unknowns tied to Intel's strategic transformation. Taiwan Semiconductor looks like a better buy for 2027 and beyond.

Hyatt is updating its rewards program in 2027, and it means you'll earn Milestone Rewards even sooner than before.

Editor/Content Strategist & Smart Travel Podcast Host

It’s going to be easier to rack up extra benefits if you’re a frequent Hyatt customer in 2027. World of Hyatt announced new Milestone Rewards, the ability to stack awards (such as Free Night Certificates and Suite Upgrade Awards) on a single stay and a simpler 365-day expiration on all awards.

The news expands on the fresh details revealed Nov. 17, 2026, around World of Hyatt’s partnership with Delta SkyMiles, which was first announced in September.

The additions to the Milestone Rewards are designed to give members more choice and personalization, according to Laurie Blair, senior vice president of global marketing and loyalty at Hyatt.

"We’re shaping the future of World of Hyatt around what our members value most. After a year of listening, one thing is clear: members want more distinctive benefits, more freedom to use their awards and the opportunity to choose awards that matter most to them,” Blair said in an email to NerdWallet.

But top-tier Globalist members will soon have to choose between perks that they previously received automatically. Most notably, Globalists will no longer receive free parking on award nights in 2027. Instead, they can choose a Free Parking Award as a Milestone Reward that they can apply to award or paid stays.

The Delta Air Lines and Hyatt partnership will also mainly benefit frequent flyers and hotel guests. With the exception of the limited-time intro promotion, only Delta or Hyatt members with elite status will earn points in both programs. Hyatt elites will have to purchase premium tickets on Delta — not economy — to earn Hyatt points on the flight.

Starting Jan. 1, 2027, World of Hyatt will extend Milestone Rewards to guests who have not yet qualified for the first level of elite status. Southwest Airlines did the same in its recent revamp to give loyal customers a thank you before they’ve reached any level of elite status.

World of Hyatt members will reach the first Milestone Reward at just 10 nights or 20,000 Base Points. Previously, it was 20 nights or 35,000 Base Points.

The reward choices at the first milestone are:

A tier-qualifying night credit, which gets you closer to the next level of elite status.

A $25 FIND Experience credit (Hyatt’s platform for local experiences such as cooking classes).

A $30 spa credit good at Hyatt Inclusive Collection resorts.

The latter two will likely still require you to pay money out of pocket to use them, as the credit will only cover a portion of your bill. For example, the cheapest spa treatment at Secrets Playa Mujeres Golf & Spa Resort in Cancun, Mexico, will still run you $109 (or $79 after the credit).

The Milestone Rewards start to get good at the higher tiers. Starting at 20 nights, you can select from the existing Milestone Rewards, as well as new items. Some of the new options include:

Free parking on award nights is going away as a Globalist tier benefit. In 2027, a Free Parking Award will be an option that Globalists can select at the 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights The parking award can be used on either a qualifying award or paid stay for up to seven nights.

Hyatt said in a call with NerdWallet that roughly 70% of Globalists weren’t using the free parking benefit at all.

Globalists who have earned status in 2026 for 2027 will be grandfathered into the automatic free parking on award stays through their tier expiration date in February 2028.

To use these new awards, the Hyatt booking process is also getting an upgrade. Previously, awards like Suite Upgrade Awards and Free Night Awards couldn’t be redeemed on the same stay. Starting in 2027, members can combine eligible awards on a single reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and Free Parking Awards.

The new booking system will also make it easier to pay for some nights of a single reservation with awards, points, cash or a combination of points and cash.

Every award earned going forward will also carry a 365-day expiration from the date it’s issued, replacing the patchwork of different validity windows. Previously, Suite Upgrade and Guest of Honor Awards expired at “rest of year plus 14 days,” which was just a tad confusing. Meanwhile, Free Night Awards earned through Milestone Rewards were valid for 180 days from the date of issuance, which was not a lot of time to plan a trip.

The Milestone Rewards kick in next year, but the other big change around the Delta partnership is available now.

Hyatt elite members can earn World of Hyatt Bonus Points on eligible Delta flights (Delta Comfort, Premium Select, First Class and Delta One). Basic Economy or standard Main Cabin fares will earn nothing from this partnership at all.

Discoverist members earn 1 Bonus Point per $2 spent.

Explorist, Globalist and Lifetime Globalist members earn 1 Bonus Point per $1 spent.

Delta Medallion members (Silver through Diamond) can earn 1 Delta mile per $1 spent at participating Hyatt properties, on top of their regular Hyatt points.

Even if you don’t have elite status with either program, it’s still worth linking accounts to take advantage of the upcoming bonus point promotions:

Those who link their accounts and complete a qualifying Hyatt stay from Nov. 17 to Dec. 31, 2026, will earn one bonus Tier-Qualifying Night Credit.

A second bonus point offer runs Jan. 4 through Feb. 15, 2027, for members who take their first Delta flight or Hyatt stay after linking their accounts. Members will earn 1,000 Delta SkyMiles after the Hyatt stay or 1,000 Hyatt points after their first flight in a premium cabin on Delta.

Hyatt and Delta are also holding a sweepstakes through Nov. 23 — no points or miles required to enter — for a free three-night trip for two at Alila Mayakoba in Riviera Maya, Mexico, plus two $1,000 Delta gift cards. Linking your accounts before entering gets you a bonus entry.

If you are interested in dual accrual in 2027, there are some routes to elite status through travel credit cards. Hyatt’s entry-level elite tier comes as a benefit of holding the World of Hyatt Credit Card, but Discoverists earn Hyatt points at half the rate of Explorist and Globalist elites on premium Delta fares.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased today, but borrowing costs are still expensive for many homebuyers.

Mortgage rates are lower today, but recent averages above 7% are still eating into buyers’ budgets.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 21 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.63% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3018. Prediction: This Cryptocurrency Will Outperform Bitcoin in 2027

Solana has a track record of significantly outperforming Bitcoin during bull market cycles.

By Dominic Basulto – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:10AM EST

Given that Bitcoin (BTC -1.68%) typically leads the crypto market higher or lower, it's no surprise that it gets the most attention from crypto investors. Bitcoin is a reliable barometer of how the crypto market is doing at any point in time.

But here's the thing: Altcoins typically have higher highs than Bitcoin, as well as lower lows. For that reason, they tend to outperform Bitcoin significantly during crypto bull market cycles.

If you're expecting the crypto market to rally next year, it will be altcoins dazzling investors with their performance. The one altcoin that I'm focused on right now is Solana (SOL +0.86%), and here's why.

Ever since its launch back in 2020, Solana has been touted as a potential Ethereum (ETH -1.82%) killer, due to its faster speeds, lower costs, and superior scalability. In 2023, Cathie Wood of Ark Invest specifically pointed to Solana as a potential disruptive force in the crypto market. After years of waiting, 2027 could be the year that Solana finally puts it all together.

For one, Solana is rapidly outgrowing its reputation as simply a place to buy, sell, and speculate in meme coins. It's moving into institutional-grade finance, and is picking up some big-name backers along the way. That's raising Solana's profile in the world of decentralized finance (DeFi).

Take tokenized equities, for example. Solana recently partnered with the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) to bring tokenized equities to the Solana blockchain. Heading into 2027, Solana is already one of the top blockchain networks for trading tokenized equities, or crypto that represents the ownership of stocks or other assets.

The same story is being repeated in other key niches of the blockchain and crypto world. That includes stablecoins, where Solana is now rapidly challenging the market-leading role of Ethereum.

When big-name corporations want to launch new stablecoins, they now turn to Solana. Case in point: Solana partnered with Western Union (WU -0.73%) in May on a new stablecoin launch.

Admittedly, the data set on market performance is limited, given that Solana has only been trading since 2020. But the numbers certainly hint at the type of outperformance Solana is capable of delivering over short periods of time (12 months or less).

In 2021, for example, Solana skyrocketed by 11,166% while Bitcoin cruised to a gain of 60%. In 2023, Solana soared by 920%, while Bitcoin rose by 155%.

On the flip side, Solana definitely has lower lows than Bitcoin. In 2022, for example, Solana collapsed by 94%, while Bitcoin lost 64% of its value. That helps to explain why Solana is down 45% this year, while Bitcoin is only down 28%.

If you're counting on a crypto rebound in 2027, then it will be altcoins leading the way, not Bitcoin. And the one altcoin that I'm expecting to be at the front of the pack is Solana.

#3015. History Says AGNC's Dividend Can Survive a Stock Market Crash -- but Not Always at Full Size

AGNC has a long history of paying dividends, but that history is actually a fairly volatile one.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than AGNC Investment Corp. ›

AGNC Investment (AGNC +0.10%) is a well-respected mortgage real estate investment trust (REIT). That, however, does not mean it is a good option for every investor. That's important to keep in mind for dividend investors, noting the stock's massive 17% dividend yield. History makes it very clear that the dividend can be volatile, as highlighted by a dividend cut during the 2020 bear market. But there's more to this story than that one dividend cut. Here's what you need to know.

AGNC Investment is a REIT, a special corporate structure designed to pass income on to shareholders. As long as a REIT distributes at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders, it avoids corporate-level taxation. Shareholders have to treat REIT dividends like regular income. (If you hold a REIT in a Roth IRA, however, you can avoid paying taxes on the dividends.) Basically, AGNC will likely always pay a substantive dividend because its corporate structure is designed to do just that.

That said, AGNC isn't a property-owning REIT, which is a fairly easy-to-understand business model. It is a mortgage REIT, which means it buys mortgages that have been pooled into bond-like securities. The company's value is essentially the value of its mortgage security portfolio. It earns the difference between its cost of capital and the interest its portfolio generates. There are two important facts here.

First, the value of its mortgage securities will change as interest rates rise and fall. The relationship is inverse: rising rates lead to a decline in value, and vice versa. This is important right now because rates are rising and AGNC's portfolio value is declining. Meanwhile, rising rates increase the company's cost of capital and can squeeze its profits. That said, falling interest rates aren't great either. While costs decline and the value of existing mortgage securities rises in that situation, new mortgage securities come with lower yields. There are a lot of moving parts, which makes AGNC and other mREITs most appropriate for more active investors.

This discussion hasn't even looked at what can happen during a bear market. Dislocations like that can cause unexpected outcomes. For example, during the 2020 bear market that accompanied the coronavirus pandemic, interest rates fell, the value of AGNC's portfolio declined, and it cut its dividend.

At the time, AGNC tied the cut directly to the decline in the value of its mortgage security portfolio. It also noted that the cut would allow it to invest for the future. However, the dividend has remained static since that cut. Meanwhile, the cash the mREIT generated in the third quarter of 2026 to pay its dividend was $0.37 per share compared to a dividend of $0.36 per share. That's not a lot of wiggle room. And it is facing the impact of rising rates on its portfolio, with its value falling nearly 17% in the quarter. To make matters worse, Wall Street is broadly concerned about the risk of another bear market. It isn't unreasonable to be worried about a possible dividend cut.

As the chart above highlights, however, the dividend has a much longer history of volatility. Note, too, that the stock price has tended to follow the dividend higher and lower. Given AGNC's corporate structure, you are likely to continue collecting dividends through both good and bad markets. But its history makes it pretty clear that the dividend simply can't be counted on if you hope to use it to pay your living expenses in retirement.

Conservative dividend investors generally look for companies that pay consistent dividends, with a preference for dividends that grow steadily over time. That's just not what AGNC has to offer. That doesn't mean it is a bad investment. It simply isn't a good fit for most income-focused investors given its history of dividend volatility. In fact, AGNC Investment makes the most sense if you reinvest dividends and focus on total return. Indeed, for many investors, this mREIT is a diversification tool rather than an income tool.

#3013. Data Residency Was The Easy Part

Nick Burling, Chief Product Officer at Nasuni.

​A company can keep every sensitive file within the required geographic boundaries and still lose control over where its information goes. An AI application processing that information through a service operating in another jurisdiction may be enough to introduce sovereignty risks.

Enterprise data sovereignty, or an organization’s control over how its data is used and which laws govern it, has traditionally been approached through data residency policies and regional infrastructure. But those safeguards can only go so far when applications process that information across national borders, potentially subjecting it to different legal requirements.

When an AI workload processes enterprise information, that data may pass through services operating beyond the jurisdiction where the original file resides. The source data can remain within its required geographic boundaries while information derived from it is processed elsewhere.

If an enterprise wants to scale AI without compromising sovereignty, it must be able to deploy workloads wherever they deliver the most value while maintaining demonstrable control over the information those workloads use.

The difficulty is that even routine AI use cases can introduce jurisdictional exposure. A financial services organization might store customer records in Europe to meet data residency requirements, then use an AI assistant to analyze them. While the original files remain in Europe, the assistant could send information to a model operating in another jurisdiction, raising sovereignty concerns even though the source data remains exactly where it belongs.

These secondary data artifacts deserve greater scrutiny because they can contain sensitive information even when they appear removed from the original documents. They may also persist in logs long after an AI interaction ends, creating additional exposure that organizations need to account for.

Under the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, transfers of personal data outside the European Economic Area are subject to specific conditions and safeguards. Meanwhile, the U.S. CLOUD Act allows authorities, through qualifying legal processes, to require providers subject to U.S. jurisdiction to produce data within their custody or control, regardless of its storage location.

These laws confirm why the location of an AI provider’s infrastructure tells only part of the story. The provider’s legal jurisdiction also determines which authorities may compel access to the information it handles.

Keeping every AI workload within the same jurisdiction as its source data may seem like the safest approach. For a hospital processing sensitive patient information, local execution may be necessary. A manufacturer analyzing internal production data, however, could have greater flexibility in using specialized models from external providers.

Applying identical restrictions across these use cases can unnecessarily limit AI adoption. Organizations should be able to choose where each workload runs based on its regulatory requirements while retaining the flexibility to use specialized AI capabilities where appropriate. That may mean keeping sensitive workloads within private infrastructure and allowing others to use external services under established safeguards.

Hybrid architectures provide that flexibility, provided governance extends across the environments involved. This becomes especially important as organizations move from AI assistants toward autonomous agents.

Autonomous AI agents make these decisions more complex. Unlike applications that respond to individual user requests, agents can independently access information and interact with services across different environments. Each interaction can introduce another jurisdiction into the workflow, making it harder for organizations to maintain consistent control over sensitive data.

The practical priority is ensuring that sovereignty policies follow information throughout an AI workflow. That starts with understanding the information an application can access and the restrictions attached to it. A document containing regulated personal information may require different processing controls from an internal knowledge article. Those distinctions need to inform which services can access the material and where processing can occur.

Those policies must extend to the information AI generates, which can carry the same sensitivity as the original documents. Organizations need to control how that information is retained and who can access it, with visibility into the providers handling it. Sensitive portions of a workflow can then remain within approved infrastructure while other functions run elsewhere.

Finally, organizations need evidence that these controls are working. An audit trail that records who accessed a source file provides limited visibility into what happened afterward. AI governance increasingly requires tracing subsequent processing steps, including which service handled the information and, where relevant, where outputs were retained.

This level of accountability can also support adoption. When enterprises can demonstrate that an AI workload operates within established boundaries, they have a stronger basis for approving it for production use.

A company may have complete records of where its sensitive files are stored and still struggle to explain what happened to that information once AI accessed it. Without that visibility, sovereignty becomes difficult to enforce and even harder to prove.

You can’t prove sovereignty for what you can’t trace. Organizations that can provide that evidence will have greater freedom to adopt AI without compromising control.

#3010. Corning vs. Vertiv: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Corning and Vertiv both ride the AI data center boom, but one carries far heavier customer concentration risk while the other trades at a lower forward multiple.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:20AM EST

As artificial intelligence drives a massive expansion in data center capacity, investors are weighing the long term potential of Corning Inc. and Vertiv Holdings Inc. (VRT +1.46%). Both companies are essential to modern digital infrastructure, but they serve different parts of the technology stack. Choosing between them involves deciding which stock is a better buy for the next several years.

Corning provides the physical glass and fiber optic cables that move data, while Vertiv supplies the power and cooling systems that keep servers running. Both companies benefit from the same high-level trends, yet their financial profiles and risk factors vary significantly. This comparison evaluates their current performance and valuation to help you determine which fits your investment strategy.

Corning operates in the materials science space, but it is often classified alongside industrial stocks because of its manufacturing breadth. The company serves a concentrated customer base, with Apple Inc. (AAPL +1.01%) being a primary partner for durable cover glass used in mobile devices. Its optical communications segment is currently seeing high demand as telecommunications carriers and hyperscale data center operators upgrade their networks for artificial intelligence. Because a small number of customers account for a high percentage of sales, this customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $17.7 billion, representing revenue growth of approximately 18.8%. Net income for this period was around $2.1 billion, a significant increase compared to the prior year. This growth is largely supported by the company's ability to innovate in optical physics, providing specialized fiber solutions that allow data centers to pack more connections into smaller spaces.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, its current ratio stands at approximately 1.6x. The current ratio measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with its current assets, with a figure above 1.0 generally suggesting healthy liquidity. The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is nearly 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $1.4 billion, providing capital for research and development.

Vertiv focuses on critical digital infrastructure, specifically power management and thermal cooling solutions. Its major customers include hyperscale and cloud providers such as Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -0.55%) and Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +1.71%), as well as enterprise clients like Walmart Inc. (WMT -0.98%). As artificial intelligence chips generate more heat, the demand for Vertiv's liquid cooling systems has accelerated. The company also maintains strategic partnerships to ensure its own supply of semiconductors for power management units.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached around $13.1 billion, showing robust revenue growth of about 35.3%. Net income during this time was approximately $2.1 billion, reflecting a net margin of roughly 16%. This significant growth in sales and profitability highlights the intense demand for physical infrastructure as new data centers are built globally to support cloud computing.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.8x. Vertiv's current ratio is nearly 1.5x, indicating a solid buffer between its liquid assets and short-term liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $1.9 billion. This strong cash generation allows the company to reinvest in manufacturing capacity to keep up with its growing order backlog.

Corning faces risks related to its high customer concentration, as losing a major electronics or telecom partner could significantly impact sales. The company is also vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and inflationary pricing for specialized raw materials. Because much of its manufacturing occurs in the Asia Pacific region, it is exposed to geopolitical tensions and potential trade restrictions. Protecting its intellectual property is also a constant challenge, as any loss of proprietary glass technology could erode its competitive advantage.

Vertiv is susceptible to shifts in data center spending, as any slowdown in cloud investment by large-scale providers could lead to decreased demand. The company competes with large industrial players like Eaton Corp. (ETN -0.60%) and Schneider Electric (SBGSF -1.30%), which can lead to pricing pressure. Vertiv also carries significant indebtedness, and its credit agreements contain restrictive covenants that could limit its operating flexibility. Managing operational costs and supply chain logistics remains critical, particularly when passing on inflationary costs to large, powerful customers.

Vertiv currently trades at a lower multiple of future earnings estimates, while Corning appears more attractive when viewed in terms of market value relative to total sales.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Vertiv has been a specialist in computer cooling systems since World War Two, and it also offers complementary products for mission-critical technological infrastructure, such as uninterruptible power supplies. The AI-driven data center boom presents a long-term opportunity for Vertiv, especially for its liquid cooling systems. Liquid cooling is better for quickly removing heat from high-powered chipsets. Vertiv believes one-third of the total addressable market for data center cooling will eventually use liquid solutions (technically, some air-cooling and heat-dissipation systems will always be needed to work in tandem with liquid systems).

For 2026, Vertiv revenue should rise 44% to $14.7 billion, with net income shooting up about 90% to $2.5 billion as AI data center demand powers the business. Those figures are much stronger than anticipated just a few months ago. For 2027, analyst consensus calls for Vertiv revenue to jump about a third, with net income up more than 40% to $4.6 billion.

Recently struck deals with Meta Platforms (META -0.17%), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA -0.36%), and Amazon's AWS division have led Corning management to believe it can execute on its so-called Springboard program to jump annual sales to $20 billion this year, $30 billion in 2028, and $40 billion in 2030. Each of the deals is in Corning's core area of expertise: fiber optics and connectivity. These are for AI data centers and new manufacturing plants being planned in the U.S. Much of the new capacity Corning needs to fulfill these deals will come from its own U.S. expansion, reducing its tariff and general geopolitical risk. In its fiscal 2026 third quarter, sales grew 19%, and net income rose about 60% to $660 million. Wall Street consensus sees net income rising 53% to $2.44 billion.

One of the keys to Corning's growth is sharing its development plans with major customers well in advance, allowing it and its partners to tweak plans and development as needed to better meet future needs. The addition of new AI customers also helps reduce its risk of overreliance on Apple, which makes the iPhone glass, among other products.

So which is the better buy for 2027? Corning's continual improvement of its fiber-optic and connectivity products has led to impressive growth, with much more on the way. Vertiv, too, is executing well on its position, meeting an essential data center construction need. Still, while Corning comes at a premium, its plans to more than double sales by decade's end seem to offer great promise for long-term investors.

#3008. ​Before You Launch Anything, Ask For The Truth

Russ Reeder is CEO of KeyDelta. Nine PE-backed CEO and COO seats; 50+ acquisitions. We fix the operating model before AI goes in.

When I was a kid, my grandfather gave me one piece of advice about books: read autobiographies. If they tell the truth, you’ll learn something.

That advice has stayed with me through 30 years of running technology companies. A story, a strategy or a product plan is only useful if it’s honest about what doesn’t work. And the person least able to see what doesn’t work is usually the one who built it.

I’m living that right now. This month I finished the manuscript for a book on leadership. Before it goes into production, I’m sending it to a small group of trusted readers: close friends, mentors and leaders I respect. After this many drafts, I know what I meant. I need to know what a reader gets.

The same step belongs before every launch a leader makes: a new strategy, a product, a reorganization or an AI pilot. Many leaders skip it. Or worse, they ask for approval and think they asked for the truth.

When a CEO presents a plan, the room tends to nod. That isn’t always agreement. Often it’s the safest thing to do in front of the person who controls budgets and careers.

Nokia shows how expensive that can get. INSEAD’s Quy Huy and Aalto University’s Timo Vuori interviewed 76 managers, engineers and outside experts and found that fear shaped how information moved inside the company. Some middle managers stayed silent or passed up filtered, optimistic information, while top managers pushed for faster delivery on an incomplete picture. Everyone shared the ambition. The facts got softer at every level.

A head nod is not a commitment. If the only feedback you’ve collected came from people who report to you in a meeting you ran, you’ve collected approval.​

I learned this the hard way. At a managed services company I led, our AI engineers built a system that automatically filled in support tickets. Months later, the support reps still weren’t using it. In a weekly standup, the engineers asked why.

The head of customer support answered: “I don’t know why they’re not using it. I haven’t asked them.”

The call went silent. We built the tool around how managers described the work, not how reps did it or how the work should be done. Once we asked, we had to start almost from scratch. We rebuilt the second version around the outcome the customer needed, and it could resolve certain issues without anyone touching the ticket.

The truth was available the whole time, but nobody went to get it. Your trusted readers should include the people who will use, deliver or be measured on what you’re launching. Their view is the one a leadership meeting rarely hears.​

“What do you think?” invites politeness. Specific questions invite the truth. Here are the three I’m asking my readers. I believe they also work for almost any launch:

1. Where did you stop believing it? This may be where a claim felt too clean, a number too convenient or a timeline too optimistic.

2. Where did you see your own work in it? That tells you which parts are landing and which are abstract.

3. Where did you lose interest? Every plan has a section people skim. Find it before your customers or your board do.​

​Then go first. Tell them what you’re worried about. In my experience, people are far more willing to point out a problem after the leader has named one.

Feedback that changes nothing teaches people to stop giving it. Before you ask, settle three things:

1. Who owns the changes. This should be one name, rather than “the team.”

2. When the review closes. Aim for a specific date so the feedback leads to a decision instead of an open-ended debate.

3. What would change the plan. Write down what you would need to hear to delay, redesign or stop. If nothing could change it, then don’t ask. You’re not asking for feedback. You’re asking for applause.

When you get answers you don’t like, thank the person who gave them. The first honest critic sets the price for the next one. If candor costs them something, it will be the last honest answer you get.​

This step comes before production for a reason. A sentence is easy to change in a manuscript and expensive to change in print. A process is easy to fix on a whiteboard and expensive to fix after it’s built into software. A strategy is easy to adjust before you’ve funded it and expensive to unwind once teams are executing it.

The truth costs the least before you launch. After that, your customers will tell you anyway, and they won’t be as kind. Find the people who will tell you where they stopped believing you, and ask them while you can still use what they say.​​​

#3007. Despite the loss, Rockets Alperen Sengun continues his career-best shooting

When the Houston Rockets traded for Alperen Sengun in the 2021 NBA draft, they knew they were getting one of the best international players. An MVP of the Basketball Super League at 19, Sengun was already dominating overseas professional leagues.

Over the years, Sengun has gone from an up-and-coming young star to one of the best players in the NBA and a two-time All-Star. Throughout his NBA career, Sengun has also been one of the best post players in the NBA. He has shown he can score in the paint against the NBA's best defenders. Even with his scoring ability in the post, his offensive game has at times been limited by struggles not only in the mid-range but also from the 3-point range.

NBA teams are smart; they have multiple scouts and entire departments dedicated to knowing every strength and weakness of their opponents. Opposing teams quickly realized that if Sengun gets to his spot in the paint, it's usually too late to stop him. So teams started sagging off Sengun on pick-and-rolls, and whenever he got the ball away from the basket, they forced him to take a shot from outside.

That defensive strategy made life a lot harder for Sengun at times, as it became every opposing team's strategy when facing the Rockets. Sengun shot just 24.8% from the 3-point range in his first season, on 1.6 attempts. The next season, Sengun shot a higher percentage at .333 but at half the volume of the first season, as he sometimes hesitated on wide-open 3-pointers, choosing to pass on them and drive into a crowded paint.

Sengun's 3-point shooting dropped over the next two seasons from .333 to a career-worst .233 in his fourth season. Sengun has often said that is the one part of his offense that needs to improve if he wants to unlock his entire game. Sengun worked tirelessly on his 3-point shooting every summer, every practice, and before every game. Sengun has talked for years about his confidence in shooting 3-pointers, as he told SB Nation three years ago during training camp.

The hard work is starting to pay off in his sixth season, as Sengun is off to the best 3-point shooting start of his career.

HOUSTON, TEXAS – APRIL 24: Alperen Sengun #28 of the Houston Rockets shoots a three pointer during the first quarter of the game against the Los Angeles Lakers at Toyota Center on April 24, 2026 in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Sengun, now in his sixth season, is starting to translate all the hard work he puts into his 3-point shot into the game. Not only has Sengun improved his outside shooting, but he leads the Rockets in 3-point shooting at 48.1 percent. It is on only 2.1 attempts per game, but that is also a career-high for Sengun. A high volume of shots from downtown has never been Sengun's goal; it is more about him being a threat from long range, which opens up the court for the Rockets' center. It's not just that he is making 3-pointers; it's that he isn't hesitating from deep when teams play him for the drive.

Sengun has made a 3-pointer in a career-high six straight games and in eight of his last ten games. For Sengun, if he keeps improving from deep, teams will have to respect him from that range, which gives him more space; with his ability to handle the ball and his court vision, it could take his offensive game to an entirely different level.

With a reliable 3-point game and improved play on the defensive end, Sengun could be in serious contention for MVP votes at the end of the season. Pretty good for a player 16 other teams passed on in 2021.

#3006. Why S&P 500 ETF Investors Don't Have to Worry (Much) About Nvidia Stock Plunging

CEO scandals drive home the value of diversification.

One of the biggest stories on Wall Street this week is the resignation of Jensen Huang, former CEO of Nvidia (NVDA -0.36%), caused by a shocking scandal involving extramarital affairs and a romantic relationship with a possible Chinese spy. Many investors are worried that Huang's departure could lead to weaker performance for his company, negative spillover effects for the entire semiconductor industry, or even a broader downturn in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

It's important to keep in mind that the stock market is much bigger than one company and one CEO. And Jensen Huang's departure is just one factor affecting Nvidia's stock price, which was already in significant decline before the scandal broke. As of Nov. 13, Nvidia shares have dropped by about 7% over the past week, by 13.5% in 2026, and by nearly 33% since reaching a record high on Oct. 6. Since Nov. 13, the stock has been turbulent, with a slight bounce in pre-market trading on Nov. 18 following its latest earnings release.

But if you own S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.02%) exchange-traded funds (ETFs), there's no reason to panic about Nvidia's scandal and a possible further sell-off in the stock. Let's look at a few reasons why.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

If you own individual shares of Nvidia, and the stock makes up a significant percentage of your portfolio, you might want to think carefully about whether you're still bullish on the company's future without Jensen Huang. Even though Huang resigned, the Nvidia scandal might not be over yet. There are significant risks and uncertainties facing Nvidia, regardless of who the CEO is.

As of this writing, Huang and Nvidia have not been accused of criminal wrongdoing. But Huang and the company are likely to face further investigations. And more news about the scandal keeps coming out. Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a Chinese businesswoman who was also an alleged Chinese spy. And according to reporting from The Information, this alleged spy might have used her relationship with Huang to gain access to billions of dollars' worth of cutting-edge Nvidia semiconductors, which she then helped provide to companies in China.

But the U.S. government doesn't want Nvidia's best chips going to China, for national security reasons. Nvidia's chips have been subject to targeted export controls since 2022. Again, this is hypothetical -- no one has accused Jensen Huang or other Nvidia employees of violating export controls or other U.S. laws. The company has said that it has no reason to believe that Nvidia corporate secrets or U.S. national security were compromised and has denied any knowledge of Nvidia chips being smuggled into China.

But what happens if more bad news comes out, or an investigation finds that the company violated export control laws or SEC regulations? What if the U.S. tightens its export controls on advanced semiconductors, making it harder for Nvidia to sell its chips worldwide? That could be more bad news for Nvidia stock going forward.

This is a lot of complexity and uncertainty, and it might be more than Nvidia shareholders want to accept. Even after a solid earnings report, the stock could have further to fall.

Nvidia is one of the largest stocks in the S&P 500. As of Sept. 30, it was the largest holding in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.08%), making up about 8.4% of the fund's assets. As of Nov. 12, after its recent sell-off, Nvidia has fallen to second place in the S&P 500 index, making up about 6.15% of the index.

What if Nvidia stock falls further from here? Let's say the stock goes into another 10% decline by the end of 2026. That's bad news for individual shareholders. But if you own Nvidia through an S&P 500 ETF, that one stock makes up only about 6.15% of the fund's portfolio. If that one stock drops by 10%, the fund's value would only drop by about 0.62%.

In this example, even if Nvidia declines by another 20% from its Nov. 12 share price, an S&P 500 ETF's Nvidia holdings would only decline by about 1.24%. And that doesn't mean the ETF would automatically go down along with Nvidia. Nvidia is only one stock; the other 499 companies in the S&P 500 index might go up. Just because one stock goes down doesn't mean all the stocks or sectors will follow.

Other semiconductor stocks or AI stocks might go up even if Nvidia goes down. Investors might shift money into other companies that they believe will be more competitive in the future if Nvidia struggles to recover. The S&P 500 is constantly sorting and rebalancing itself as some companies gain or lose market cap.

The S&P 500 is not guaranteed to go up or be a "safe" investment. The entire stock market can still go down by 10%, 20%, or more in any given year. But the S&P 500 tends to be steadier than any individual stock, and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has delivered annualized returns of about 12% over the past five years.

The Nvidia scandal shows the value of diversification. It's easy to be confident about individual stocks when the economy is booming, and everything is going well. But when crisis hits, prominent CEOs resign in disgrace, and companies are suddenly thrust into uncertainty and face allegations of serious misconduct, that's when putting too many eggs in one stock's basket can hurt investors.

#3004. The Most Important Number In Nvidia's Earnings Report Was 75%

Nvidia’s next-year forecast says more about its post-Huang confidence than any quarterly beat.

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:28AM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -0.36%) had plenty to prove when it reported its fiscal third-quarter earnings after the market closed Nov. 17. It was the company's first earnings report since Jensen Huang's sudden departure. Investors wanted to know whether the artificial intelligence chipmaker could maintain its momentum without its longtime CEO.

The numbers were outstanding. But I think the most important figure in Nvidia's earnings report wasn't its revenue, earnings, or even its guidance for the current quarter.

That's how much Nvidia now expects its revenue to grow in fiscal 2028, up from its previous forecast of 70%. And that increase tells us something important about the company's confidence in its ability to keep delivering AI processors to customers – even without Huang running the show.

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (ending Oct. 25, 2026), Nvidia reported revenue of $115.84 billion, up 103% from a year ago, and topping analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion. Its data center business generated $107.6 billion in revenue, up 110% year over year, as demand for AI computing infrastructure continued to grow.

"Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said. "Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater."

Nvidia also projected fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $130 billion, ahead of the $125.1 billion consensus estimate compiled by LSEG. While that number stands out, it's also important to know that Nvidia's fiscal fourth quarter includes an additional week of revenue. Melius Research estimates that accounts for approximately $9 billion to $10 billion of the roughly $14 billion sequential increase in Nvidia's guidance.

That's why I'm paying more attention to what Nvidia expects to happen next year.

The increase in Nvidia's fiscal 2028 growth forecast is what really got my attention. In August, Nvidia projected 70% revenue growth for its 2028 fiscal year, and acknowledged that its ability to supply enough processors would limit how quickly it could expand.

Now the company is bumping that projection up to 75% growth.

During the company's earnings call with analysts, Kress said that Nvidia evaluated both customer demand and the additional supply it expects to make available. The company believes it can deliver that growth despite ongoing supply constraints and new U.S. export restrictions.

Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress. Image source: Nvidia.

Nvidia's ability to grow depends on more than designing powerful chips. It needs manufacturing capacity, advanced memory, packaging, networking components, and customers with enough data center capacity to put its systems to work.

And just as importantly, Nvidia needs to keep those relationships going even in the post-Huang era. Huang was forced to resign Nov. 12 after the board began investigating allegations that he had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Other extramarital relationships with Nvidia employees also came to light.

There are some, including President Donald Trump and people at Nvidia, who suggest that Huang be reinstated. And Huang issued a lengthy statement on the social media platform X saying he would return if asked.

But Nvidia closed that door on Tuesday, stating that Huang would not be reinstated and citing his "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms."

Huang's departure created legitimate questions about Nvidia's leadership and its relationships with customers and suppliers. Those concerns won't disappear after one earnings report. But the company's higher fiscal 2028 forecast suggests its manufacturing partnerships, customer relationships, and product roadmap remain intact.

I think the increased forecast is more significant than a quarterly earnings beat. While its first earnings report without Huang suggests the business can continue delivering exceptional results, a revenue growth rate of 75% in the next fiscal year shows Nvidia is hardly running out of momentum.
