#3002. Dillon Brooks’ intensity remains essential to the Suns’ identity

There are plenty of things in this world that you love 85% of the time and can't stand the other 15%. Group texts immediately come to mind. You love being part of the conversation, whether it's with family members, lifelong friends, or your sports buddies discussing the latest developments surrounding the Phoenix Suns. But sometimes those conversations go completely off the rails, your phone starts vibrating like it's sitting on a washing machine during the spin cycle, and you find yourself eternally grateful for whoever developed the technology to mute group text notifications.

As it pertains to the Phoenix Suns, the same could be said about Dillon Brooks.

We were baptized in the Dillon Brooks experience a season ago, and the overwhelming majority of the returns were positive. He's a culture setter and an attitude definer, somebody whose presence dictates the level of physicality with which your basketball team operates. Last season, he also showed us that he has considerably more tools in his offensive arsenal than many of us anticipated, averaging a career-high 20.2 points on 17.1 field-goal attempts per game.

But with that tenacity comes an edge, and navigating it without going over can be a delicate exercise. That's where the other 15% of the Dillon Brooks experience resides. The technical fouls. The flagrant fouls. The moments when the very characteristics that make him such a valuable member of your basketball team become the source of your frustration. And oftentimes, it's the timing of those infractions that makes them particularly maddening. Late-game situations and high-leverage possessions are instances in which discipline needs to supersede emotion, and Brooks doesn't always recognize when that transition needs to occur.

You love what he brings to your basketball team 85% of the time. The other 15%? You find yourself wishing Dillon Brooks had the same mute button as your group texts.

That being said, we've seen a different version of Dillon Brooks thus far this season. He's averaging 13.8 points on 12.0 shot attempts per game. Maybe it starts with the haircut, but whatever has changed, it's manifesting itself in his performance on the basketball court.

With the acquisition of Miles Bridges, Brooks has looked somewhat out of place to begin the season (as has Bridges). Much akin to the duplicative nature of Devin Booker and Jalen Green's skill sets, the same can be said of Brooks and Bridges. They occupy similar spaces on the floor and are asked to perform similar functions within the starting unit. Be a quality point-of-attack defender, knock down the three ball when called upon, and provide some physicality and assistance on the glass.

The Suns have found themselves in an interesting conundrum as the season has unfolded. There are instances when neither player appears entirely certain of where he should be positioned, whom he should be covering, or how to navigate switches on the defensive end. That uncertainty creates a particularly frustrating defensive dynamic because it compromises the very aggression that makes both players effective.

When they're aggressive, miscommunication leaves somebody exposed, and the opposition makes them pay for it. And then there are possessions when it appears they're being overly cautious, almost hesitant to do anything for fear of doing it wrong. That too burns them defensively. For two players whose effectiveness is predicated in large part on their physicality and assertiveness, indecision can be debilitating. It's difficult to impose your will on a basketball game when you're still trying to figure out where you're supposed to be.

This conundrum has contributed to the challenges the starting unit has faced throughout the early stages of the season. They're not a horrible offensive unit, primarily because Devin Booker's consistency has served as the rising tide that lifts the boats around him. Defensively, however, this group has yet to establish an identity. And when you juxtapose that against what we're experiencing from the second unit, a group that clearly understands its individual roles and how those roles complement one another, it becomes glaringly apparent how discombobulated the starting five has been.

Last night against the Denver Nuggets, we saw head coach Jordan Ott make an adjustment that appeared to unlock Dillon Brooks. That adjustment? He opened the second quarter with Brooks alongside members of the second unit, and almost immediately we saw Dillon being Dillon again.

Through his first three minutes as part of that lineup, Brooks attempted four shots. Granted, he went 1-of-4 from the field, but what stood out to me was the decisiveness with which he was operating. There was a familiarity to his approach, an aggressiveness that we'd grown to appreciate a season ago. He looked empowered to assert himself offensively without having to navigate the overlapping responsibilities that exist within the starting five.

The shots weren't necessarily falling, but the mentality was there. And from that point forward, Brooks delivered one of his best performances of the young season.

Now, I'm not about to head to my group text and flood its participants with messages advocating for Dillon Brooks to take 17 shots a night again. As Brooks has shown us throughout his career, his inefficiency can be his downfall. He attempted more shots than any member of the Phoenix Suns last night, going 6-of-17 from the field to get his 15 points. Not exactly great.

What this team needs more of is an engaged Dillon Brooks. Somebody who's emotionally invested in the game, actively disrupting what the opposition is attempting to accomplish, and embracing the alpha mentality that has become synonymous with his brand of basketball.

Brooks is the emotional leader of the starting unit, much like Jordan Goodwin is the emotional leader of the second unit. When Brooks is passive and isn't asserting himself, it affects his individual performance and, by extension, the performance of those around him. His intensity has a trickle-down effect on his teammates, and when that intensity is absent, you can feel it throughout the lineup.

Again, it's a fine edge to navigate. But it's one Brooks has navigated throughout his NBA career. It's his X factor, the characteristic that makes him special and gives him value beyond his statistical production.

Hell, he even picked up a horseshit technical foul last night after knocking down a three-pointer and barking at the opposing bench. Apparently, only Dillon Brooks can earn a technical foul for doing something we routinely see across the NBA. As frustrating as the whistle was, it was another indication of how engaged he was in the game.

It was his third technical foul of the season through 13 games, meaning he's averaging one every 4.3 games. That's a slightly more disciplined pace than a season ago, when he averaged one every 3.3 games en route to accumulating a league-leading 17 technical fouls.

The ideal balance, in my eyes, is a version of Brooks who takes somewhere around 11 shots per game, assumes greater offensive responsibility when sharing the floor with the second unit, and remains the emotional leader of the starting five. Defensively, you want him to take charge, communicate, dictate physicality, and impose his will, rather than operate with uncertainty and defer to those around him.

There's no perfect formula for finding that balance, particularly for a player whose greatest strength can occasionally become his greatest weakness. The Suns need Brooks to understand when to turn the volume up and when to dial it back. But they also need him to remain the emotional heartbeat of that starting unit. His aggression, physicality, and willingness to get under somebody's skin are part of what makes him valuable.

Give me an engaged Dillon Brooks, and I'll live with having to mute the group text from time to time. Now do me a favor, send this article to one of your friends via group text.

#3000. This Magnificent Vanguard ETF Could Turn $500 per Month Into $1 Million in Under 30 Years

Investors can build life-changing wealth in the stock market with a combination of patience and consistency.

By Anthony Di Pizio – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:29AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF ›

The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (VUG +0.37%) is an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that exclusively invests in America's most valuable growth stocks. These stocks are known for delivering high capital returns, separating them from value stocks, which typically generate comparatively modest gains, supplemented by dividend income.

Here's how the Vanguard ETF could turn a consistent investment of $500 per month into $1 million in under 30 years.

The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF holds 135 stocks from 11 different economic sectors. However, a whopping 72.1% of its assets are parked in technology companies alone, which is fitting given their tendency to generate faster revenue and earnings growth than companies in other sectors. High exposure to tech is a key reason why the ETF tends to outperform the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.02%) index over time.

The Vanguard ETF is also top-heavy because its 10 largest holdings alone represent 66.1% of the value of its entire portfolio.

Data source: Vanguard. Portfolio weightings are accurate as of Oct. 31, 2026, and are subject to change.

Following a recent decline in Nvidia stock sparked by the departure of founder Jensen Huang, Apple is now the world's most valuable company once again. The company continues to expand its Apple Intelligence suite of AI features and applications, bringing new capabilities to the iPhone, iPad, and Mac lineup of computers. With over 2.5 billion active devices globally, Apple could soon be the largest distributor of AI software to consumers.

While the future of Nvidia's leadership team remains uncertain, there is still an unprecedented amount of demand for the company's data center chips, which do most of the heavy lifting in AI workloads. Nvidia has already revealed some of its product pipeline through to 2030, with the Feynman AI semiconductor architecture slated to replace the latest Rubin architecture from 2028. As a result, the data center business is likely to grow nicely no matter who leads the company.

While Apple could dominate consumer AI, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon are battling for market share in the enterprise AI space. They have each enhanced their legacy product platforms with AI, and their respective cloud computing platforms provide businesses with all of the tools they need to leverage this revolutionary technology themselves.

These AI powerhouses have led the Vanguard ETF higher over the last few years. However, it does hold a number of stocks from outside the tech sector, including payment giants Visa and Mastercard, retail behemoth Costco Wholesale, industrial powerhouse Boeing, and even Starbucks.

The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF has delivered a compound annual return of 11.8% since it was established in 2004, but it has delivered an even faster annual return of 24.6% over the last three years specifically, thanks to the AI boom.

Here's how long it could take the ETF to turn a monthly investment of $500 into $1 million, based on three different average annual returns.

It's unrealistic to expect any ETF to deliver an annual return of over 20% indefinitely, because the law of large numbers eventually becomes a headwind. For example, if Apple's market cap grew by 20% annually for the next 20 years, it would become a $198 trillion company, making it more valuable than the output of the entire global economy, which was $118 trillion in 2025.

But even if the Vanguard ETF's annual return reverts back to its long-term average of 11.8%, it could still turn $500 per month into $1 million in under 30 years.

With that said, I think above-average returns are likely for the foreseeable future. Although the AI boom is facing some headwinds, this technology is laying the foundation for the industries of the future, from robotics to autonomous vehicles to quantum computing. Given the Vanguard ETF's concentrated exposure to the technology sector, it's likely to hold the companies driving those potential revolutions.

However, that can be a double-edged sword at times, because a concentrated portfolio will also experience higher volatility than a diversified portfolio. This is something investors should keep in mind when buying the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF.

#2998. Applied Materials vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Two chipmakers, two very different bets: one sells the tools that build the chips, the other designs the networking silicon that moves data between them.

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:38AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Applied Materials ›

As the race for dominance in artificial intelligence intensifies, choosing the right infrastructure provider is critical. Should you invest in equipment giant Applied Materials (AMAT +0.00%) or connectivity specialist Marvell Technology (MRVL -0.51%)?

Applied Materials supplies the tools that actually build the chips, making it a foundational player in the semiconductor ecosystem. Marvell designs the custom chips and networking components that move data between servers. Comparing these two reveals different ways to play the ongoing shift toward high-performance computing and massive data center expansion.

Applied Materials sells materials engineering solutions used to produce nearly every new chip and advanced display in the world. It serves a concentrated customer base of logic, foundry, and memory manufacturers, including giants like Intel (INTC -1.11%) and Micron Technology (MU -1.08%). Two specific customers accounted for approximately 19% and 15% of net revenue, respectively. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached nearly $34.4 billion. This represented growth of roughly 21.4% compared to the prior period, driven by strong demand for advanced chipmaking equipment. Net income totaled approximately $10.1 billion, showcasing the profitability possible at this scale.

As of Applied Materials' October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3. This ratio measures total debt against shareholder equity, with lower numbers typically suggesting less financial leverage. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is roughly 2.3. For those following semiconductor stocks, strong cash flow is vital for R&D. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $6.2 billion.

Marvell Technology operates as a fabless supplier, meaning it designs high-end semiconductor solutions but outsources the actual manufacturing. The company focuses on data center core networks and the network edge, serving original equipment manufacturers and cloud service providers. For its most recent annual reporting period, two customers each accounted for 10% or more of net revenue, and the 10 largest customers collectively accounted for 82% of net revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $9.5 billion. This figure reflects growth of close to 30.6% over the previous 12 months as the company expanded its footprint in AI infrastructure. Net income for the same period was approximately $2.6 billion, marking a significant turnaround from previous years.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.3. Its current ratio is approximately 2, indicating a solid ability to meet short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was close to $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Applied Materials faces significant geographic concentration, with a heavy reliance on customers in China. This exposure makes the company sensitive to trade policies and export restrictions. It also manages legal risks involving export controls, including a $252 million settlement reached in February 2026 for export violations involving Semiconductor Manufacturing International. Furthermore, its reliance on complex global supply chains creates vulnerability to regional disruptions or inventory obsolescence.

Marvell Technology has high customer concentration. Its 10 largest clients account for nearly 82% of revenue, and it often competes with rivals like Broadcom(AVGO +2.17%). The company is also navigating a massive $115 billion pending acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE +0.01%). This deal introduces risks related to shareholder dilution and the complex process of integrating two large organizations. Additionally, Marvell's dependency on third-party foundries in the Pacific Rim creates supply chain risks if regional political conflicts arise.

Applied Materials currently appears to be the more conservative value choice, while Marvell Technology commands a higher premium given its faster growth profile.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, helping you see how much you are paying for every dollar of projected profit. The P/S ratio measures the market price relative to sales over the past 12 months.

Marvell and Applied Materials are riding the current tech boom, with both stocks hitting all-time highs earlier this year. They've since pulled back a considerable amount, but they're still handily outpacing the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.02%) by massive margins:

There's not a ton of daylight between the two stocks' recent returns. And as for business performance, Applied Materials has a slightly higher net margin, while Marvell is posting stronger revenue growth.

I lean toward Applied Materials in this matchup. Marvell's revenue growth is impressive, but its pending acquisition of Lumentum introduces a fair amount of risk. There's the possibility of dilution, but there's also the potential that the combined company doesn't create the cost-savings and synergies management had hoped for. That could lead to significant writedowns, which would almost certainly impact the stock negatively.

Applied Materials just seems to have less risk, which makes it my pick for 2027 and beyond.

#2996. The 3 Best AI Stocks to Buy Now (Yes, Nvidia Is One of Them)

Nvidia may be going through a tumultuous period, but the business is still strong.

By Keithen Drury – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:44AM EST

The artificial intelligence sector of the stock market isn't the most popular place to invest right now. There are questions surrounding how the AI build-out will be allowed to proceed, with Democrats sweeping the U.S. midterm elections. This could put a pause on some data centers, affecting companies that provide the components. Still, many projects are underway, and many builds will likely be allowed to continue as-is, with newer facilities coming under greater scrutiny.

While AI investment sentiment is currently negative, I think there are plenty of great investment opportunities right now. They include Nvidia (NVDA -0.36%), Broadcom (AVGO +2.17%), and Micron (MU -1.08%). While Nvidia is in a bit of a mess with its CEO resigning last week, I think the stock has cratered to the point where it makes sense to buy shares. The other two are also genius buys and make for timely investments, with the market not being bullish on the AI outlook.

First, let's look at Nvidia. CEO Jensen Huang resigned due to relationships with staff and a potential Chinese spy. This is a huge loss for Nvidia because Huang co-founded the company and built it into what it is today. At the same time, Nvidia's products are so impressive and have such a dominant market share that they practically sell themselves. This means business will likely go on as usual at Nvidia, and investors should use the global sell-off as a buying opportunity for the stock.

After the sell-off, Nvidia trades at a dirt cheap price of 10.5 times next year's earnings estimates.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

That's a huge discount, and considering the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.02%) trades for about 20 times forward earnings, I can see Nvidia having an impressive rebound in 2027.

While Nvidia is a timely buy, it still has some troubles. So, investors should also look to other stocks.

Broadcom has been taking market share from Nvidia for a while. Instead of making a broad-purpose GPU like Nvidia, it's partnering directly with AI hyperscalers to develop custom AI chips that are tailored to their workloads. This has major cost advantages, as running workloads on these chips is far cheaper than on GPUs. However, they cannot be used in every situation, so there will always be a large place for Nvidia GPUs.

Next year, Broadcom expects its AI semiconductor revenue to double, and double again in 2028. That's huge growth and will also outperform Nvidia over that time frame. As a result, I think it's a top option to buy in addition to or instead of Nvidia.

Micron is a key supplier to both Broadcom and Nvidia, as it makes memory chips for computing devices. The memory chip industry has seen practically all of its production capacity consumed by the AI build-out, causing chip prices to soar. This has led to a record-setting year for Micron, but it could get even better.

During Micron's latest earnings report, its management team noted that market conditions will be worse in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026. When Micron says "worse," it means worse for its clients, not for itself. The company will do well because high demand for memory chips has driven up prices, translating into pure profit for Micron.

Historically, Micron has been a cyclical stock, which is why the market isn't valuing it at its full potential.

The market is valuing Micron's stock as if its business will evaporate tomorrow; we know that won't happen for several more years, given the strength of the AI build-out. This mismatch is your investment opportunity, and I think Micron is a top stock to buy now.

#2995. Dan Campbell sends Lions clear celebration message after Aidan Hutchinson injury

With the Lions losing star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson for the season in their 35-10 overseas win over the Patriots, head coach Dan Campbell stood firm on his stance regarding player celebrations.

Hutchinson's season came to an unfortunate end after a sack on Patriots quarterback Drake Maye in the first quarter; the five-year veteran landed awkwardly after jumping in the air in celebration and tore his ACL in the process.

During Tuesday's appearance on Detroit's 97.1 The Ticket, Campbell verified the defensive star's injury status and how it will affect an already depleted defense.

Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (97) sits on the field after an injury during a game in Munich, Germany, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. AP Photo/Matthias Schrader

"What a gut punch, just because … he's such a phenomenal player," Campbell said. "This guy's an impact player, but more importantly, he's an unbelievable teammate, and he's one of our captains.

"It just stinks, man. It hits you. And I hate it for him, man, because he was on a heater. What a hell of a year he was having. He's just improved every year and to come off the injury he had [in 2024]. But I also know this, man: this guy will overcome this and he will come back better than he was, too. It's just the way he is, it's the way he's wired, and he'll come out better for this."

Regarding whether the celebration caused the injury, Campbell played it off as a freak accident.

"No, I don't believe that," Campbell said. "I think what happened speaks for itself. We're not talking to 8-year-olds here. And I'll give you a story. I remember one time I made a big play and I freaking pumped my arm up and I'm pretty sure I tore my bicep, but I didn't tell anybody. I was just excited. I just pumped my arm. It's not like I — so if you say, 'Hey, don't pump your arm next time, make sure you stay stoic,' man, this game is built off of emotion. And if you have to contain yourself after a play is made … then you're really becoming something you're not."

Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell speaks at a press conference after an NFL football game in Munich, Germany, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The gesture was similar to the typical goal celebration in soccer that fans of FC Bayern Munich would see at Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, where the latest European NFL matchup was held.

Lions fans remember the outcome vividly, as former linebacker Stephen Tulloch suffered the same fate as Hutchinson back in 2014 against the Green Bay Packers.

Hutchinson had 24 tackles on the season and six sacks before getting hurt.

This marks the defensive end's second season-ending injury in the span of three seasons.

The injury, Campbell said, was "one of those things that happened."

"I hate it, I know he hates it. But I mean, the number of moves that I've seen Hutch make and the number of plyometrics, explosive movements, the spins, the one leg lateral movements, lateral balances, I'm just like, it was one of those things, man," the coach said. "I hate it. I think we all understand what it is, and let's be smart, but no, I'm not gonna say, 'Nobody celebrates anymore.'"

The Lions went into the international matchup without middle linebacker Jack Campbell, who left Week 8's 19-15 win over the Minnesota Vikings on a stretcher.

#2992. The Urgency Premium: The Clock AI Can't Control

Adam Thier is the Chief Product and Technology Officer at Anaplan, a leading AI-driven scenario planning and analysis platform.

One of the most hyped benefits of AI is that it will speed up decision making from weeks to minutes. It’s a good story, and parts of it are already true.

But as any technology leader who’s tried to operationalize AI knows, moving fast means nothing if the rest of the world doesn’t move as fast as you do. ​

Here’s a simple example that has nothing to do with AI and everything to do with why “faster decisions” alone won’t fix the problem. ​

You have a document that needs to arrive at your client’s office on Friday. If you send it a week ahead of time, it costs $0.82, the price of a first-class stamp. Wait until two days before, and it costs maybe $12. The day before? The cost of express delivery can jump to over $30. ​

In every version, the mail truck didn’t get faster because you decided faster—all that changed was how much of its schedule you had left to use. ​

Most leaders write this off as a rounding error, a one-time tax on poor planning. But the same dynamic plays out across hiring, procurement, sales and product launches. In each, waiting can destroy significant value.​​

I call this the “urgency premium,” the avoidable value lost to insufficient lead time. ​

There’s a tendency for leaders to treat lateness as binary: you either hit your deadline, or you didn’t. But value deteriorates long before the deadline arrives, whether or not anyone notices. ​

Technology is especially exposed to the urgency premium because some of its most critical resources disappear quickly. I’ve seen this play out repeatedly leading product and technology organizations.

For example, consider a product launch that’s scheduled for three months out. At this stage, you have multiple implementation partners available, time to secure specialized engineering support and plenty of runway for technical reviews and testing.

If you wait until one month out, you may still be “on track,” but the conditions for reaching your launch look very different. Here’s how: ​

1. Your options disappear. There is no alert when the specialist you wanted commits to another project, a competitor moves first or a technical decision becomes too costly to revisit. Options disappear while the project still looks healthy on a dashboard.

​2. The remaining options get more expensive. Once the preferred path is gone, preserving the same delivery date comes at a premium. Contractors replace internal expertise; vendors charge for expedited support; and overtime fills gaps that more lead time would have avoided. On a $1 million procurement commitment, even a modest rush premium can translate into thousands of dollars in avoidable costs before you even count the preferred suppliers you no longer have access to.

3. The quality of execution declines. Technical reviews get compressed, vendor evaluations become less thorough and teams make trade-offs they wouldn’t have made with adequate lead time. You pay more and get less. ​

The specialist who commits to another project, the vendor whose calendar fills up, the review that takes however long it takes—all run on clocks you don’t control. Repeat those issues across dozens of projects at enterprise scale, and an organization can stay consistently “on time” while quietly leaving millions on the table. ​

AI can help you decide in seconds instead of weeks, but it can’t move any of those clocks. ​

Most organizations plan backward from the last possible date an action can be taken.

My take: That’s the wrong target. By that point, your highest-value options are likely already gone. Instead, leaders should track option cliffs, or the points where a preferred resource, path or choice stops being available. ​

Let’s go back to the product launch example. The launch date is one deadline, but there are many others hiding in the months leading up to it.

There is a date when your preferred implementation partner can no longer guarantee availability, and a point when compressing testing or security review begins to compromise quality. Those are the cliffs leaders need to identify before work begins. ​

To find them, ask three questions for all major decisions:

1. How fast do costs escalate as time runs out?

2. How fast does execution quality decline?

3. When do your best options actually expire? ​

Of the three questions, the third is especially important. If a preferred option disappears weeks before a launch, managing to the launch date means managing to the wrong deadline. ​

Not every decision should be made as early as possible. Sometimes waiting has real value. Requirements may become clearer, markets may shift and new information can lead to better decisions.

Make that trade-off explicit: what you gain by waiting has to be worth more than the options you’ll lose, the costs you’ll incur and the execution quality you’ll sacrifice. ​

AI may make decisions dramatically faster, but that only makes timing more important.

To sum up, investors may want to consider both of these consumer stocks, given their impressive growth rates and profits. However, in this particular head-to-head comparison, Airbnb has the overall edge, in my view. The company's profitability, combined with its more reasonable valuation, complements its revenue growth, which exceeds 15%, making it my choice in this battle of consumer stocks.

#2987. The Real Value Of Enterprise AI Lives In The Boring Work

Rajat Bhargava is an entrepreneur, investor, author and currently CEO and cofounder of JumpCloud.

The technology industry is racing toward bigger AI breakthroughs, from autonomous agents to increasingly sophisticated models. Inside most organizations, however, the most valuable opportunities are less exciting. They sit in repetitive tasks such as preparing customer handoffs, reviewing sales opportunities, compiling reports and managing routine IT requests. These activities rarely make headlines, but they consume time employees could spend solving problems or building customer relationships. For business leaders, the question isn’t how much AI an organization can deploy but how much better it operates because of AI.

Getting there requires more than adding another tool. Organizations need to understand where employees lose time, improve the processes behind that work and define what success looks like. They also need to recognize that AI agents acting on employees’ behalf create new responsibilities around access and oversight. Moving quickly matters, but deploying AI everywhere is not a strategy. The organizations that gain the most will start with everyday problems, test their assumptions and expand what works.

A common mistake is starting with technology rather than a business problem. Leaders may pursue ambitious AI projects while overlooking smaller workflows that could deliver value sooner. Consider a sales representative preparing for a customer meeting by gathering account details, reviewing past conversations and summarizing open issues across several systems. AI could handle much of that preparation, leaving more time to understand customer needs. The goal isn’t necessarily to replace a process; it’s to remove the administrative work slowing it down.

A useful starting point is to ask employees which repetitive tasks consume the most time without requiring much judgment. Rather than launch a company-wide initiative, leaders can evaluate promising workflows against three practical criteria:

• Find Recurring Bottlenecks: Prioritize tasks that happen frequently and slow down employees or customers.

• Set A Baseline: Record how long each task takes, how often errors occur and what delays cost.

• Test Before Expanding: Pilot one defined workflow, then compare speed, accuracy and employee feedback with the original process.

Even a promising workflow may not be ready for automation. When teams follow different procedures or store information in disconnected systems, AI can reproduce confusion at greater speed. Automating customer handoffs, for example, won’t help if sales and customer success disagree on which details must be shared. Before deployment, organizations should clarify responsibilities, standardize the process and agree on a successful outcome. Fixing these gaps first prevents teams from spending money automating inefficiency.

AI makes it easier to produce content, process information and complete routine tasks, but more output doesn’t automatically mean better performance. Thousands of AI-generated sales summaries won’t matter if they don’t improve customer conversations. Weekly reports add little value if nobody uses them to make decisions. Counting prompts, agents or completed tasks therefore offers an incomplete picture of progress. What matters is whether AI improves the quality, speed or cost of a meaningful business outcome.

Each initiative needs a baseline and a result that can be checked after deployment. Customer support leaders might measure resolution time alongside customer satisfaction, while IT teams could track how quickly routine requests are handled without weakening security. Sales teams could examine whether automated preparation creates more time for conversations that move opportunities forward. Measurements should include the effort spent checking AI output and correcting mistakes. If automation saves 30 minutes but requires 20 minutes of rework, the real gain is only 10 minutes.

It is essential to distinguish time saved from value created. Giving employees five hours back each week sounds promising, but the benefit depends on what happens next. That time might support faster customer service, more thoughtful decisions or stronger relationships, none of which is captured by an automation dashboard alone. Small pilots help teams test those connections before committing to larger investments. Scaling then becomes a decision grounded in results, not excitement about the technology.

An assistant summarizing a document presents different risks from an agent updating customer records or acting inside business systems. As AI moves from answering questions to taking action, organizations need clearer rules about who and what can access sensitive information. A recent report our company conducted found that 72% of surveyed organizations reported a moderate-to-large gap between what AI was permitted to access and what they could prove it accessed. That gap shows why productivity and oversight cannot be treated as separate projects. Agents need clear ownership, limited permissions and records of their activity from the start.

Before deploying an agent, IT and security teams should define its task, permitted systems, approval requirements and accountable owner. An agent preparing a sales report might need to read CRM data but not modify customer records or open unrelated financial files. Access should be restricted to what’s necessary and removed when the task or agent is no longer active. Activity logs should help teams investigate mistakes and identify unusual behavior. These safeguards make it easier to expand automation without losing visibility or control.

Governance cannot end when a pilot goes live. Business needs change, employees encounter exceptions and automated workflows can drift away from their original purpose. Teams should regularly review accuracy, outcomes, permissions and whether an agent is still needed. Frontline employees should remain involved because they often spot problems before a dashboard does. The real advantage in enterprise AI will come from improving ordinary work, measuring what changes and keeping control as automation grows.​

Despite this double-digit top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of approximately $62.9 million. This loss reflects the ongoing costs of scaling its global infrastructure and investing in its edge computing capabilities to compete with larger rivals.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintains a current ratio of approximately 2.6x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term obligations with current assets. Its debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.5x, showing a moderate level of debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $65.8 million. However, note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 124.2% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

(NET +2.61%), as well as hyperscale providers such as Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +1.98%), Google, and Microsoft. Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

For Docusign, sales in its current fiscal year are seen growing by nearly 9% to $3.5 billion, with a slightly better percentage gain in net income to $346 million.

Docusign's launch and global expansion of the IAM platform with the introduction of AI-powered tools should position the company for future growth. However, the not-so-great projected revenue growth rates suggest that Docusign may be entering a phase of more mature growth and a landscape of increasingly competitive digital agreement and contract management software. In particular, news reports OpenAI would launch a ChatGPT product that would compete head-on with Docusign in the document summary field caused some investor fears. Right now, however, the signature and identity verification part of Docusign's business appears unthreatened by ChatGPT.

Fastly, meanwhile, processes over 5 trillion requests a day, a huge number that is actually just a small part of the total addressable market (TAM) for the business. Management sees the TAM as $22 billion, giving it a long runway for growth. The company has posted three straight quarters of more than 20% growth (year-over-year).

One of the company's competitive edges, it says, is that it delivers its resources dynamically, allocating them in real time to whatever the load is on a global basis. So, for example, one Thursday night, its network might be delivering Thursday Night Football. On Black Friday, the exact same network is handling e-commerce. The next week, it might be handling a video game release. Fastly says that makes it a much more efficient network than competitors, who have siloed networks for security, compute, and delivery, et cetera.

For the current fiscal year, look for sales to grow to $741 million, a 19% rise over the prior year, with a much narrower net loss of about $72 million.

Fastly shares come at a premium to Docusign's, at least through the prism of forward P/E, but it brings along faster growth for the price. For 2027, Fastly is the stock that's the better buy here.

#2984. AI Observability 2.0: Why Enterprises Need To Measure The Full Cost And Value Of AI

Yuri Gubin is Chief Technology Officer at DataArt, working with organizations integrating AI into complex engineering environments.

​As we’re approaching the end of 2026, it’s interesting to look at what we expected from AI this year and what really happened. If you go back a few years, many of the predictions were based on guesstimates and wishful thinking. Now we do see that AI is everywhere, agentic development is quite good and there are methods evolving with examples of how AI really boosts development. We also see the impact on individual productivity, even outside engineering, in knowledge management and other areas.

What we’re still missing, despite all the efforts, is an industry-proven methodology that has become a standard for AI-enabled development. We have different frameworks explaining the stages of AI adoption, and examples of what works and what doesn’t, but we’re still some way from having an approach that everybody can use, regardless of which LLM they’re working with.

And then there’s the ROI question. We still need better measurements and evidence of the benefits, particularly when it comes to understanding whether the same approach will work in different environments. This is where observability could become particularly interesting.

Organizations will be rethinking the costs of AI, and I’m not talking about subscriptions or tokens alone. It’s the cost of data, infrastructure and everything you put in place to make AI happen in your company. All these expenses add up, and we’ll likely see more scrutiny and greater demands for results.

This is already happening, of course. We’ve been anticipating this and advocating for reasonable use of AI, where you validate results with data rather than relying on expectations. Some organizations will try to spend less without substantial changes in quality or delivery, and others will spend more, but this rethinking is already underway.

If you look at the work companies were doing three or five years ago, they were paying for people, cloud infrastructure and other operational expenses. Now you may be doing the same work, but you’re also consuming AI resources, and the value of that work may be different. So the economics change, including margins and how companies capture the value created. This may affect business models across the board, including outside IT services.

One area we’ll likely see developing is observability, but in a different sense from how we’ve traditionally understood it. Before, we would talk about operational telemetry and system metrics, while with AI, we need to understand where it’s being used and how much value it has created.

I would call it AI Observability 2.0, because there should be a new standard and a new wave of technologies that help us understand the impact of AI.

Right now, I don’t think the ecosystem is there to tell us exactly how much we spend on each action when we consider the end-to-end flow. And it’s not only about pure numbers. You have the technology, the decision-making, the judgment, the quality of the result, the spending and the value created. We need to understand the entire chain, including what happens when something doesn’t work well and how we can troubleshoot, evaluate and react faster. Some of this may come through new technologies, or it may be changes to the same technologies we’ve had in our toolboxes before.

One thing we still haven’t resolved is how to measure ROI in a way that gives us reliable, repeatable results. Let’s say AI works well in one team and you see productivity improvements. If you apply it to another team, even within the same organization, will it work the same? The technology stack might be different, the problem space is different and it’s difficult to say whether you should expect the same benefits.

There’s something similar happening with data. Its importance was already on everyone’s mind at the beginning of 2026, but as you start making progress, you discover new depth to the challenges you already knew about.

You may have created a data lake and put all the data in one place, but then you discover that it doesn’t help you improve the use of AI as much as you expected. Maybe the conventional data lake is too slow, or maybe you’re still missing some data. You wanted to transform the company, and now you realize that having the data in one place doesn’t necessarily solve the problem.

I hope 2027 will be a year of AI growth, but in a more reasonable, pragmatic and mature way, rather than explosive experimentation. Hopefully, as an industry, we’ll make progress on methodologies and standards for AI-enabled development, because those are still to be defined.

I also expect technologies that help us understand the value AI creates will become more important. Observability is an interesting area because we’re still missing that understanding of the complete process, and we’ll need it to make better decisions about AI investments.

#2982. Does Intelligence Need The Railroad?

Charles Yeomans is the chairman and founder of Atombeam.

​In Fortune’s recent Term Sheet (paywall), Allie Garfinkle asked investor Hans Tung to take the Industrial Revolution analogy for AI seriously, which he did. His argument runs from Britain’s steel steamships to the railroads that helped decide the American Civil War, and he casts data centers as the railroads of this century. The models that make a difference, he argues, are the ones with the infrastructure behind them: “The models that win are the ones that are available.”

As history, I find the argument persuasive. As a prediction, it rests on an assumption almost nobody examines: that intelligence has mass. We have accepted it as settled that AI needs all of this infrastructure. We should be asking whether that is a fact about intelligence or a fact about one design.

Railroads were important because cargo was heavy. Steel ships became critical because trade goods had to cross oceans in hulls. Data centers matter today because the dominant AI architecture makes every act of machine intelligence heavy. A large language model answers a question by driving it through billions of calculations on specialized processors, and it does so again for the next question, and the next, forever. Usage rises, and the compute bill rises with it. Under that architecture, Tung is simply right. Intelligence must ship to the railhead, and the nation with more track wins. One estimate he cites puts the American buildout at an average of 3.6% of GDP every year into the next decade, which tells you how heavy we have decided intelligence has to be.

But heaviness is a property of the architecture of AI. The way our brains work suggests there is a different way to build machine intelligence: Hold knowledge as durable structure, and compute each answer directly from it. The engineered version can go one step further than biology: The structure can be explicit and inspectable, so a machine can show the basis for what it concludes. In a system built this way, learning is the expensive step, and it happens once. After a subject is learned, producing an answer would be computationally trivial, small enough to run on an ordinary processor, with no round trip to anyone’s railhead.

We do not need much compute to identify a car when we see it, or a person we know. Our brains run on 20 watts, not megawatts, so we know this kind of efficiency is possible. The economics would be the reverse of the token meter: Cost falls as the machine learns, because knowledge would persist instead of being recomputed. Something else follows from structure: A machine that computes from what it actually knows can decline to answer when it does not, instead of generating a plausible guess. The reliability problems keeping AI out of high-consequence work are, at root, the same architecture question.

If this idea for a new kind of AI proves possible, and prototype work by my own team and others gives me reason to believe it is, the strategic picture inverts in two ways. The first concerns Tung’s own Civil War detail. He points out that most battles clustered near the railroad because the railroad was the dependency, and dependencies are what adversaries target. A force, a hospital or a factory whose machine judgment lives locally needs no railhead; everything stays behind the firewall, and the whole thing runs on the power budget of a laptop, or even less, rather than a substation. Local AI is not just more secure and more available; it steps almost entirely out of the energy problem, because computing an answer from learned structure draws watts where generating one from scratch draws megawatts.

The second is the geopolitical race itself. We need to face the fact that we are betting on out-pouring concrete against China, perhaps the most formidable builder of physical infrastructure on earth. The asymmetric answer to that is not more gigawatts. It is more intelligence per watt, which is an architecture question before it is an energy question.

The railroads will be built, and much of that buildout will be valuable; training, research and the broad models that benefit from scale will use every mile of track. But the assumption that all intelligence must ride those rails deserves the scrutiny we give any assumption worth trillions. Tung says the winning models are the available ones. I agree. The most available intelligence is the kind that never has to travel.

#2976. Investors Love the S&P 500 Index. Here’s Why I Don’t.

The S&P 500 Index isn't what it used to be.

By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:56AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

The S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.06%) is one of the most popular stock market indexes in the world. Roughly $16 trillion is invested globally in index funds and ETFs tracking the S&P 500. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.13%) alone has $1.7 trillion in assets.

Charlie Munger, the longtime business partner of Warren Buffett, once claimed that "95% of people have no chance of beating the S&P 500 Index." But I'm not sure that advice is true in today's market. And there's one glaring reason why.

Most investors believe that the S&P 500 is a diversified basket of stocks that captures the valuation of the entire U.S. economy spanning a broad range of industries and sectors. That's true, but only up to a point.

During the dot-com bubble, technology stocks accounted for roughly one-third of the index. When the bubble burst, S&P 500 investors learned they weren't as diversified as they had believed.

The same proved true during the financial crisis, when financial stocks comprised roughly one-quarter of the entire index. When that bubble burst, the S&P 500's supposed diversification benefits proved less reliable than initially thought.

Today, nearly half of the S&P 500's value is tied up in either AI stocks or companies that supply the AI industry. The math isn't perfect, as many AI stocks engage in many other business activities besides AI. But the lofty valuations of these companies are very much tied to their AI efforts. If the AI story stumbles, nearly half of the S&P 500 could see their valuations compress sharply.

"Artificial intelligence concentration is increasing, both across the economy and in investor portfolios," research from Franklin Templeton warns. "[I]nvestors are now considering how to best mitigate concentration risk without sacrificing the gains from AI, which include economywide productivity growth and potentially superior investment returns."

In almost all cases, sticking with an index fund tracking the S&P 500 is prudent, even during market peaks. If you had purchased shares of an S&P 500 index fund at the peak of every bubble in history, you'd still be sitting on a healthy long-term profit. That's the power of long-term thinking.

The issue today is that the S&P 500 no longer functions like it did in the past. In past bubbles, peak industry concentrations ranged from 25% to 35%. Today's AI concentration hovers around 45%. The decline of a single industry, therefore, could drag down your entire portfolio.

Many long-term, risk-tolerant investors may do well sticking with their traditional index fund exposure. Risk-averse investors such as retirees and those on a fixed income, however, should reassess just how "diversified" their portfolios are. The S&P 500 remains a great index to track long term. But it's no longer the no-brainer investment it used to be.

#2975. Your AI's Confidence Score Won't Catch Products You Don't Carry

Srijith Ravikumar is a Principal Engineer at Amazon building AI search and recommendation systems. Published at ACM CIKM and IP&M.

In 2024, a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to compensate a customer who had relied on its website chatbot’s advice about bereavement fares, and it rejected the airline’s argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions. Retailers face a version of that exposure: AI recommendations for products the store doesn’t carry. A tempting way to decide when to trust those suggestions is a score the model reports about itself.

Ask a recommendation model how confident it is, set a threshold and drop everything below it. That guardrail is easy to build and easy to report upward. In my tests, it barely worked. Across 48 test settings, filtering on stated confidence cut the share of out-of-catalog suggestions by a median of 0.02 percentage points, and in 18 of them, the filtered list came out slightly worse.

My study measured how often suggestions miss the catalog, not what a miss costs. The likely costs are easy to name. A customer taps a suggestion, finds nothing to buy and trusts the feature a little less. A slot that could have sold something goes to an item that can’t. An assistant that names products the store lacks invites complaints. Treat those as hypotheses to check against your own numbers.

This year I tested four widely used large language models from four different developers. Each suggested 10 items from a user’s history, working from memory with no access to the catalog, on three public datasets covering movies, local businesses and retail toys. I checked every suggestion against the catalog it was meant to come from, using a matching method validated against about 200 human judgments, and counted anything not in that catalog as a miss, whether or not it exists elsewhere.

The out-of-catalog rate depended heavily on the catalog. Across the four models and three catalogs, it ran from 0.6% to 61%. Every model stayed under 3% on movies and reached roughly half or more on toys, with identical instructions. A rate measured in one domain tells you little about another, and a vendor demo is one domain.

Confidence barely moved. Each model’s stated confidence on toys stayed within about four points of its confidence on movies, while its out-of-catalog rate rose twentyfold or more. Researchers have already shown that models stating their own confidence tend to be overconfident, a bias you could at least correct for. Here the bias wasn’t stable. Across the 12 model-and-catalog combinations, the models were underconfident in seven and overconfident in five: All four were underconfident on movies, and all four were overconfident on toys. A correction tuned on one catalog would point the wrong way on the next.

One explanation fits the data, though the data don’t prove it. Asked how confident it is, a model seems to rate how good it thinks the suggestion is. It can’t check whether the item sits in your catalog from memory.

The filter I used is split conformal abstention, which uses conformal prediction, a standard statistical technique, to drop the least-confident suggestions while guaranteeing that a set share of the good ones survive. Its best result across the 48 settings was a cut of under two percentage points. The method largely kept the good items, as designed. Its guarantee says nothing about removing bad ones.

I tested only the confidence a model states in words. Token probabilities, agreement across repeated samples and constrained generation are different signals I didn’t test, and they may do better. If your model only picks among candidates retrieved from your catalog, the failure changes shape: The risk becomes a poor pick among real items, and this study doesn’t speak to that.

Within that scope, these are the questions I’d bring to a product review, an AI governance meeting or a decision to fund the next phase.

Is every suggestion checked against the live catalog before a customer sees it? It removes items you can’t sell, though it won’t fix relevance.

How was the out-of-catalog number measured? If items are matched by title, the matching rule can move the answer more than the model does. On identical model outputs, plausible off-the-shelf matching rules disagreed on the toy catalog’s out-of-catalog rate by more than a factor of 10. Ask for a check against a couple of hundred hand-labeled cases, with the remaining error reported next to the number. Having the model return product IDs avoids the problem.

Is a promising fix being tested as an experiment? On the business catalog only, I told two models to recommend from a fixed catalog that I didn’t show them and asked how sure they were that each title was in it. Out-of-catalog suggestions fell from 12.9% to 1.5% for one model and from 14.4% to 8.9% for the other. Each cut is at least three times the filter’s best result. The paper reports the figures and compares the first cut directly against that result. That prompt changed the instruction and the confidence question at once, and it covers two models in one catalog. Before a rollout, ask for a test that changes one prompt element at a time, runs on a held-out sample of the live catalog and reports both the out-of-catalog rate and whether the suggestions stayed relevant.

Was it measured on your own catalog, including the long tail of products customers rarely look for? A benchmark from someone else’s data, or a pilot on your bestsellers, says little about those.

Keep the confidence score for sorting results or deciding where a person looks first. The governance question is a different one: What share of our AI suggestions aren’t in our live catalog, measured across the long tail? The confidence score can’t answer it.​

"The way I play, I can get to it off the bench, I can get to it as a starter. I'm mature enough to be able to handle different roles, different minutes."

With McCollum sidelined, the keys to the offense will belong to Flemings, whom the Hawks selected with the No. 8 pick in June's draft out of Houston. In 12 games including five starts, Flemings is averaging 7.8 points, 4.1 assists, 2.5 rebounds and 0.7 steals in 21.5 minutes per game.

Flemings' shooting efficiency has stood out, especially for a rookie. He's shooting 51.4% from the field and 42.9% on 1.8 3-point attempts per game. He's done so in limited playing time as McCollum has continued to play heavy minutes off the bench.

Flemings has been day-to-day with back tightness, but was reportedly able to practice on Tuesday. He projects to have an opportunity to build on his success with increased volume and playing time in McCollum's absence.

The Hawks also announced Tuesday that second-year backup forward Asa Newell will miss at least four months with a plantar plate tear in his left great toe that required surgery. Newell was averaging 3.6 points and 2.6 rebounds in 11 minutes per game in five appearances this season.

#2970. If Stocks Tumble, History Says Investors Who Own This 1 Type of Stock Lose About Half as Much as Those Who Don’t.

In market drawdowns of 10% or more since 1973, dividend payers fell about half as much as non-payers. Here's the data and how to use it.

By Matt DiLallo – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:03AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.02%) fell 4.4% on Nov. 5, its worst day since April 2025. It was another reminder of how quickly stocks can tumble.

However, when stocks fall, not all tumble as much. Research from Hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data, shows that since 1973 the stocks that held up better in big declines have been dividend payers. In market drawdowns of 10% or more, dividend-paying stocks fell 14.4%, versus 28.2% for non-dividend-paying stocks. That's about half as much.

Here is what to look for in a dividend stock to help cushion the blow of a future stock market slump.

Hartford Fund's analysis covers every S&P 500 drawdown of 10% or more from 1973 through 2025. In those periods, dividend-paying stocks fell an average of 14.4%. The equal-weighted S&P 500, a good proxy for the average stock, fell 19%. Meanwhile, stocks that didn't pay dividends tumbled 28.2%.

In other words, dividend payers lost about half as much as non-payers during a stock market correction. While they still lost money, they helped preserve more wealth during a market downdraft.

Hartford suggested two reasons why dividend stocks tend to hold up much better than non-payers during a market downturn. Many dividend stocks tend to be concentrated in industries less sensitive to the economic cycle. For example, most consumer staples and utility stocks pay dividends because companies in these industries generate stable cash flow due to resilient demand.

Additionally, a company typically needs to have a track record of profitability and relatively predictable cash flow before it initiates a dividend. That business maturity would also make a company's stock price less volatile.

While dividend payers have historically delivered higher total returns with less volatility than non-payers, one group of dividend stocks stood out from the pack:

Companies that grew their dividends outperformed the average dividend stock and had lower volatility. Companies that cut or eliminated theirs lost money on average, with the most volatility of any group.

Hartford also found that the highest yields haven't been the best bet. Since 1930, stocks with the highest payout ratios (which typically have the highest yields) outperformed the market about half the time, similar to companies with much lower payout ratios. However, the sweet spot was companies with an average dividend payout ratio of 49%. These companies prioritized dividend payments while maintaining plenty of flexibility to continue growing their dividends even during more challenging times.

Those results point to a few simple ways to put the data to work before the next pullback.

While dividend stocks have historically helped cushion the blow during downturns, that doesn't guarantee they will outperform during the next one. For example, S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats® (the term Dividend Aristocrats® is a registered trademark of Standard & Poor's Financial Services LLC) -- S&P 500 members with 25 or more years of annual dividend increases -- outperformed the market during the dot-com crash and global financial crisis. However, they underperformed during the COVID crash.

Further, weaker companies tend to cut their dividends during periods of market stress. As we saw before, dividend cutters and eliminators have historically delivered negative total returns. That's why it's important to check a company's dividend payout ratio to ensure it has plenty of cushion to weather a market downturn.

When stocks tumble, history shows dividend payers tend to fall about half as far as stocks that don't pay dividends, and dividend growers have done even better over time. It's a cushion, not a guarantee. If you're worried about a potential pullback, lean toward investing in companies with growing, well-covered dividends rather than non-payers and those with the highest yields.

The Dallas Cowboys lost a game to the San Francisco 49ers. That's not a shocker to anyone, as this Cowboys team has struggled all season, and the 49ers are the best team they've played so far, and by a good margin. Looking at their opponents, San Francisco is the only offense the Cowboys have faced this year that is ranked in the top eight in scoring, now averaging over 31 points a game. In fact, the Cowboys haven't fared well against offenses that average over 22 points a game.

They've played five teams that average more than 22 points/game. Their record against those teams is 1-4.

They've played five teams that average fewer than 22 points/game. Their record against those teams is 3-2.

Clearly, playing decent offenses is not ideal for this Cowboys defense, so when they faced the NFC's highest-scoring offense, it was a huge problem for a unit that has struggled immensely all season. Even so, it shouldn't have been that bad. The defense gave up 584 total yards on the day. It was the most yards they have ever given up at home during their 67-year existence. The most ever is never good.

The frustrating part about this game is that when you take a closer look, it's easy to tell that the Cowboys never had a shot. The defense was just outmatched. It was like playing one of those games where you play against an older sibling, where they might toy around with you for a bit, only to flatten you when it's time to get serious.

The 49ers did that to the Cowboys' defense. That doesn't mean they were playing opossum at any point during the game. It's just that whenever the 49ers found themselves in a crunch, they always had a go-to play where they knew they could take advantage of the Cowboys' vulnerabilities.

The Cowboys had several defensive breakdowns in the game, with multiple third-down letdowns and explosive plays. One of the most embarrassing plays came on the Deebo Samuel reverse play in the third quarter. When fullback Kyle Juszczyk went in motion, the entire defense was lured into a trance. Follow the Juice because that's where the action goes most of the time. Only this time, the Juice wasn't worth the squeeze.

Sadly, the entire defense took the bait. It was crazy to see how many defenders continued chasing running back Kaelon Black. That left an entourage of blockers out in front of Samuel, leaving very little chance for the Cowboys to make a stop. Malik Hooker and Shemar James were the first to figure it out, but they were so far out of position that by the time they caught up, they were left gambling and taking poor angles. Cornerback Joey Porter Jr. was the last hope. He's not the greatest tackler as it is, but he's even worse when he's washed out by multiple blockers.

In our game preview article, we mentioned that "Shanahanigans" would be an issue due to the Cowboys' over-pursuing nature, and right on cue, they obliged. It was one of the poorest-defended reverse plays we've seen.

Mental lapses are common for this defense, but more frustrating is when their effort is so lackadaisical. The touchdown run by the rookie Black was horrible for different reasons. It starts with Juice looping around with banana motion. He and wide receiver Jordan Watkins take on the outside defenders, leaving a nice hole for Black to run through. With no defenders to impede his path, Black gets a full head of steam and commits some terrible Big 10 rookie-on-rookie crime by running over Caleb Downs.

Yes, that's the Cowboys' top draft pick being leveled, but in fairness to Downs, he squared up well. It's just hard to defy physics when the running back comes plowing through with that much force.

The rest of the Cowboys' defense is sealed off from clever run-blocking that creeps to the second level. Cornerback Cobie Durant has one final chance to bring him down, but he gets run over like he's not even there. It wouldn't be a Cowboys game without a humiliating run-stop attempt against a team's backup running back.

Getting their playmakers in space was the name of the game for the 49ers, and they did it often. They just meandered off to one side, got the defense to cha-cha-cha in that direction, and then boom, sealed off! On the quick pass to Samuel, the Cowboys' defense was so out of position that their lone, helpless cornerback wasn't even able to get a hand on him.

And then there were the two long touchdown passes to Christian McCaffrey. To be fair, McCaffrey is a handful all of the time, so game planning for him isn't easy. The first touchdown catch was especially hard because the defense actually played well for 90% of the play. It was just hanging on for that last 10% that got them in trouble. McCaffrey was a sneaky sneakerton and, at the last second, leaked out into the secondary, and as soon as Brock Purdy saw that, it was over.

The second touchdown was a harder pill to swallow for a couple of reasons. First, it essentially iced the game. Any hopes of a comeback were crushed. Second, in the defense's biggest moment, they were once again escorted out of the play. It was a simple play for the 49ers, with all their receivers basically running away from where McCaffrey was, taking the defense with them. It was like Moses parting the Red Sea, only Kyle Shanahan was holding the staff, and it was the Cowboys' defense that opened up for the easiest pitch-and-catch you'll ever see.

The Cowboys' defense has been a problem all season, and the 49ers exploited every element of it. The same things keep happening, and they aren't showing any sign of improvement. And it's not going to get any easier with four of their final five games against offenses averaging over 22 points a game. This defense has fallen into troubling times with very little chance of escape.

#2965. Your AI Roadmap Is Really A Planning Problem

Monisha Somji | Senior Digital Transformation & AI Executive.

Walk into almost any large enterprise today, and you will find AI everywhere: copilots in the inbox, pilots in every function, a steering committee or two. Yet the financial results rarely match the activity.

In my experience, the pattern is consistent. The demo works, the pilot succeeds and the initiative stalls anyway because nobody owns the step between a working prototype and a changed way of working.

The data agrees. McKinsey’s latest global survey found that 88% of organizations now use AI in at least one business function, but only 39% report any enterprise-level EBIT impact, and just 6% qualify as “high performers.” Gartner predicts that “over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls.”

The usual explanation is that the technology is not ready or that employees need more training. Having led digital transformation and product programs across technology, retail and mobility, I see a different culprit: the planning and funding machinery wrapped around the model.

Across industries, leaders often avoid saying out loud that this is a leadership problem, not a technology problem. Pilots are popular because they are politically safe. They let every executive show AI progress without consolidating a team, giving up a budget or killing a sponsored project. Redesigning a workflow forces decisions about who owns it, who loses control of it and what stops.

Those decisions are hard because incentives point the other way. Leaders are rewarded for launching initiatives, not retiring them. Budgets belong to functions, not workflows, so no one gains by consolidating. Risk teams are measured on avoiding incidents, so they review late and cautiously. Everyone behaves rationally inside a system that quietly rewards the wrong thing.

Most large organizations still run on annual budgets, quarterly planning and intake queues designed for software that ships a few times a year. AI capabilities shift in months. A use case approved in one cycle can reach production two cycles later on a model already a generation behind.

That is why McKinsey’s research keeps landing in the same place. Of the 25 organizational attributes it tested against EBIT impact, workflow redesign had the strongest effect. The companies capturing value are not adding a tool to an old process. They are rebuilding the process.​

Every function runs its own AI queue, with its own vendors and its own definition of success. It is common to find three teams funding near-identical summarization tools from three vendors, each unaware of the others, until a budget review puts the requests side by side.

A pilot gets a budget and a deadline. When the money ends, the initiative ends, whether or not it worked. Pilots routinely hit their targets and still die because the funding line closes the same quarter the results arrive and no one owns the workflow they were meant to change.

Consolidate the front door. Create one intake and prioritization path for AI work, shared by product, technology and the business. One view of demand makes it possible to sequence work, reuse components and kill duplicates early.​

The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by whoever licenses the most capable model, because those models will be available to everyone. It will be won by organizations that decide quickly, fund the right workflows, govern as they build and change how work actually gets done.
