#2963. Datadog vs. Figma: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Datadog and Figma pull in opposite directions, one with real profits and one with rapid growth, and the valuation gap may be the deciding factor.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 9:20AM EST

As cloud complexity grows and digital design becomes more collaborative, choosing the right software platform is essential. Investors must weigh whether Datadog Inc. (DDOG +0.51%) or Figma Inc. (FIG -0.30%) provides the better long-term opportunity.

Datadog focuses on observability and security, helping companies monitor their cloud infrastructure and applications. Figma provides a collaborative platform for teams to design and build digital products together. Both companies have become staples in the software ecosystem, but they navigate different market dynamics and financial stages as they look toward 2027.

Datadog sells an AI-powered observability and security platform to organizations of all sizes. The company is a key player among tech stocks, offering tools that monitor infrastructure, logs, and data. It serves approximately 32,700 customers across more than 160 countries and maintains over 1,000 integrations to support various IT environments.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $4.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 33.2%. The company reported net income of roughly $262.0 million during this time, resulting in a net margin of about 6.1%. This profitability marks a steady progression as the business scales its suite of cloud-native services.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.4x. This measures the company's total debt against its shareholder equity. The current ratio is 3.4x, indicating the company can comfortably cover its short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached about $1.0 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 71.5% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Figma provides a collaborative design platform used by global product teams to build digital interfaces. Roughly 85% of its monthly active users are outside the U.S., with India serving as its second-largest market. In its latest annual report, the company noted it moved to an administrator-controlled provisioning model to streamline enterprise adoption and manage complex procurement requirements.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $1.4 billion, reflecting growth of roughly 44.4%. However, the company reported a net loss of about $562.5 million for the period, with a net margin of approximately -40.2%. These figures show a company prioritizing rapid expansion and AI investment over immediate profitability.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x. The current ratio is 2.6x, demonstrating a healthy ability to meet its near-term financial commitments. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $246.2 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 544.2% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

Datadog faces intense competition from established technology companies like Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -0.55%), open-source solutions, and native tools from cloud providers. It also competes with specialized rivals such as Dynatrace (DT +1.96%) and Cisco Systems (CSCO +0.35%). The company's reputation depends on protecting against cyber-attacks and data breaches. Rapid expansion into international markets adds risks from complex local regulations, while its reliance on Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +1.98%) for cloud infrastructure presents ongoing operational challenges.

Figma relies heavily on the successful adoption of its AI-powered features, though these investments currently pressure operating margins. The company faces stiff competition from design suites like Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE -1.78%) and emerging AI-native tools. Its reliance on Amazon for hosting its platform exposes it to risks of service outages. Additionally, recent shifts in billing models, including the transition to AI credit-based pricing, risk customer dissatisfaction and create challenges in maintaining high retention rates.

Figma appears cheaper than Datadog based on its P/S ratio, measuring value against sales over the past twelve months, and its Forward P/E.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Datadog is fast-growing, with revenue expected by Wall Street analysts to jump more than 31% to $4.47 billion in fiscal 2026, and net income to nearly double to more than $203 million. Yet there is some customer concentration risk. It is believed OpenAI is Datadog's largest customer, accounting for more than $100 million--perhaps well more--according to various analyst reports. There are also vague concerns that AI could develop tools that can replace Datadog's services, but that is a general concern for just about any software provider these days.

The good news is Datadog usage continues to increase with both new and established customers. Spending by its largest customer group is rising, with the number of customers providing annual recurring revenue of more than $100,000 accelerating, up about 20% in the third quarter compared to the year-ago period. That cohort rose 23% in the second quarter. Demand seems broad-based across both its AI and non-AI customers. Revenue growth from its non-AI customers climbed meaningfully, too, signaling a ramp in its enterprise segment.

Figma, meanwhile, has seen its user experience design solution become the industry standard for digital asset and mobile application development. The company uses this niche dominance to introduce additional modules, helping transform it from a single-point solution into a full design platform.

One differentiator from competitors is that Figma has done an excellent job not only presenting itself to developers, but to marketers and product managers who have to collaborate on designs. That gives the company more champions in an organization for its products.

For the current fiscal year, revenue should grow quickly, at about a 40% rate, to $1.49 billion. Look for a dramatic reduction in its net loss, from nearly $1.3 billion to about $490 million. Wall Street still sees similarly sized losses ahead for the foreseeable future, however.

So which cloud tech stock is the better buy? Datadog registers profit, which can sometimes be an overlooked metric for tech stocks. It comes at a growth stock premium, but rising sales and net income suggest Datadog can keep the momentum going through 2027 and beyond.

#2962. Preparing For Changing ABA CPT Codes In 2027

Juan Pablo Montoya is Founder and CEO of Solum Health, which automates insurance verification and prior authorization with AI.

When a code set changes, the first thing practice owners ask me is which codes are new. I understand why, but it’s the wrong place to start. A new code can’t really hurt you because your billing system has never seen it and will say so. Deleted codes are also noisy since the claim usually bounces within days.

What hurts is a code that keeps its number and changes what it means. That claim goes out clean, and you find out weeks later from a denial or an auditor’s question nobody on the team can answer.​

On January 1, 2027, applied behavior analysis gets that kind of change. Speech therapy gets a big dose of the other kind.​

The ABA Coding Coalition’s crosswalk spells out the ABA CPT code changes: six new codes, revised descriptors for 97151 through 97158 and two Category III codes deleted. The change that matters is 97155. Under the 2019 descriptors, it covered protocol modification by the behavior analyst, with or without directing a technician, so it was where the analyst’s own hands-on treatment got billed. Beginning in January, it will mean the analyst directing a technician, and the analyst’s direct treatment will get its own code (97173).​

In speech, 92507 is deleted on January 1. ASHA described 10 replacements across five clinical categories, each built as a base code for the first 30 minutes plus an add-on for every additional 15 minutes. The group code, 92508, is revised into a stand-alone code. Outside Medicare, each payer decides when to add the new codes to its fee schedule.​

This is a data problem before it’s a billing problem. If your system treats a CPT code as a plain label, “97155” in July and “97155” in January are the same string, and nothing downstream knows they describe different work. A code is really a definition with a start date. An authorization approved under last year’s definition doesn’t carry over to this year’s on its own.​

The timing makes it worse. Most ABA authorizations I see run six months, so almost anything approved since midsummer will still be open in January. Those approvals funded 97155 hours that belong to two different codes from January 1, and unless the payer says otherwise in writing, the authorization won’t tell you how to split them.

The claim to worry about is the one that pays. If an analyst keeps billing hands-on treatment as 97155 out of habit, it matches the old authorization and goes through, and it stays wrong until someone reads it against the 2027 definition. The speech authorizations I see are usually written as a number of 92507 visits, which in January becomes a count of visits for a code that no longer exists.​

Don’t expect payer reporting to flag any of this for you. The largest Medicaid-managed care insurers denied 14% of standard prior authorization requests in 2025, and the published figures can’t show which services those were. If the cutover produces a run of mismatches, you’ll see it in your own data or not at all.​

This should be a single query: every authorization ending after December 31 that references 97151 through 97158, 0362T, 0373T, 92507 or 92508. If it turns into a week of opening PDFs and reading notes fields, that’s your real finding.​

Your code table needs start and end dates, so a December session is read against the 2026 definition and a January session against the 2027 one. Keep last year’s descriptors instead of overwriting them because sooner or later, someone will ask you to justify a 2026 claim. Load the crosswalk as reference data that your claim logic actually reads.​

HIPAA-covered payers must accept code sets valid on the date of service, but each one decides when it will cover, price and authorize the new codes. For a stretch, one payer may have 97173 loaded and priced while another hasn’t, so your system needs to know which payers have moved. Ask each one, in writing, how it will treat authorizations that cross January 1.​

Splitting an authorization between technician direction and the analyst’s own treatment is a clinical call. Your behavior analysts have to make it, and the payer has to amend the authorization to match, ideally before the first January session.

While you’re asking, consider whether you also need the new code for non-face-to-face analyst work, 97180, which no 2026 authorization could have listed. For speech teams, the equivalent job is turning approved visits into base and add-on units.​

Set up a weekly view of rejections, denials and authorization mismatches on every new and revised code, and keep it running through February. Put paid 97155 claims in that view, too. Nobody reviews claims that paid, which is exactly where the habitual billing errors will sit.​

Most of January’s coding problems will announce themselves with a rejection. The expensive one won’t; it’ll be a familiar number on an authorization you approved months ago now describing different work. I’d treat the cutover as a data migration rather than a coding update, and I’d start that inventory now while payers still have time to process amendments.​

#2961. Is Palantir Overvalued, or Is It Still a Buy at This Price?

Palantir trades at a high P/E ratio, but investors need to factor the company's expected growth into the equation before jumping to conclusions.

By Will Healy – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:22AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Palantir Technologies ›

Palantir (PLTR -0.41%) has attracted considerable attention among businesses and investors alike in recent years. Its data analytics tools have driven eye-popping productivity gains for its clients. As such, interest in its products has soared, and annual revenue growth is approaching triple-digit percentages.

Unfortunately, this has also drawn attention to its valuation, as rapid revenue growth typically means a stock will trade at a considerable premium. Despite its impressive revenue growth, I believe Palantir stock is overvalued. Here's why.

Palantir began as a company focused on supporting national defense and intelligence agencies. Its tools employ artificial intelligence to analyze data and deliver insights. In its early days, the help it provided to U.S. intelligence services in finding Osama bin Laden gained the company considerable attention.

However, seeing the limits of growth within that field, it turned its expertise to the commercial sector. While that broadening of its customer base led to increased growth, it was the release of its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) that was the game changer.

Palantir began offering potential customers the opportunity to enroll in “boot camps” where they were able to immediately see how AIP could be applied to their actual business problems, and as a result, many of its clients began to discover ways to use it to noticeably increase productivity.

Among these companies is GE Aerospace, which applied AIP to fleet management and supply chain coordination, thereby increasing engine production. AIP also helped AIG automate insurance underwriting for more complicated commercial lines of business.

Such improvements helped drive Palantir’s revenue to nearly $5.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 92% from the prior-year period, with a blowout Q3 boosting that growth.

Moreover, since its costs and expenses grew more slowly than revenue, its net income was nearly $3.1 billion during the same period. That was a 201% year-over-year increase. Amid this performance, it is not too surprising that Palantir stock is up by more than 2,300% since the beginning of 2023.

For 2026, revenue will grow 91% if the company's forecasts hold. However, analysts predict that growth will slow to 53% in 2027.

Even though a 53% yearly revenue increase is still impressive, investors tend to frown on slowing growth. That could bode poorly for Palantir, particularly given its lofty valuation.

Palantir now trades at 110 times trailing earnings. Moreover, its forward P/E ratio of 92 is similarly pricey. When also considering the forward 1-year P/E ratio of 62, these metrics suggest Palantir's stock price has years of expected growth already baked into it.

However, as high as these numbers sound, they also offer some hope to investors. The current stock price is around $165 per share as of this writing, a level it first reached in August 2025.

At that time, its P/E ratio stood at 575, while its forward P/E and forward 1-year P/E were 239 and 102, respectively. Over the past year or so, its valuation ratios have eased down to somewhat more reasonable levels.

That may not bode well for near-term stock price gains, though, since its valuations remain high and the stock has been essentially trading sideways for 15 months. On the other hand, Palantir's rapid revenue growth and rising profitability dramatically reduce the odds of this SaaS stock suffering a steep correction, suggesting it is more of a hold than a sell.

Based on Palantir's financial metrics, the stock is overvalued, but that does not mean investors should necessarily dismiss it as a potential portfolio holding.

Its stock price growth in recent years stemmed from the company’s ability to deliver palpable productivity gains to its customers. That has led to massive revenue growth that prompted investors to bid the shares up to high valuations.

Fortunately, Palantir's valuation has contracted somewhat in the past year. Since rapid revenue and profit growth have persisted, the stock offers current shareholders good reason to hold while also suggesting that future investors could buy at a lower premium. These factors alone make Palantir a stock that investors should continue to watch.

#2958. The 5% Redesigned The Work First; The 60% Got Nothing Back

Manu Khetan is Founder and CEO of Rolling Arrays, a LinkedIn ‘Top Voice’ Influencer and Creator of the R7 Framework.

​The most common thing a CEO says to me about AI this year is some version of the same sentence: We invested, and we cannot find the return.

In 2025, BCG put a number on that feeling. It surveyed 1,250 senior executives across 68 countries and nine industries. About 60% of companies reported no material value at all from AI, despite substantial investment. Around 35% are scaling. About 5% are getting value at scale. Note what is being counted: companies, not pilots.

Most boards read that and blame the models. BCG’s own reading points somewhere else. The firms getting value, it says, “go well beyond automation and incremental productivity improvements to reshape current workflows and invent new ones.”

They redesigned the work first, and brought the agent to the redesigned work.

BCG describes what the winners do. What the 60% did is my own reading, from 17 years inside enterprise workforces and from every AI budget I have watched up close, and I want it labeled as mine rather than as something the survey says. In those rooms, the pattern is consistent. They bought agents and left the work exactly as it was.

The ones who got something back did the unglamorous thing first. They took a process apart, decided which tasks should stay human, redesigned what was left and only then went shopping.

The public cases show the same order of operations. Octopus Energy has AI answering customer emails at a workload of around 250 people, with satisfaction higher than on the human-handled queue, 80 against 65. JPMorgan’s COIN took roughly 360,000 hours a year of document review off the desk, and that was nearly a decade ago.

IKEA is the one I keep coming back to. AI-powered chatbot “Billie” absorbed about 47% of inbound customer inquiries, over 3 million conversations. Billie’s savings over two years came to around 13 million euros. Then they retrained roughly 8,500 call-center workers into remote interior-design advisors, and that remote channel sold about 1.3 billion euros in the 2022 financial year.

Those two figures measure different things, a year of sales against two years of savings, so they are not a ratio. But nobody builds a billion-euro channel by shopping for agents.

Every AI budget I see falls into one of four patterns.

Redesigners are the 5%. They cut the work, not the people, and the people who stayed moved into work worth more than what left. IKEA is the archetype.

Reversers automated the moments their customers needed a human, paid for it in quality and corrected course. Klarna did this in public, which took some courage.

Experimenters are most of the 60%. Pilots everywhere, nothing at scale, a conclusion that AI is overhyped. Their skepticism is accurate about their own deployments and wrong about the frontier.

Installers take the output, and the humans simply exit. Output up, humans out. It is proof of power, not of governance, and I will come back to what it costs in Part 5.​

We run a 400-person business across six countries, and we are adopting AI as we speak, so I am doing this while also advising on it. The order was harder to follow than to describe.

Our delivery work runs through 18 roles, three ladders of six, from associate to director, and like every professional services firm, we allocated it by asking who could do it. That habit was the first thing in the way because real people sat in those roles, and we couldn’t cut them into tasks.

What unlocked it was stopping looking at the roles and starting to look at the client’s work. In a services firm, the work is defined the day the contract is signed. It lives in the scope. Read task by task, asking what kind of work each is—physical, cognitive or relational—and who should own it: execution, judgment or trust; it could be cut without anyone’s job title in the room. Cognitive execution became a candidate for agents. What stayed human became the new roles.

Mindset is the second thing in the way. The instinct is still to ask who fills the integration consultant slot, not what the work is. Hiring is where we are weakest. The new roles concentrate judgment, client relationship and accountability and need less of the configuration depth we used to interview for. The job descriptions changed faster than the interviews did. What helped more than I expected is a framework to teach, not a slogan to repeat. A grid people can apply to their own tasks gets you arguments, then adoption, slowly.

I am not going to tell you that puts us in the 5%. That is a result, and you don’t get to announce a result on the day you decide to go after it. Don’t buy an agent before you know where the work lives, and don’t hand it whatever it can take and leave the rest to roles designed for humans. Cut the work, not the people.

Whether AI is good enough is not the question, or rather, it is a question with no general answer. It gets asked task by task and only about today.

The question that separates the four patterns is different. Ask which of them you are funding. Then ask the harder version. Take the last AI investment your board approved and find the work that changed shape because of it. Not the tool that got installed. The work. If a process looks exactly as it did before, only faster in one spot, you have bought a tool and kept a workflow, and the 60% is where that lands.

And it points to a sharper money question: If the winners were not buying salary savings, what exactly should the agent dollar buy, especially if agents keep getting more expensive rather than cheaper? That is Part 4.​​​

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

#2957. Nick Bosa’s shocking drought comes with a 49ers silver lining

The San Francisco 49ers hold an 8-1 record, the best in the NFC, and yet they still haven't gotten quite the same type of production out of Nick Bosa that they're accustomed to.

NBC Sports Bay Area 49ers insider Matt Maiocco was asked if Bosa would ever be productive again and provided his insight on why he's a key contributor to the 49ers' pass rush.

"Nick Bosa does not have a sack in the four games he has played this season. Never before has he gone four consecutive games in the same season without a sack since coming into the NFL in 2019," Maiocco said.

San Francisco 49ers edge rusher Nick Bosa during team warmups at AT&T Stadium. Getty Images

Since Week 2 of last year, Bosa has missed an extensive amount of time dealing with a torn ACL last season and a calf injury this year.

Maiocco added that Bosa not being able to participate in training camp this past summer put him behind the rest of his teammates, and then when he was cleared to play again, he played in two games, and then strained his calf.

Bosa returned two weeks ago against the Raiders and recorded one tackle. He played 57 snaps against the Cowboys last Sunday, finishing without a tackle but registering a quarterback hit.

Nick Bosa coming out of the tunnel before an NFL game against the Cowboys. Getty Images

Maiocco added that Bosa is still winning despite the longest drought of his career.

"Bosa leads the 49ers' defensive line with a pass-rush win rate of 16.7 percent. That is down from past seasons, when he typically is around a 20 percent figure," Maiocco said.

On Monday, 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan appeared on a conference call that included Maiocco, and he was asked if he was worried about Bosa and told reporters, "I'm not worried about Nick."

"Nick is going to get better each week, and he'll eventually get there," Shanahan said.

While San Francisco is waiting for Bosa to reform himself, the 49ers defense can be patient.

Nick Bosa attempting to tackle Raiders tight end Michael Mayer. Getty Images

The 49ers rank second in the NFL in run defense, allowing 82.6 rushing yards per game. They're also giving up an average of 21.8 points per game.

Their pass rush has been inconsistent, especially Sunday, when the 49ers managed just one sack of Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott, who threw for 343 yards and five touchdowns.

The 49ers are tied with the Eagles for 30th in the NFL with 16 sacks, underscoring their struggles to get after opposing quarterbacks.

Perhaps if Bosa can get back to his old self soon, he could give the 49ers' pass rush the jolt that they desperately need.

#2955. If You'd Invested $1,000 in Berkshire Hathaway (BRKB) Stock 20 Years Ago, Here's How Much You'd Have Today

Spoiler: Your stake would have grown impressively -- and at a slower rate than the stock has grown in the past.

By Selena Maranjian – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:35AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Just about all of us know that Warren Buffett is one of the greatest investors ever, and many of us are familiar with the company he built into a trillion-dollar enterprise -- Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -1.02%) (BRKB -0.98%). He grew the company's value by nearly 20% annually over some 60 years!

Let's say you parked a modest $1,000 in Berkshire Hathaway 20 years ago. What would it be worth today? Well, the answer is $8,310. The shares would have been trading for around $71.29 per share in November 2006, and more recently, they've been around $590 apiece. That's a total gain of 732%, and an annualized one of 11.16% (which still tops the S&P 500's average of 9.3% over the same period).

Whenever I report these kinds of numbers, I like to include reinvested dividends. Berkshire is not a dividend-paying stock at this point, as its leaders have preferred to plow excess earnings into furthering its growth -- and they've occasionally repurchased some shares, too. The S&P 500 does feature dividends, though, and with dividends reinvested over 20 years, its average annual gain would come to 10.6% -- still below Berkshire's gain, but not by a lot.

Multiplying your investment's value eightfold is pretty great. Can you expect that kind of growth over the next 20 years with Berkshire? Well, maybe. I certainly wouldn't count on average annual gains of 20% or more, as the company has delivered in the past -- because it can be especially hard for really large companies to grow.

But Berkshire is built to last, and features a lot of diversification. It owns many businesses in the insurance, energy, transportation, and manufacturing sectors, among others, and has a large portfolio of stocks, too. It's reasonable to hope or expect it to surpass the S&P 500's performance over the long run.

#2951. Coca-Cola vs. Monster Beverage: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Coca-Cola's global scale and steady bottler network go head-to-head with Monster's 20% revenue surge, but the valuation gap may settle the debate.

By Jake Lerch – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 9:45AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›

Investors often choose between established dividend stability and high-octane growth. Choosing between Coca-Cola (KO -0.85%)and Monster Beverage (MNST +1.87%)involves weighing a massive global powerhouse against a rapidly expanding energy drink leader.

While both companies operate in the same broader industry, they serve very different market needs. Coca-Cola offers a diversified portfolio of sodas and juices, while Monster Beverage specializes in the high-growth energy category. This comparison examines their financial health and risk profiles to help you decide which is better.

Coca-Cola sells brands like Sprite, Fanta, and its namesake cola through a vast network of independent bottling partners and retailers in over 200 countries. One significant bottler accounts for nearly 10% of net operating revenues. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. The company also manages the dairy subsidiary, fairlife, LLC, and maintains an equity investment in Monster Beverage to expand its reach.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 2, 2026, revenue reached approximately $51.1 billion, representing growth of nearly 7.1% over the prior year. Net income for the same period was roughly $14.6 billion. This growth reflects a steady recovery and pricing power in global markets despite varying economic conditions across its geographic segments.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.5x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio is roughly 1.5x, indicating its ability to cover short-term liabilities with current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $5.3 billion, reinforcing its position among beverage stocks.

Monster Beverage develops and sells energy drinks, including Reign and NOS, and relies heavily on the Coca-Cola distribution network to reach 158 countries. Its primary customers include Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP -0.21%)and Coca-Cola Consolidated (COKE -1.04%), which account for roughly 15% and 10% of net sales, respectively. Such concentration adds a layer of risk to the business, as these two partners account for a significant share of distribution.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $9.6 billion, a significant growth of nearly 20.2% compared to the previous year. Net income for this period was roughly $2.2 billion. This expansion highlights the increasing consumer appetite for energy beverages and the company's ability to successfully scale its brands globally.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x, indicating it has no total debt relative to its equity. The current ratio is approximately 3.7x, suggesting a very strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $2.0 billion. This financial flexibility allows for continued reinvestment into new product lines.

Coca-Cola faces pressure from global economic volatility and geopolitical instability that can disrupt its complex supply chain. The company must navigate intense competition from rivals such as PepsiCo (PEP +0.02%)and Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP +1.06%). Additionally, it manages ongoing tax litigation with the IRS and regulatory scrutiny regarding sugar-sweetened beverage taxes and environmental impacts of packaging.

Monster Beverage is vulnerable to category-specific regulations, such as potential age restrictions or limits on caffeine content in energy drinks. The company relies heavily on the Coca-Cola distribution system, meaning any strategic shift by its partner could impact market access. Furthermore, it faces increasing competition from nimble competitors such as Celsius Holdings (CELH +6.38%)and rising costs for raw materials like aluminum.

Monster Beverage carries a higher Forward P/E and P/S ratio, which divides market cap by sales over the past twelve months, than Coca-Cola.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

When comparing Coca-Cola and Monster Beverage, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.

Firstly, we should consider revenue growth. In this category, Monster gains a real edge. Over the last three years, it has averaged 11.8% year-over-year revenue growth, while Coca-Cola has averaged about 4.9%. Moreover, in recent quarters, Monster's revenue growth has surged well above its average, clocking in at 16.7% in its most recent quarter. Coca-Cola has also delivered above-average revenue growth, at 7% in its most recent report.

Another factor to consider is each company's profitability. Over the last 10 years, Coca-Cola has had an average operating margin of 27.1%, while Monster's was 31.7%, seemingly giving Monster the edge here. However, in recent years, Monster's profitability has drifted lower, while Coca-Cola's has increased. In fact, Coca-Cola has now overtaken Monster. Coca-Cola's operating margin is now 32.1%, while Monster's has fallen to 28.5%, giving Coca-Cola an advantage in this category.

Finally, there's valuation. Since both companies are profitable, it makes sense to compare their price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples. Coca-Cola has a P/E multiple of 29x, while Monster's is 40x. That gives Coca-Cola another edge, as its stock is more affordable.

To sum up, investors may want to consider both of these consumer stocks. However, given its more reasonable valuation and its higher profitability, Coca-Cola wins the battle between these two beverage giants, in my opinion. Nevertheless, given its impressive revenue growth, solid profitability, and reasonable valuation, Monster also remains a stock worth considering.

#2949. IonQ Stock Plunged 48% in Six Months. Is It a Bargain Buy?

A sharp share price decline doesn't always equal a bargain.

By Chris Neiger – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:47AM EST

Shares of IonQ (IONQ +0.20%) are down about 48% over the past six months as investors have headed for the exits amid worries the company is spending too much on acquisitions and raising too much capital at the expense of existing shareholder value.

IonQ has always been a speculative bet on an unproven market — quantum computing — but some investors may wonder whether the recent share price pullback makes IonQ stock a bargain right now.

Unfortunately, even with the recent drop, its shares still aren't in the bargain bin. Here's why investors are betting on IonQ, what the company has going for it, and why IonQ stock still isn't a good deal.

The biggest reason for IonQ's recent share price drop was the October announcement that the company would acquire Elisity, a zero-trust cybersecurity company. IonQ said it would make the $1.2 billion acquisition in an all-stock deal, diluting existing shareholders.

IonQ announced just a few days later that it was holding a $2 billion equity offering, cementing investors' concerns about share dilution. By the end of the month, IonQ's stock was down 31%.

This decline came months after IonQ's shares tumbled over the summer as investors fled riskier tech stocks. The AI trade came under pressure during that time as investors questioned the hundreds of billions of dollars tech companies are investing in data centers, and some of the negative sentiment spilled over into quantum computing stocks.

The result was a near-meltdown of IonQ's stock, pushing it down 48% since June.

It's not all bad news for IonQ. The company has a unique edge in the quantum computing space with its trapped-ion technology helping to reduce error rates (a major problem for quantum computers), and its revenue is climbing.

Sales jumped 336% to nearly $174 million in Q3 2026, and management recently raised its full-year guidance to $510 million, at the midpoint. The company also said it has an impressive backlog of $1.2 billion.

IonQ also has $3.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents, so there's no real concern about the company's ability to keep the lights on for the next few years.

There are two simple reasons the stock isn't a bargain: The company remains highly unprofitable, and its shares still look expensive despite the recent drop.

IonQ's operating losses were $433 million in Q3, and its trailing free cash flow was a negative $689 million. It's worth noting that while the company reported a GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) net profit of $564 million in Q3 2026, management said this was due to an $896 million non-cash accounting gain from warrant revaluations rather than operational profitability.

IonQ CFO Inder Singh said on the latest earnings call that the company is thinking about profitability, but it hasn't publicly estimated when that will occur. "Now that we are moving forward toward potentially being the first quantum company to deliver $1 billion of revenue in the future, it is also time to begin to think about charting out our path to both revenue growth and profitability," Singh said.

What's more, IonQ stock is still expensive. Even after its sell-off, IonQ's shares have a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 29.6, which is far higher than the technology sector's average P/S ratio of 6.5.

That's nowhere near bargain territory for a stock, and given that IonQ won't be profitable anytime soon -- not to mention that it's betting on a very speculative quantum computing market -- investors should proceed with caution before buying this one. If you do pick up some shares right now, it's probably a good idea to add a little to your portfolio over time instead of going headfirst into a large position.

#2948. Tuesday Miami Dolphins Thoughts With The Earl

This game really depends upon your outlook for the season. If you are a "get the first draft pick at all costs" person, then you like this outcome. If you want to see a win and positive development, this was a horrible outcome. It was another of the "close, but no cigar" games the Dolphins have played this season. Here's what I saw.

In previous games, there was a tradeoff between the offense and defense over which would show up. In this game, the offense was expected to be worse than the defense, with a backup QB getting his first-ever NFL action. However, the Dolphins still couldn't go a game without some form of tradeoff. In this matchup, it was a tradeoff between the pass defense and the run defense. The Dolphins allowed a completion percentage over 70% and had a run defense that allowed less than 4 yards per carry. The pass defense had its best performance of the season. They held Danny Dimes to 50% completion and a 4.9 YPA average. They picked him off twice, one of which was returned for a TD. They allowed a passing TD and a couple of big plays but were solid in coverage. In a shock to everyone, the Dolphins allowed more rushing yards to TE Tyler Warren (3) than receiving yards (1). Warren was held without a catch until the 4th quarter and was a complete non-factor.

Unfortunately, while the Dolphins pass defense stepped up covering the one receiving threat the Colts had, the run defense couldn't stop the other threat the Colts posed. The Colts rushed for 172 yards on 34 carries, 106 of those yards coming in the 1st half on 19 carries. That's a 5.6 YPA allowed. They improved a little in the second half, allowing 66 yards on 15 carries and a 4.4 YPA. But on the final drive, they allowed 12 yards on 2 carries that finished off the game. Just once, the team needs a complete performance on both sides of the ball. Now they need a complete performance on both sides of the ball. I will give them some due credit. They limited the Colts to 17 offensive points and were hamstrung by a limited offense, but the run defense was the backbreaker in this game. With the injuries mounting on the DL, I don't know how they can fix it.

We'll get to the obvious problem in a moment. Bradley Pinion had 3 punts for 134 yards, with a 55-yarder. That's an average of 44.7 overall and 39.5 on the other two punts. Indy's punter had 6 for 290, averaging 48.3. The league average is 47.5. Miami still allowed too many yards in the kick return game. They had the 15-yard penalty on Louis, though I won't complain about penalties since the total was lopsided in Miami's favor and that penalty was ultimately inconsequential. It is still unacceptable, though.

I said on Friday that the Dolphins simply aren't good enough to win without winning in the margins. This is a young team working to find its identity. They come to work every day and put it all on the line every game. This isn't the 2024 or 2025 Dolphins with players obviously checking out and Tua laughing on the sideline or Hill taking himself out of a game. This is a bad team playing like they are trying to get the top seed in the AFC. When the kicker, the second oldest player on the team, shanks not one, but two FGs and misses a PAT as the icing on the cake, that is a level of terrible that cannot be measured. After I watched the game and went to bed thinking of all I planned to say about how he cannot remain on the team if the coaches wanna keep the locker room, the Dolphins made my job easier and waived him on Monday. So that is a non-issue now.

And I've seen the tweets about how the misses keep the tank alive and all that. But I cannot stress enough how not only is tanking a bad idea in general, but you really only tank for a QB, and the 2027 QB class is buns. They are bad. It's an elevated class due to absences and wouldn't be considered top prospects in a class like 2018 or 2020. I would love for the Dolphins to get Jeremiah Smith as much as any other fan. But this team is NOT trying to lose. They aren't playing like they are trying to lose. They are talent deficient, but they aren't tanking. So when you play as hard as they do and the veteran kicker can't do the basic requirement of putting the ball through the uprights, then a message needs to be sent, and it was.

Kyle McCord's play will be dissected by many others, so I don't want to get deep into it. I thought he played ok. I thought he played like a player getting his first NFL snaps. His performance isn't worth getting worked up over one way or another. I said in Friday's post that a healthy Willis wins this game by 2 scores, and I still believe it. But McCord played well enough for the Dolphins to get a win against another equally terrible team and was let down. The next step will be to see what, if any, level of improvements can be made.

The run game has disappeared, and it probably won't come back for a while. I tried to watch to see how much Indy loaded the box, but I didn't truly keep track. Indy is a bad team, but Miami will face some good teams coming up; teams with solid to great defenses. My guess is they will load the box and force McCord to beat them. Having Meyer in there instead of Brewer hurt as well, but the OL can only do so much. The good news for the RBs is they were involved in the passing game. All three RBs were targeted 9 times with 8 catches for 62 yards, including the 4-yard loss for Kaytron Allen. If the RBs can contribute in the pass game, then the offense can function about as normally as we can expect. Even with the drop-off, Gordon is still on pace for a 1000 yard season.

Caleb Douglas was invisible for most of the game but stepped up late. He will continue to be a force. Washington had the play of the game IMO with the one-handed catch down the sideline. He continues to improve in getting separation and being a factor in the offense. The TD throw was nice also.

The TEs were invisible, and that's a concern. I like Dulcich, and he has potential, but he is playing his way off the roster for 2027.

The passing defense stepped up as I mentioned, and its leaders are two rookies. Michael Taaffe logged his 3rd INT this season, and Chris Johnson got his 2nd in consecutive weeks. It should have been his 3rd in 4 weeks, but that Jets WR fell down and they said Johnson interfered. He was a ballhawk in college, and it is showing up now. There are 17 players in the league with 3 or more INTs and only 7 with more than 3. Taaffe has the instincts to be around the ball a lot. His development going into the rest of this season will be interesting to watch.

Regarding the kicker position, I would not be opposed to the Dolphins adding a young player – an undrafted rookie or second-year player – to fill the position. Vets are what they are, and while they offer some reliability, I'm all for giving a young player a chance to make his mark. They probably won't because, well, they are trying to win games. But if they swing and miss with young players, at least they tried. If they get a hit, that's something they can build on moving forward.

Circling back to the opening paragraph, I am not a fan of losing games for a draft pick. I want the Dolphins to win. This game was frustrating because they had it and gave it away. They lost by the margins and lost the game. Unfortunately, this was the last win on the schedule for a while. Unless McCord magically turns into Tom Brady in the next few games, the Dolphins are looking at 1-16. They host the Jets in 2 weeks, but I don't like that matchup with McCord. They host the hapless Chargers in week 16, and if Willis is back healthy, they'll have a good chance of winning. They have the 8-1 Bills and 7-2 Broncos on the road in 2 of the next 3 games. They get the 7-2 Bears and 6-4 Packers, all battling for playoff seeding and that division title. Perhaps the Bills will lock up home-field advantage by week 17, and the Dolphins will get backups. Otherwise, the outlook is grim. To paraphrase Captain Jack Sparrow: if you were waiting for the opportune moment to get a win… that was it.

We all knew this season wasn't about the wins, but 1-16 is a tough mark for anyone. Even if the Dolphins go 12-5 over the next 2 seasons (they won't), that is still 25-26 over 3 seasons. It's going to be much worse than that. It is going to be a long road back to relevance for this franchise. I'll cover that later on (either this week or next), so stay tuned.

#2946. Booking Holdings vs. MercadoLibre: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Booking's 25.5% net margin meets MercadoLibre's 47% revenue surge, but their valuation gap tells a sharper story than growth rates alone.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 9:50AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Booking Holdings ›

Investors often choose between proven global leaders and high-growth regional powerhouses. Deciding between Booking Holdings Inc. (BKNG +0.17%) and MercadoLibre Inc. (MELI +1.06%) requires weighing stable profitability against an expanding digital ecosystem in Latin America.

Booking serves the global travel market through its massive network of accommodations and flight options. MercadoLibre dominates Latin American e-commerce and digital payments, functioning as both a retailer and a bank. While both companies operate in the consumer discretionary space, they offer very different risk-reward profiles for long-term investors looking toward 2027.

Booking operates a massive network of consumer-facing brands, including Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, and OpenTable. The company focuses on its "connected trip" strategy, which aims to integrate accommodations, flights, and rental cars into a single, seamless itinerary for travelers. By managing nearly 4.7 million accommodation properties, it relies on a broad network of travel service providers that typically operate on non-exclusive terms.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $28.1 billion, representing roughly 8% growth compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of approximately $7.2 billion, reflecting a net margin of about 25.5%. This performance demonstrates the company's ability to generate significant profit while expanding its presence in the international travel market.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a negative debt-to-equity ratio of roughly -3.5x, indicating that its total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to the equity held by shareholders, measures how a business balances its obligations against its assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow, which is cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, was about $9.1 billion.

MercadoLibre operates the leading commerce and fintech ecosystem in Latin America, driven by the Mercado Libre marketplace and its Mercado Pago payment platform. As a leader among consumer discretionary stocks in its region, it relies on a vast network of third-party sellers and logistics partners. Its integrated strategy combines retail, lending, and asset management to serve over 136 million unique buyers.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $38.5 billion, marking about 47% growth over the previous period. The company reported net income of approximately $1.9 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 4.9%. This rapid top-line expansion highlights the scaling nature of its integrated digital services across major markets like Brazil and Mexico.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.7x, while the current ratio is roughly 1.2x. The current ratio measures the ability of a company to cover its short-term debts with its short-term assets, providing a view of its immediate financial health. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $10.8 billion, reflecting the strong cash generation of its marketplace and fintech platforms.

Booking faces intense global competition from other online travel agencies like Airbnb Inc. (ABNB -0.51%) and technology giants like Alphabet Inc. (GOOG +1.23%). The company depends heavily on third-party traffic sources such as search engines and faces the risk of disintermediation by artificial intelligence assistants. Furthermore, it must navigate complex legal and regulatory landscapes, particularly in the European Union where its status as a gatekeeper imposes restrictive obligations.

MercadoLibre operates in highly competitive markets where it faces pressure from global retailers like Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +1.98%) and low-price regional entrants. The business is exposed to significant macroeconomic volatility, including high inflation and currency devaluation in core markets such as Argentina and Brazil. Additionally, the company manages credit risk associated with its lending operations and faces potential cybersecurity threats across its integrated fintech and commerce services.

Booking carries a lower Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, while MercadoLibre has a lower P/S ratio which compares stock price to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

MercadoLibre has evolved from the so-called eBay of Latin America to something more akin to a combination of Amazon and PayPal Holdings Inc. (PYPL -0.79%). In 2025, the company made large investments in its Brazilian logistics network, cut down the free-shipping threshold in Brazil in June, and nearly doubled its consumer loan book. This drove impressive growth for the company and investors, with an increasing focus on financial services over delivering goods.

Yet the immediate concern with left-of-center Luis Lula winning the Brazilian presidential election last month is that the new administration will start addressing Brazil's high government and consumer debt levels, which will keep interest rates there around their current very high levels. That's bad for a consumer-loan-focused business like MercadoLibre, and shares have been hammered this week as a result.

Long-term, however, such fears are probably overblown. In fact, in the current fiscal year, revenue is expected to jump 45% to $41.9 billion, with slightly higher free cash flow and slightly lower net income. Overall, it's a good picture for MercadoLibre.

Booking Holdings is successfully shifting from an agency model to a primarily merchant model. That means it used to make its money as an agent--connecting travelers to a hotel and collecting a commission while the hotel manages collecting payment from the traveler. In the merchant model, Booking buys capacity from hotels and other providers on its platform and collects payment directly from the traveler. This tends to lead to fatter margins.

The company is also in excellent financial shape. It has $16 billion in cash, which makes its balance sheet investment grade. Another plus for shareholders is that the company has a $20 billion share buyback program. The brand is increasingly a destination for travelers, which means it is paying less to companies like Google for search engine visibility. Today, two-thirds of Booking.com's visitors are organic, meaning they are direct visitors rather than from paid ad traffic.

Revenue will grow about 9% this year to $29.3 billion. And net income takes a healthier 50% leap to about $8.1 billion.

Booking's shares are priced at a discount to the average S&P 500 stock and well below travel rival Airbnb. Yet the company provides more total sales and has good growth, expanding margins, and a pile of cash. It's too good a bargain to pass up at these prices. For 027, go with Booking Holdings

#2944. Jaylen Brown to miss 76ers game Wednesday vs. Magic due to 'hamstring strain'

The Philadelphia 76ers will take on the Orlando Magic on Wednesday night, but without star shooting guard Jaylen Brown.

He is dealing with a hamstring strain and has already been ruled out for tomorrow night's game. Brown picked up the injury during Philadelphia's win over the Brooklyn Nets on Monday.

The guard is in his first season with the 76ers after the infamous trade that sent him to Philadelphia from Boston. Brown has played in 14 games so far this season and is averaging 22.6 points, 6.6 rebounds, and 3.6 assists.

The Philadelphia guard had a slow start with his new team, scoring 19 points in his team debut. The 76ers have tried to find the best fit among Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, Brown, and free-agent signee LeBron James.

It finally seemed to be clicking for Brown ahead of the injury. He logged back-to-back games with 31 points, his season high. The guard finished Monday night's win with a double-double: 31 points and 13 rebounds. He shot just 47.4% from the field, but he made 10 of 11 attempts from the charity stripe as Philadelphia beat Brooklyn 135-123.

Without Brown in the lineup, the 76ers will likely give more minutes to Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Jabari Walker.

Wednesday's game against Orlando will be Brown's second missed game this season. He also missed Philly's first game of a back-to-back against the New York Knicks.

Brown was dealing with both a head and a hamstring injury coming out of Monday's win against Brooklyn. After the game, he said that he may have to get imaging done on Tuesday. Brown has been diagnosed with a left hamstring strain, but it remains unclear whether it will keep him out beyond Wednesday's game.

Philadelphia has the Magic, Milwaukee Bucks, Portland Trail Blazers, Miami Heat, and Indiana Pacers in its next five games.

#2943. 5E Advanced (FEAM) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Early V-BOR ramp and grid-independence plans take center stage.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:53AM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

5E Advanced (FEAM +8.12%) transitioned from a development-stage entity into an operating producer of borates and industrial minerals following the acquisition of Searles Valley Minerals on Oct. 1, 2026. Management reported that the acquisition includes three processing sites, 54 megawatts of cogeneration capacity, and established infrastructure acquired free and clear of legacy liabilities. The company is currently executing a strategy focused on commercial resets, cost optimization through grid independence, and volume recovery across its California assets. Management stated that boron's status as a critical mineral strengthens the company's strategic position as a domestic supplier to energy and defense markets.

Operator: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us today for 5E Advanced Materials Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Conference Call and Shareholder Update. During today's call, management will reference the company's quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended September 30, 2026, which is available in the Investor Relations section of the company's website and on the SEC's website. For a copy of the Form 10-Q, you may also contact PRA Communications at [email protected].

As a reminder, remarks made on today's conference call will contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including statements regarding the acquisition of the Searles Valley Minerals assets and the integration of the acquired operations, the bridge facility and promissory note entered in connection with the acquisition, the transition of customers to take-or-pay and fixed price offtake agreements, the ramp of V-BOR sales volumes and the recovery of V-BOR production towards approximately 100,000 short tons annually; the restart of the SAC plant, the restart of idle boric acid production, the well field development program, reducing reliance on purchase power and the expected cost savings, expected future results, cost, production capacity, market dynamics, capital expenditures, liquidity, cash spending, finance objectives and options, customer demand, purchase order commitments, offtake arrangements, customer qualification activities, commercialization strategy, development plans, engineering and project financing activities, including FEED-related work and the timing and scope of future engineering phases, advancement of supply chain initiatives and products, the potential benefits of our ASX delisting, the potential application of our products across energy, defense and industrial markets, government-based financing opportunities, including EXIM-related diligence, the company's ability to continue operating the small-scale facility and developing the project and the potential development of advanced boron derivative projects, including meta boric acid and ferroboron.

These statements are based on management's current expectations and involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially and adversely from those projected or discussed. Additionally, information concerning factors that could cause actual results to differ materially and adversely from these forward-looking statements is contained in our disclosures and public filings with the SEC, including our Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. The company undertakes no obligation to update forward-looking statements, except as required by law.

Today's call may also include a discussion of non-GAAP financial measures as that term is defined in Regulation G, non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered in isolation from or as a substitute for financial information presented in compliance with GAAP. This afternoon's conference call is hosted by 5E Chief Executive Officer, Paul Weibel. Management will first lead off the call by making prepared comments, after which we will open the call for your questions. I will now turn the call over to Paul. Paul?

Paul Weibel: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us today. The first quarter of fiscal year 2027 marks a defining moment for 5E Advanced Materials. On October 1, one day after quarter end, we closed our asset acquisition of Searles Valley Minerals, acquiring them free and clear of the prior owner's legacy liabilities and historical claims. With that closing, 5E transitioned from a development stage company into an operating revenue-generating producer of borates and industrial minerals. It is worth pausing on what we now own.

Searles Valley includes 3 processing sites, 54 megawatts of on-site cogeneration capacity, the Trona Railway short-line railroad, water utility, approximately 25,000 acres across 3 California counties and mineral tenure across more than 9,000 acres at Searles Lake, operated by an experienced workforce of approximately 250 people. The operation produces V-BOR, which is borax pentahydrate, sodium sulfate and salt, and it includes boric acid production capacity that is currently idled. Together with our Fort Cady project, 5E now holds 2 boron assets in Southern California at a time when boron has been added to the U.S. Department of the Interior's Critical Minerals list. We believe that positions 5E as a strategically important domestic supplier of critical minerals.

Because the acquisition closed just after quarter end, today, I want to focus on our first 5 weeks of ownership and our plan to grow the value of this platform moving forward. That plan is built on the 3 levers we laid out on our acquisition call, price, cost and volume. The focus is now on operational excellence and execution. Each one is already underway, and I will walk you through our progress. First, I'll look at our first month of operations. In October, we produced 6,200 tons of V-BOR, adding to approximately 3,000 tons of V-BOR inventory we carried into the month, and we sold approximately 2,500 tons.

We prioritized our domestic customers in October, while we build out export logistics through the Port of Long Beach. That network is now established, opening container shipments into Asia and the inventory we built in October is positioned to ship into that channel in November. With logistics in place and product on hand, we expect V-BOR sales volumes to ramp as we move through November and into December. Now to the levers starting with price. Through the bankruptcy process, the legacy below-market sales contracts were rejected. That gives us a clean slate on commercial terms, and we have transitioned customers onto new take-or-pay and fixed-price V-BOR offtake agreements.

In our first month, we achieved a V-BOR netback of approximately $767 per ton. Importantly, many of our November V-BOR orders have been prepaid, which speaks to the demand we are seeing for our product. Turning to cost. Power is one of our largest opportunities, and the solution is already on site. We plan to reduce the Westend plant's reliance on purchased power through greater use of our existing 54 megawatts of on-site cogeneration capacity. To enable that, we have engaged a third-party engineering firm to finalize the specifications for a capacitor. We are targeting having that capacitor on order by January with the objective of reducing our reliance on the grid by next summer.

We expect this initiative to require approximately $0.5 million of capital, and it would save approximately $38,000 per day on grid electricity purchases or roughly $14 million gross on an annualized basis, which we expect to reduce operating expenditures by approximately $8 million to $9 million. Beyond power, we are resetting the cost structure through organizational and procurement efficiencies and the elimination of duplicative corporate costs. On to volume. Current V-BOR production is approximately 82,000 short tons on an annualized basis.

Our objective is to recover production towards approximately 100,000 short tons annually through 2 initiatives: the restart of the SAC plant and an engineering-led well field development program, together with incremental byproduct production, including sodium bicarbonate and additional boric acid. We also plan to restart the idle boric acid production at our Trona facility, adding another product line from assets already in place. Reliability underpins that growth. On November 1, we commenced our first planned 5-day maintenance turnaround at the Westend plant. The team completed the work and restarted production on Friday, November 6. This planned downtime allowed us to address equipment reliability and maintenance items that are important to sustaining higher operating rates.

And it is one part of a broader effort to reduce unplanned downtime and strengthen operating performance. During our last update call, we emphasized the restart of the SAC plant, and it remains our most immediate volume catalyst. For those new to the story, SAC stands for Soda Ash Consolidation. It is a small existing facility that was idled as part of the soda ash exit last February, and it can operate independently of the legacy soda ash operation. The SAC plant is designed to capture natural gas emissions into the brine and reduce brine pH, improving brine chemistry and V-BOR output. Bringing it back online is a capital-light way to add volume.

I'm pleased to report that our team has begun the necessary prep work, including maintenance, readiness activities and the steps required for a safe startup. Our target is to have the SAC plant operational in January. Sustained volume growth starts with the resource. So we are also focused on the brine and well field system that underpins production. October brine grade was in line with our modeled expectations, consistent with the assumptions behind our production plan. Today, we kicked off a drilling and workover program addressing 205 wells with new and reworked wells targeting fresh tincal ore with the goal of recovering brine grade towards historical levels.

We also improved heat delivery on the lake by bypassing an underperforming heat exchanger, resulting in more consistent heat. Together with the SAC restart, these initiatives are intended to support stronger brine grades and higher V-BOR production. Beyond borates, our industrial salt and sodium sulfate businesses give us a diversified revenue base serving established industrial customers. Industrial salt operations transitioned seamlessly, averaging approximately 28 trucks per day, delivering industrial salt to key oil and gas customers in Bakersfield, California. In sodium sulfate, we used October to establish the rail and export logistics serving our customers in Mexico.

That work is done, and we are now moving product by rail to the Union Pacific line and onward into Mexico, setting up volumes to build from here. Searles Valley platform also gives us opportunities beyond our current operating plan. We have commenced 2 independent work streams focused on lithium and tungsten, both of which have the potential to become important byproducts that enhance our economics. Reputable third parties have received brine samples and will work to perform initial testing, analytical procedures and process recovery work. These opportunities are at an early stage, but we see them as meaningful optionality on top of our core borates business. We also see longer-term potential in borates expansion and sulfate of potash.

At Fort Cady, we continue to advance our advanced boron material strategy. In August, independent x-ray diffraction analysis confirmed the formation of iron boride in our ferroboron samples. We have since initiated testing at 1,400 degrees Celsius and are planning an approximately 500-gram batch with a third-party metallurgical processing partner as next steps towards producing samples for prospective customers. All of this is being done alongside the integration of the Searles Valley organization into 5E. We held our first employee town hall, and we are working closely with our employees as they transition on to 5E systems, and we have identified critical positions that we intend to fill. I want to personally recognize the Searles Valley team.

Their experience operating this asset is a real advantage for 5E, and I'm grateful for the work they have done during this initial transition. On financing, we ended the quarter with $15.6 million in cash and cash equivalents. And we received $7 million under our bridge facility at closing and are diligently working on the remaining CPs to draw on the remaining $3 million. Customer prepayments on November orders are supporting our working capital and our go-forward plan includes a working capital debt facility supported by our contracted offtake structure, which we are working now to finalize. We remain focused on solutions that optimize 5E's cost of capital.

To sum up, our first 5 weeks have been about establishing a reliable operating platform and a foundation for increasing production, and we have made strong progress. We completed a successful first month, streamlined logistics to drive sales, began resetting our commercial terms, completed a planned maintenance turnaround and advanced the SAC restart that can unlock additional production and sales volumes.

Looking ahead, our milestones are clear: ramping V-BOR sales through November and December, transitioning customers onto new take-or-pay and fixed-price offtake agreements, restarting the SAC plant in January, restarting idle boric acid production in Trona, placing the capacitor order by January, reducing our reliance on the grid by next summer and recovering V-BOR production towards approximately 100,000 short tons annually. Our focus remains on safely increasing volumes, improving reliability and cost and strengthening commercial execution. We believe the combination of Searles Valley's operating platform today and Fort Cady's long-term resource opportunity positions 5E for its next phase of growth, and we are excited about the road ahead. With that, we're ready to open up the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question is coming from Dmitry Silversteyn from Water Tower Research.

Dmitry Silversteyn: I just wanted to clarify your numbers on the sale of V-BOR -- production of V-BOR. You talked about 6,200 tons that you produced in November, and you had, I think you said 1,300 tons in inventory. So that's about 7,500 tons and you sold 2,500. So when you talk about ramp-up in November versus October, are you looking at kind of selling the rest of that? I'm just trying to understand what the run rate in November and December is going to be given the 2,500 ton sale in October.

Paul Weibel: Yes. Inventory was a little over 3,000 tons when we...

Paul Weibel: Yes, 3,000 tons. No, targeted production is about 8,200 tons. So I think we got in, met with the team and I think kind of came out of the gates and then planned for the kind of first downtime. We had a power outage that knocked us down for a day in that month, and then we kind of build back up the rates. So I think the goal and the target right now for November is approximately 8,300 tons. And I think you did 6,200 on month 1. I didn't quite know what it would look like once we came in, Pleasantly surprised to see about 3,000 tons in inventory.

And I think targeting on kind of hitting those rates.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Got it. Okay. And then just to clarify on the cost savings from the switching off the power grid and going to your cogeneration plant. You talked about $40 million in gross savings and then you talked about $8 million to $9 million in savings. Is that -- are both of those annual numbers?

Paul Weibel: Yes. No. So what will happen here is -- and it's good to get into those details. So approximately what we're buying from the grid at Westend is about $38,000 a day, right? So $38,000 times 365 gives you kind of your gross number that we're paying to SoCal Edison. The lines and the infrastructure are set up to fully decouple from the grid, but we get a voltage sag. And so we require a capacitor to ultimately stand that up. And so once we do that, we'll -- there's going to be an incremental MMBtu of natural gas we'll procure.

But all day long at $6 to $6.20 all-in MMBtu, that makes sense to buy that every day of the week. So the net savings, like the OpEx kind of reduction on a net basis is targeted to be $8 million to $9 million.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Understood. So that's -- okay. So that's the cost savings minus the purchase of gas and the cost of operating the plant.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Got it. Okay. And then in your 5-day outage -- maintenance outage, you talked about everything kind of going according to plan. Any -- maybe not surprises, but anything you've learned as you've worked through the maintenance of that equipment that affected you one way or the other about your plans?

Paul Weibel: No. Like it's a good question. I think there was a handful of safety fixes and get-rights that needed to occur right away. There was a tank that hadn't been cleaned out and emptied in about 10 years, hadn't seen the bottom of the tank. That was effectively drained and then cleaned out and the agitators were -- rigs were kind of maintained or working in good order. And there's a lot of leaks -- and we can quantify based on our concentrations, where we are in the process and the solution. A leak of 10 gallons a minute, if it's got 2% to 5%, whatever borax in it, that's dollars that are going on the ground.

So a lot of the focus was on that and just fixing a lot of the leaks and starting to build in redundancies that really focus on uptime reliability. So I think it's -- I think the punchline and takeaway was, listen, it needs TLC. That was a big focus out of the gate and kind of did that. And I think we -- it was very planned. So that's why I think we started November 1st or 2nd and came right out of it on the 5th.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Excellent. So it sounds like you're getting your hands around in at least the first 5 weeks around this asset and really starting to understand what levers you need to pull. So that's good to see.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Adam Kelsey from Titan Partners.

Adam Kelsey: Paul, just one point of clarity. How much of the current V-BOR output falls under the new take-or-pay contracts? And how quickly do you expect to address any remaining legacy contracts?

Paul Weibel: We have -- you're probably about 90% all in. The take-or-pays have -- when I look at them, there's minimum 62,000 tons under contract, but then they also have maximums. And I think not required to sell the maximum, but they're really great customers, and we want to service them. And I think there's a small percentage that are kind of spot or kind of smaller 1,000 tons a year to 1,500 tons that they're kind of contracts via a simple 1-page doc, but there's 5 customers right now, and that accounts for the majority of our volumes.

Adam Kelsey: And with respect to the customer prepayments in November, is that going to be a regular standard course of business? Or is this just kind of a onetime exception?

Paul Weibel: No. I think it's funny. The demand is very real. So I think some of the customers have figured out that, okay, happy to prepay if I can go higher in line and get my allocation. But all these offtakes come with about 60 days of documentary letters of credit. And so the goal here is to actually transition them from prepays. We're working with a financial institution that will basically stand up a working capital facility at basically SOFR plus 4%. And so all of these customers have been vetted. And once we're in the process of transitioning them over to the documentary LCs, which give us the working capital, that's for probably 3 out of the 5.

One of the other offtakes, actually, the customer negotiated, they're prepaying for the first 6 months. So you kind of -- you have a bit of a mix, and it is quite helpful on the working capital draw.

Adam Kelsey: Got it. And obviously, it's still early days with about 6 weeks since you acquired the asset. I would appreciate, though, to see any early learnings or anything that surprised you from the last 6 weeks?

Paul Weibel: No, great question. Listen, I think I don't -- I want to give the team a lot of credit for opening up those supply chains for all the exports. All the -- the majority of the sodium sulfate is going down into Mexico and 4 out of our 5 contracted by customers are all based out of Asia. And so you're dealing with -- they've been navigating. -- there's a new union contract getting negotiated in Long Beach that have kind of caused -- it's been moving, but like everyone is paying attention to that.

And I think there's inspections that have been required and just bills of lading needs to match and we stood up a new entity, the actual contracting entity was stood up probably maybe September 15th, 5E SVM was the buyer, but below 5E SVM are 3 stand-alone entities. And so all that -- there's a lot that goes into the basic execution of taking product up in Trona, packaging it, getting that onto a truck with a container, making sure that gets them into the right loading dock in Long Beach that gets on the right container destined for Malaysia, getting to then Malaysia and then to customers.

So that was probably -- we knew it would be not so straightforward. And maybe a little bit of turbulence there, but I think a lot of lessons learned, and we now are -- we're stood up and we're going. I think we're 15 trucks a day picking up all that product that's staged in the warehouse and it's moving.

Adam Kelsey: Great. Final question for me, and I'll jump back in the queue. You mentioned that there are some positions that you need to fill. I just want to clarify, are these existing legacy positions? Or are these newly created positions? And is there a theme amongst what you need to address?

And so then there was some employees based at Overland Park that didn't get offers. And I think we didn't want to mess too much with org charts. And there was some kind of -- there was definitely a population of open roles that were on the org chart, but we sort of just said, let's get in, let's assess, and then go from there. And so I think HR has a role that we've posted, there's a mechanic. Utilities has 3 operators that they need to fill.

So we're gearing up to start posting those roles. So we want to get those roles kind of filled to get people trained up. And it's -- we're not talking about a bunch of roles, but there's probably 5, 6, 7 roles that are going to get filled here in the next kind of 4 to 6 weeks.

And to the extent that SAC comes online here in January, as we expect, we have a 30-day drill program going into fresh tincal ore, if that can drive a higher brine grade, that drives more primary borax production, and that brings on Trona and restarting boric acid and maximizing Westend sooner than later. So I think we kind of -- my model is pretty conservative, but like we'll kind of see how it goes.

Heiko Ihle: Paul, I somehow got into the queue a little later than I thought, so bear with me here. But just building on the last question a little bit. It sounds like you're hiring additional staff, at least to a certain extent. Maybe just walk us through what you're seeing in the tranches and maybe give a bit of color beyond what we saw in the press release.

Paul Weibel: Yes. Heiko, glad you're here. Appreciate the question, too. Listen, the culture and that integration is probably one of the more taller orders in this acquisition. I think in the first kind of -- it took about 1.5 weeks or so, and then I've been up there twice a week with the team and just really getting to know our people. We had a town hall. It was definitely a bumpy -- for a lot of the employees, we went from 25 people to 250 people as of October 1, approximately. And we had 5E benefits. Now we're a smaller company.

So our benefits weren't as good as what they previously had. But we were able to at least offer benefits and bolt everyone on. Now we'll go back to market here in the new year. And so I think out of the gate, there was definitely received skepticism as I think would be kind of normal, but I think there's a rational reason on why we've done something or made a decision. And similar to how I need to answer to shareholders, the leadership team here at 5E needs to answer to our employees. And there's not just an arbitrary decision.
