So I'm trying to catch people at turnovers and just talk through them. And there's -- we're having leadership meetings on a weekly basis that basically can ensure that everyone is over the details of the organization because it really is an integrated facility and platform where power drives heat to the lake, lake drives brine and borates to Westend, Westend puts out tons, and they need power and good brine to run. So it's very much an integrated organization and just making sure people are informed and there's a rhyme and a reason for decision has been critical.

Heiko Ihle: Fair enough. Walk me through -- just as a follow-up, I guess, walk me through your conversations with clients. And I think customers are quite uncomfortable being that this is an oligopoly structure, and they do like that it's an American-owned company that they're able to buy from.

#2940. Under CEO Satya Nadella, Microsoft Stock Has Soared at a 23% Annualized Rate for 12 Years. Can the Tech Titan Keep Up the Pace?

Microsoft's AI spending is generating solid results, but sustaining rapid growth gets progressively harder for multitrillion-dollar companies.

By Marc Guberti – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:57AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Microsoft ›

Microsoft (MSFT -0.55%) has enjoyed a roughly 14-fold share price increase since CEO Satya Nadella took over in 2014. That amounts to an annualized growth rate of 23%, but some investors worry that the company’s heavy spending on AI could disrupt future gains.

Such worries are justified, since experienced investors may remember that the tech stock went through a “lost decade” of long-term negative returns before Nadella took over. No Microsoft shareholder wants a repeat of that, and while those concerns appear overblown, they shouldn’t be ignored.

In its fiscal 2027 Q1, Microsoft's results featured 19% year-over-year revenue growth. That was a little lower than prior quarters, but was still a respectable growth rate. One thing that stood out is the relative lack of growth in non-AI segments.

Microsoft groups all of its revenue under two categories: "agents and infrastructure" and "devices and consumer." The latter segment made up $15.5 billion of Microsoft's $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue. That part of the business was down by 3% year over year, with Xbox sales growth remaining sluggish for multiple years.

Unsurprisingly, the agents and infrastructure segment performed well, posting 25% year-over-year growth. Microsoft's AI spending goes toward this category, and its 73% year-over-year increase in commercial remaining performance obligations is a meaningful result.

Azure has been the company's bread and butter from a growth perspective, and it certainly didn't disappoint at the start of the tech giant's fiscal 2027. This part of the business was up 48% year over year, and Microsoft Cloud revenue was up 30% year over year.

It's important to keep this context in mind when assessing its rising AI infrastructure costs. Microsoft is the second-largest cloud infrastructure provider in the world, and is investing hundreds of millions of dollars a year into expanding and enhancing its cloud platform. If it reduces its capital expenditure, then No. 1 Amazon Web Services and Alphabet-owned No. 3 Google Cloud will be more than happy to take big bites out of Microsoft's market share.

Maintaining high growth rates for Azure will be critical to the stock's performance. If Microsoft’s cloud computing growth decelerates, it could trigger a prolonged correction for the stock. The company is sitting on enough cash to support higher AI spending, and each additional investment in infrastructure makes it that much harder for competitors to take any of Microsoft's AI data center market share.

Right now, its AI investments are bearing positive results. Elevated revenue growth rates and net operating income are some of the highlights. It's powering the remaining part of Microsoft's business that is still gaining market share, at a meaningful price that justifies the current price.

Although AI spending is necessary for Microsoft to keep up with the competition, that doesn't mean it will be able to maintain its long-term 23% annualized growth rate.

The company produced only a 16.1% annualized revenue growth rate over the past five years. It's hard for a company to deliver annualized stock returns that exceed its annualized revenue growth rate. That partially explains why Microsoft stock has only an annualized return of 9.9% over the past five years.

Microsoft is also approaching a $4 trillion market cap. It's harder for trillion-dollar tech giants to deliver the type of growth required to justify significant share price gains compared to smaller tech companies.

Microsoft's net income has been trending higher as its margins expand, but the company would likely have to deliver at least 23% year-over-year revenue growth over an extended period to achieve a steady 23% CAGR in its stock price again. That prior period of rapid stock price growth also included a time when Microsoft's cloud segment was much smaller, and a smaller amount of revenue and earnings gains were required to move the needle for the hyperscaler.

#2938. Should You Buy the Worst-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026 Before 2027?

Tesla’s EV business is beating expectations again. Its stock is still the worst performer among the Magnificent Seven this year.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:05AM EST

The Magnificent Seven refers to a group of prominent market leaders. It includes Alphabet (GOOG +1.23%) (GOOGL +1.17%), Amazon (AMZN +1.98%), Apple (AAPL +0.85%), Meta Platforms (META -0.04%), Microsoft (MSFT -0.12%), Nvidia (NVDA -0.36%), and Tesla (TSLA +1.52%). They have been called "magnificent" because they are among the top players in their respective industries and have crushed broader equities over the long run. However, some of them haven't been so magnificent this year -- several have lagged the S&P 500 to date. And the worst-performing, as of writing, has been Tesla (though Nvidia is a very close second). Is the electric vehicle (EV) company a buy on the dip before 2027?

One puzzling fact about Tesla's performance this year is that despite lagging the market, its core EV business has beaten expectations. In the second and third quarters, Tesla's deliveries exceeded analysts' projections. There were several reasons for that. Here are two of the most important. First, Tesla benefited from macroeconomic factors. Conflicts in the Middle East led to soaring oil prices and, as a result, many consumers decided to buy EVs instead of gas-powered cars.

This led to a boost in sales across much of the industry. Second, Tesla's management has argued that the company's Full Self-Driving (FSD) software is increasingly attracting buyers. In the third quarter, the company's FSD attach rate (the percentage of new car buyers who opt in for the monthly FSD service) grew almost 20 percentage points quarter-over-quarter in North America, reaching over 75%.

Total FSD subscriptions for the period came in at 1.74 million, up 67% year-over-year (including lifetime subscriptions purchased upfront, though Tesla no longer offers those). On the earnings call, management confirmed FSD subscriptions are now generating revenue at an annual run rate approaching $1 billion.

That's a small fraction of the company's trailing 12-month revenue of $103.57 billion, but at the rate they are growing, FSD subscriptions could become a meaningful growth driver over the medium term. That could matter for the bottom line, since subscription revenue arguably comes with juicier margins than car sales. Over time, it could give Tesla's profits a lift.

So why has Tesla's stock dropped so much this year despite EV deliveries beating expectations and FSD subscriptions growing fast, which is driving demand for the company's vehicles? One reason is that its actual financial results have been mixed. In the third quarter, Tesla's revenue of about $28 billion remained pretty much flat year over year.

But the company's GAAP earnings per share of $0.22 dropped 44% compared to the year-ago period. Tesla R&D spending has increased significantly as the company continues to invest in future opportunities. The question is whether these projects can pay off. Consider Tesla's robotaxi ambitions.

It has also made some headway in that market this year. In September, Tesla launched the Cybercab, a two-seat autonomous vehicle built without a steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors. Tesla hopes it becomes the cornerstone of its robotaxi fleet. If it can scale its fleet over the next few years and attract significant business, robotaxi sales -- and profits -- might soar.

Tesla also recently announced it would start selling the Cybercab to select customers. It will cost about $30,000 upfront, pretax, plus a mandatory $299-per-month Autonomy Subscription (without it, the car can't go anywhere). It can be operated only in certain geographic locations.

At that price and with those subscription fees, Tesla could collect more than $35,000 in subscription fees alone over 10 years on each Cybercab -- so customers would essentially be spending a little more than the initial purchase price every decade they own it, assuming no price changes. If Tesla can attract enough customers, this business could become highly lucrative for the company.

With all that said, Tesla faces considerable uncertainty. First, the Cybercab may not attract the kind of business the company hopes for, whether as a robotaxi or for personal use. Second, Tesla could face significant pushback from regulators. In fact, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an audit into how Tesla certified the Cybercab's compliance with federal safety standards as soon as it hit the roads back in September.

Third, Tesla's shares trade at a steep premium, which may be one of the most important reasons the stock has gone nowhere this year, despite progress in its robotaxi and core EV businesses. Shares are currently trading at 159.3x forward earnings. At current levels, I'd rather stay away. If Tesla stock falls much further before 2027, perhaps it'll be worth investing in the company.

#2935. Ramona Shelburne doubles down on inaccurate Lakers take

Ramona Shelburne gave her honest thoughts on the Lakers this season.

"It's easy to find your way when you're playing one of the easiest schedules in the league," Shelburne said on ESPN.

Luka Doncic (77) and Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers look on during a game against the Toronto Raptors on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

While Los Angeles' 12-2 record hasn't come by defeating all the NBA's best teams, the Lakers' early strength of schedule ranks around 14th to 16th. That means the cumulative strength of schedule is around league average, not one of the easiest as Shelburne implied.

NBA on ESPN's post of Shelburne's take was not received well by many as a Community Note was added, stating: "Analyses rank the Lakers' played schedule near average or slightly easier than league average in strength, not one of the easiest; Spurs and Memphis rank easier per opponent records and models."

Shelburne chose to defend her take the following day and went on an unfiltered rant on ESPN's radio show Tuesday morning.

"I don't think people understand what it's like to be a female reporter," Shelburne said. "It's an objective thing here that they have not played any of the top teams in the West yet."

Shelburne's assessment is correct; the Lakers have not played a juggernaut like the Spurs or Rockets. But as the saying goes, you can only beat what's in front of you.

The Lakers' early-season schedule has featured more teams above .500 than the Spurs have faced. and LA has won more of those games.

But fans were quick to criticize Shelburne.

"ummmm what…??? this is not a male/female thing

"You were factually wrong, got a community note, just apologize and move on," another user wrote on X.

For many, the NBA insider's Lakers reporting has drawn skepticism in recent years.

ESPN's Ramona Shelburne attends The Annual espnW: Women + Sports Summit day 1 at The Lodge at Torrey Pines on October 18, 2021. Getty Images

Fans have been critical of her MVP voting history, including her past ballots in which she ranked Luka Doncic at No. 4. In 2023, she placed Jalen Brunson at No. 2 over Doncic in the fourth spot.

ESPN's John Ireland said Shelburne is an apologist for the Clippers, which could contribute to her seemingly one-sided opinion on their crosstown rivals.

"You are an apologist for the Clippers," Ireland told Shelburne last December on ESPN LA. "And you're not the only one."

Los Angeles Lakers' Austin Reaves shrugs during the first half of an NBA basketball game against the Milwaukee Bucks, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Milwaukee. AP Photo/Aaron Gash

"For whatever reason, the media is in love with the [Clippers] front office," Ireland said.

Shelburne remains a brilliant writer and respected NBA insider, but her reporting on the Lakers, at times, lights a fire under fans.

Key among the many recent developments was the completion of our manufacturing relocation to our new headquarters in San Jose. As we outlined on our last call, a change in our manufacturing address requires re-registration in a number of international markets, and this creates short windows where we cannot ship under the new registration. To protect our distributors and their customers during those windows, we built safety stock utilizing the old address. That increased inventory is now starting to convert to revenue as international regulatory clearances are completed, and we continue to receive orders tied to upcoming blackout periods. This will become a tailwind for cash flows as working capital and inventory is steadily converted back into cash.

The combination of our inventory investment and the lower-than-expected third quarter revenue resulted in a cash use of roughly $1 million in the quarter. As safety stock converts to revenue and we collect the related receivables, we are driving towards a return to cash flow break-even. Glaucoma developments continue to be very encouraging, and the U.S. G6 product family revenue grew, supported by higher average selling prices and an increase in system placements. Internationally, probe orders were lower in the quarter as distributors worked through inventory they purchased in the first half, a pattern we flagged last quarter. In retina, U.S. PASCAL sales were the highlight of this segment, with year-over-year sales increasing by approximately 50%.

The rest of the retina business was challenged as a mix of deferred orders, regulatory constraints, and competitive pricing in specific international markets impacted results. I will now discuss each segment in further detail, starting with glaucoma. We saw several bright spots in U.S. glaucoma performance throughout the quarter, driven by the same 3 factors we highlighted last quarter: Medicare LCD tailwinds, targeted outreach through MedScout, and higher average selling prices. First, the Medicare LCD changes continue to improve the reimbursement environment and are encouraging physicians to consider MicroPulse TLT with G6 earlier in the treatment pathway. Our 2-year clinical follow-up data on MicroPulse TLT reinforces that shift.

Longer-term outcome data gives us a strong foundation for physician education and supports earlier use of the therapy, including in selected patients with mild to moderate disease. Second, our utilization platform continues to sharpen our commercial focus. MedScout helps our team target mid-utilization accounts and high-volume MIGS surgeons, where we see the clearest path to greater adoption. We also left the American Academy of Ophthalmology Conference with strong physician interest and active commercial conversations, which we expect to support adoption and utilization in the months ahead. Third, pricing remains a meaningful contributor. U.S. G6 probe ASP increased in 2025, and we have held that higher price level consistently throughout 2026.

We believe this reflects the value physicians place on MicroPulse therapy. G6 probe volume in the U.S. was 6,900 units, roughly in line with the prior year period, and we placed 8 G6 systems in the U.S. compared to 7 in the prior year quarter. Global G6 probe volume was approximately 11,900 units versus 14,900 in the prior year, with the declines coming primarily from international distributor ordering patterns. On systems, we placed 28 G6 systems in the quarter compared to 30 in the third quarter of 2025. Going deeper into details impacting our international glaucoma business, in Europe, Middle East, and Africa, results were shaped mainly by order timing.

Distributors accelerated G6 console and probe orders in the first and second quarters, which reduced third-quarter demand, and tighter inventory and purchasing controls at one of our larger distribution partners added to the effect. Supply constraints also delayed fulfillment of some G6 Probe Illuminate orders. In Germany and Austria, they continue to perform above plan as we recover business previously handled by our former distributor. New G6 console placements remain competitive, particularly against the A.R.C. FOX platform. In Asia, continued economic challenges in China contributed to relatively stagnant order activity in the third quarter.

In Japan, customers had placed significant orders in the second quarter ahead of our headquarters relocation and the associated business transition, resulting in lighter third-quarter purchasing as anticipated. Stocking orders in Korea and Malaysia ahead of the address change helped partially offset softer demand elsewhere in the region. Importantly, all outstanding EndoProbe backorders carried over from the second quarter for customers in China and Japan have now been fulfilled. In Latin America and Canada, G6 probe sales were stable. Orders from Peru and Chile offset lower purchasing in Brazil, where our distributor built inventory in the second quarter. Canada continues to deliver steady results following the commercial changes we made earlier this year.

Overall, the drivers of our glaucoma business remain intact: favorable reimbursement, a growing body of clinical evidence, more focused selling, and disciplined pricing. We remain focused on turning those advantages into steady probe volume growth and additional system placements. Now turning to retina. Our retina strategy continues to rest on 3 priorities: advancing the PASCAL upgrade cycle in the U.S., expanding PASCAL's international reach, and securing regulatory clearances for our next-generation platforms. We saw several bright spots domestically this quarter: U.S. PASCAL revenue increased approximately 50% year-over-year. Internationally, retina faced challenges concentrated in Asia and Europe. Turning first to Asia, in Japan, our partner deferred PASCAL shipments into the fourth quarter after building inventory ahead of our manufacturing relocation.

This deferral included 1 particular order of approximately $300,000 that we expect to ship in the fourth quarter. In China, economic weakness, regulatory challenges, and slow tender cycles continue to limit activity. In India, registration delays continue to limit our business to PASCAL sales only. In Europe, Middle East, and Africa, medical retina faced aggressive pricing pressure from larger competitors across Europe. Delays in PASCAL MDR certification also continued to restrict sales in key markets, including Germany and Austria. We continue to expect PASCAL MDR approval in the first half of 2027 and anticipate solid demand once completed. In Latin America and Canada, PASCAL sales have resumed after early market disruption, and we expect further improvement through year-end.

We anticipate some of the third-quarter retina impact, especially the Japan shipments, could be realized in the fourth quarter. Competitive pricing and regulatory timelines likely could take longer to work through, and we are planning accordingly. I will also want to acknowledge the Middle East. We removed the region from our guidance earlier in the year, and recent developments in Saudi Arabia will continue to weigh on the activity in the region. We will continue to serve customers in the region where we can, but we are not including recovery in our near-term outlook.

Looking at the remainder of the year, particularly to the fourth quarter, we expect financial results to benefit from the release of remaining safety stock, open international orders, and the deferred Japan PASCAL shipments, along with the typical year-end seasonal lift. At the same time, we expect these benefits to be offset by a continuation of headwinds discussed today, namely regulatory delays and competitive pricing pressure in retina, along with continued volatility in international ordering. Accordingly, we are updating our full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $46 million to $48 million, which continues to exclude revenue from the Middle East.

While this lowers our outlook for 2026, these same decisions are why we believe 2027 to be a more profitable year for IRIDEX. Romeo will provide more detail in a moment. Looking ahead to 2027, we expect to see, for the first time, the combined benefit of our cost-saving and margin initiatives. This includes the San Jose facility savings, the administrative function transfer, and the operating expense reductions we have made over the past 2 years. Beyond these activities, we are evaluating and planning additional meaningful operating expense reductions, which we expect to further lower our cost base in 2027. Second, we expect meaningful gross margin improvement as our major products move to third-party contract manufacturers.

We remain on track to complete that transition in 2027, and once our major products are contract manufactured, we expect gross margins to increase. Third, we are undertaking a comprehensive strategic review of our product portfolio and distribution model with the objective of sharpening our focus on higher-margin, more profitable revenue streams. As part of this effort, we are evaluating opportunities to streamline our product lines and reduce the overall size and complexity of our portfolio. A more focused product offering will not only improve operational efficiency, but also help reduce the ongoing costs and complexities associated with product obsolescence, inventory management and maintaining regulatory clearances across multiple markets.

In parallel, we are assessing distribution alternatives in select international markets to better align our commercial structure with our profitability objectives. In some regions, this may mean accepting lower revenue in exchange for stronger margins, a lower cost to serve, and more predictable ordering patterns. Ultimately, we expect these efforts to result in higher margins, a lower cost structure, and a more consistent cash flow-generating business model. With that, I'll turn the call over to Romeo to review the financials.

Romeo Dizon: Thank you, Patrick, and good afternoon, everyone. Total revenue for the third quarter of 2026 was $10.2 million, compared to $12.5 million in the third quarter of 2025. The third quarter decline came primarily from international retina and lower international probe orders, partially offset by growth in our U.S. glaucoma business. Retina product revenue was $5.1 million compared to $6.7 million in the prior year quarter. The decrease was driven by international markets where deferred shipments in Japan, continued weakness in China, registration delays in India, and competitive pricing and MDR regulatory timing in Europe restricted our revenues. Total product revenue for the Cyclo G6 product family was $3.2 million, compared to $3.5 million in the third quarter of 2025.

The decline is attributed to a decrease in international revenue, as distributors worked through inventory purchased earlier in the year, partially offset by higher U.S. probe ASPs and higher system revenue. Other revenue was $1.9 million compared to $2.2 million in the prior year period, mainly reflecting lower paid service revenue and the absence of royalty revenue in the current period. Gross profit for the third quarter was $4.3 million, translating to a gross margin of 42.4% of revenue, compared to $4.0 million, or 32.1%, in the third quarter of 2025. As Patrick indicated previously, in the third quarter of 2025, we recorded a one-time, non-recurring, non-cash $0.8 million charge to cost of goods sold due to an inventory write-down.

Excluding this write-down, gross margin as a percent of revenue would have been 38.7%, an improvement of approximately 370 basis points versus the prior year. The improvement reflects a more favorable geographic mix, along with sustained pricing discipline. We expect the move to third-party contract manufacturers to be the next significant driver of margin expansion as we move through 2027. Operating expenses for the third quarter were $5.5 million, essentially flat with $5.4 million in the prior year period. Net loss for the quarter was $1.4 million, or $0.08 per share, compared to a net loss of $1.6 million, or $0.09 per share, in the prior year period.

Non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter was a loss of $0.6 million compared to an adjusted EBITDA loss of $0.1 million in the third quarter of 2025. Moving to the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with cash and cash equivalents of $3.7 million as of October 3rd, 2026, compared to $4.7 million at the end of the second quarter. Net cash used in operating activities was $1.0 million in the quarter. The main driver was a $1.6 million increase in inventory as we built safety stock to support distributors through the registration blackout periods, along with lower revenue in the quarter. Moving forward, cash utilization should decrease significantly with stronger sales and reversal of the inventory stocking process.

Turning to guidance, for the full year 2026, we now expect revenue in the range of $46 million to $48 million. As a reminder, our outlook excludes revenues from the Middle East given the ongoing conflict in the region. We continue to expect adjusted operating expenses, which exclude depreciation, amortization, and stock-based compensation, to be in the range of $19 million to $19.5 million for the full year. We are not providing 2027 guidance today. Looking further out, we expect 2027 to reflect the full year benefit of our operating expense reductions, headquarters relocation, and the progressive move of products to contract manufacturers, resulting in a more profitable IRIDEX.

With that, I'll turn the call back to Patrick for closing remarks.

Patrick Mercer: Thanks, Romeo. The foundation for next year is strong. Our manufacturing relocation is complete and delivering the cost savings we anticipated, with more to come as the site is fully integrated. Gross margin improved meaningfully from the second quarter, and the safety stock we built is now becoming revenue-generating. Our glaucoma franchise continues to show its strength with year-to-date probe volume growth, higher U.S. pricing, and new 2-year MicroPulse TLT data that adds to our confidence in the therapy's long-term role. For the rest of 2026, our priorities are clear: complete our international clearances, continue advancing our contract manufacturing transition, and return to cash flow break-even.

We expect to enter 2027 as a more efficient IRIDEX with better margins, a lower cost base, generating operating profits, and a business model built to generate cash. Thank you for your continued support of IRIDEX. We look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter. Operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question comes from the line of Scott Henry with AGP. Your line is open.

Scott Henry: A lot to talk about. I'll try to take a higher-level, bigger-picture approach, but I do have a couple questions. Starting with retina, we've seen double-digit declines year-over-year for the last 3 quarters, and it looks like Q4 will be -- based on your guidance, it appears it will probably be close to double digits if not a double-digit decline. How do you think about -- and granted there's some moving parts impacting this year. But how do you think about the organic growth for that segment?

I think we were hoping we would be single digits or higher if it was gaining share, but how do you think about the category and I guess, that would likely play out in 2027 as well?

Patrick Mercer: Scott, and thank you for your question. You know, we've had this year -- this quarter in particular was a challenge for us. Even going into Q4 we see weakness in China. For example, last year we had $4 million in orders from China. This year we're up to -- we have about $400,000 from China. That's really been -- that's really hit us hard. We'd like to have had that $3.6 million. Japan, we've had a lot of volatility due to our blackout periods and working with the distributors to get those orders placed. Some have been cautious, some have wanted to wait.

For example, Japan placed a stocking order in Q2, so they didn't place any orders in Q3. We're seeing rising energy costs from the Iran war, which has affected our business in other regions outside the Middle East, particularly Asia and Europe. We are -- we're working through the headwinds as far as the regulatory delays and some of the competitive pricing. We are taking -- you talked about how we see '27; we are taking a strategic review of our product lines as we discussed in the script, mainly aimed at creating more profitable revenue streams for us. We're not going to sell in regions that aren't profitable anymore.

We're not going to go to countries that aren't profitable, and we're not going to put product lines forward that aren't profitable. So that's our 2027 plan. We're going to look at reducing -- continuing to reduce our OpEx, but really focusing on profitable segments of our business. And that's really what's going to help us overcome these things. We still believe in glaucoma. Glaucoma growth is really strong. So...

Scott Henry: Yes. I don't want to -- let's finish this line of questioning, if I can. Do you think you're gaining share in the markets you're in? Or do you think -- I mean, the numbers would suggest you're not, but I wanted to hear what you think.

Patrick Mercer: In the U.S. we certainly are. We grew the IP, which is our flagship product, by 50%. The OUS has been challenged by the issues I talked about previously. But in the U.S., we certainly are with our PASCAL system.

Scott Henry: And just for clarification, because I did see the breakout by geographic segment in the 10-Q, I understand the issue in China and Japan. In Europe, when you speak of regulatory delays, I mean, you're already in those markets. Are they taking products off the market, which would be negatively impacting you? Or -- because I feel like if you're being delayed on new products, you would still have your base business, but it seems like you're losing business. Could you just explain where the regulatory delays are impacting you?

Patrick Mercer: Yes, the regulatory delays, they're -- our new PASCAL product is our IP product, IRIDEX PASCAL, and that product has a lot more feature sets than our existing PASCAL. You are correct, we are selling the existing PASCAL in Europe today; however, a lot of those distributors know that the new IP product is going to be getting approved. So they're waiting to place orders for those products. So that's been the challenge. We've submitted everything to the notified bodies to get the MDR approval. We've had our BSI audits complete, our TUV audit. We are now just waiting for those approvals, which we hope will come in Q1. But yes, you're correct, we are selling in those markets.

However, a lot of the distributors have told us they're waiting to get approval before placing new orders for the new product.

Scott Henry: Okay. That's helpful. And then on the G6 business, I mean, you can see the, kind of, a lump in probes, particularly in Q2, perhaps a little in Q1. How are you thinking about probes in Q4? I mean, do you think we're back to a steady state? Or do you expect more inventory burn in Q4?

Patrick Mercer: Q4 is generally our largest quarter for not only probe sales, but G6 systems. So I anticipate that our probe volume will increase -- the amount of probe sales will increase in the Q4.

Scott Henry: Okay, and I assume you're speaking sequentially? Or do you think they'll increase year-over-year?

Patrick Mercer: I believe they'll increase year-over-year, but certainly sequentially.

Scott Henry: Okay. Well, year-over-year would imply pretty good growth. How about on systems? Do you think that -- I mean, that would increase sequentially and year-over-year? Last year was particularly good for Q4, and I think it was 44 systems.

Patrick Mercer: We still believe that's the case. Nothing's changed as far -- certainly over this quarter it will increase, but year-over-year we anticipate it will increase also. All the things that we've discussed previously with the LCD and [ we ] treated more moderate patients early in the continuum of care. We've been holding -- we didn't get a lot of orders in G6 systems for Q3 from OUS, so we expect those numbers to turn around.

Scott Henry: Okay, I -- your guidance would imply, I believe, an $11.5 million to $13.5 million revenue for Q4. Do you think that would be adjusted EBITDA positive for operations based on what we're seeing?

Romeo Dizon: Scott, this is Romeo. Thanks for the question. For the quarter, yes, if we reach the higher end of that revenue range, we will be, but not for the full year because of the prior 3-quarter losses that we've incurred.

Scott Henry: Yes, of course, Romeo. And then, final question, if you start to rationalize sales towards profitable sales, which, unless you're going to grow your way into profit, makes sense, that would imply that we would see gross margins increase or at least net margins because the losses are going to either come -- either going to add to gross margin or come out of expenses. What would you -- where would you expect that to show up? Because one of those metrics should improve, and in, sort of, what magnitude should we expect in 2027 for that improvement, just general terms?

Romeo Dizon: We expect it to come from both increases in margins as well a reduction in operating expenses. As you know, we've moved into the facilities already back in October, and we're starting to -- we've got -- we're 6-month free rent, and our rent's a lot lower. So a lot of that -- more than half of that, is allocated to cost of sales. So that'll lead to further expansion in the margins. And given the strategic product portfolio, like Patrick indicated earlier, we're going to start -- we're going to stop selling low margins and just focus on the profit. So that will add to that.

And we are also constantly still looking for reduction in operating expenses, such as perhaps moving some more things overseas or what have you. So that's always in the play.

Patrick Mercer: Thanks, Scott. Thanks, Romeo. Now I'll turn the call back over to the operator.

Operator: Thank you. And that actually concludes our question-and-answer session. So I would like to turn the conference back over to Mr. Patrick Mercer for any closing remarks.

Patrick Mercer: I want to thank everybody for joining us today, and we look forward to updating you on IRIDEX in the future. Thank you.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, this concludes today's call. We thank you for your participation, and you may now disconnect.

#2929. LeBron Log No. 5: Popcorn in hand, a viral chorus and ‘basketball AI'

LeBron Log No. 5: Popcorn in hand, a viral chorus and 'basketball AI' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James spent Monday night in street clothes.

He still managed to argue a call with popcorn in his hand, practice his golf swing during a timeout and reject a report about himself before the Sixers left Brooklyn with a win.

That followed a Sunday afternoon in which James passed Jason Kidd on the NBA's career assists list and received an unusual description from Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle.

Welcome to the fifth edition of the LeBron Log.

James sat out the Sixers' 135-123 win over the Nets because of low back and sciatica management.

It was his fourth absence through 15 games. James has yet to play both ends of a back-to-back this season after logging nearly 33 minutes Sunday against Indiana.

He watched Monday's game from the end of the Sixers' bench in a yellow hat and an "Ohio Baby" sweatshirt. James snacked from a small bag before switching to popcorn.

When Joel Embiid believed he was fouled on a first-half drive, James stood and pleaded his case to official Jacyn Goble without putting down the box. He also joined conversations between teammates and officials during several timeouts.

James found another way to pass a third-quarter stoppage. As "Hot To Go" played inside Barclays Center, he practiced his golf swing near the bench.

His most pointed contribution came on Instagram.

An ESPN story by Dave McMenamin cited a Sixers source who said James had asked the coaching staff to remain patient while he worked toward finding his rhythm and conditioning by December.

James reposted ESPN's graphic and rejected the account.

"🧢! Those words never came out of my mouth!" he wrote.

The Sixers improved to 4-0 without James. They have beaten the Bucks, Hornets, Raptors and Nets in the games he has missed.

Brooklyn pulled within five points during the final five minutes Monday, putting the Sixers in another clutch game.

Philadelphia has reached 10 clutch wins more quickly than almost any team since the statistic began being tracked in 1996-97. The 2026-27 Sixers are the second team in that span with at least 10 such victories through their first 15 games.

The other was the 1997-98 Atlanta Hawks, who had 12.

James was also on the last team before Philadelphia to open a season with at least 10 consecutive clutch wins. The Lakers started 13-0 in those games last season.

James did not play in the Sixers' latest close finish, but he has now been part of the last two teams to start at least 10-0 under those circumstances.

Before Sunday's game, Carlisle explained why he tries to limit his play calls against James.

"LeBron James is one of the reasons we try not to have play calls, 'cause he knows all of them," Carlisle said. "He's a walking NBA basketball AI machine. That's what he is."

James followed with 15 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds in the Sixers' 131-124 win.

His pass to VJ Edgecombe for a layup with 1:19 remaining gave him 12,092 career assists and moved him past Kidd for third in NBA history. Only Chris Paul and John Stockton remain ahead of him.

Noah Levick wrote more about James' milestone and the anticipation behind his passes.

When told what Carlisle had called him, James appreciated the description.

"So, yeah, Rick is great," James said. "He's one of the greatest coaches of all time, and I've had my battles with him over the years. That's super humbling coming from a guy like that."

Philadelphia has found its soundtrack for James' biggest home moments.

The Sixers have played the viral "LeBron, LeBron, LeBron" song after several of his baskets, including his late putback against the Knicks on Oct. 30.

The refrain comes from a version of Steve Lacy's "Oh Yeah?" that replaces "Come on" with James' name. The Baylor University Men's Choir performed its own rendition, helping the song spread across social media.

Lacy later joined in. During an Oct. 15 concert at Freedom Mortgage Pavilion in Camden, he performed the LeBron version as the crowd sang along.

James has noticed Philadelphia's use of it.

"I've seen it. I've heard it. It's pretty hilarious, to be honest," James said. "I heard it towards the end of a game when we were winning. I made a play, and I heard that song. I was just chuckling to myself on the inside."
