#2916. NRx (NRXP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

First FDA approval reshapes NRx as it becomes a commercial biopharma company.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:09AM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

NRx (NRXP +7.75%) reported a transition from a clinical-stage firm to a commercial biopharmaceutical company following the first FDA approval of its preservative-free ketamine product. Management stated the company restructured into four distinct divisions: NeuroRx Pharmaceuticals, HOPE Therapeutics, NRx Defense Systems, and GeNeuro. The company reported the elimination of all convertible debt and the acquisition of clinical revenue streams through its HOPE clinics. CEO Javitt noted that the recent FDA approval of the blow-fill-seal packaging platform offers a cost-effective alternative to traditional glass bottling, aiming to address national security concerns regarding the sterile injectable supply chain.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the NRx Pharmaceuticals Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the conference over to Brian Korb of Astr partners. Please go ahead.

Brian Korb: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Joining me on today's call are Dr. Jonathan Javitt, Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; and Michael Abrams, Chief Financial Officer of NRx Pharmaceuticals. Following their prepared remarks, we'll open the call for questions. Yesterday, NRx filed its quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The 10-Q is available on the Investors section of the company's website and on the SEC's website. Before we begin, please note that statements made on this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements.

Actual results may differ materially due to risks and uncertainties, including those described in the Risk Factors section of our most recent Form 10-K and subsequent filings with the SEC. I'm now pleased to turn the call over to Dr. Jonathan Javitt, Founder, Chairman and CEO of NRx Pharmaceuticals. Jonathan, go ahead.

Jonathan Javitt: Thank you, Brian. Good morning, and thank you for attending our third quarter conference call. The third quarter of 2026 has been the quarter in which seeds that were planted 2 years ago have begun to grow into a sustainable orchard. As you recall, exactly 2 years ago, we announced the resignation of the company's former management and the Board's recognition that we needed to chart a new path forward. The company at that time had no near-term path to an approved drug. It was paralyzed by toxic debt and lacked a strategic direction. Our market capitalization was $15 million, and the company reported $1.6 million in cash at the end of the quarter.

Two years later, we've shed all the convertible debt from our balance sheet. We've attracted healthcare specialists and institutional investors led by the B Group who provided us with a path to profitability. We've been granted our first FDA drug approval. We have a 17-person veteran sales force led by a seasoned commercial team engaging customers every day, one of whom gave us our first order yesterday. Our market capitalization is approximately $95 million and has reached twice that in the past 6 months. We ended our third quarter with about $20 million in cash and cash equivalents. We have clinics that are generating revenue.

We have earned the trust of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, and we've been tasked with leading the clinical development of their most promising solution to treating depression and PTSD in the military. We are gearing up for a commercially successful 2027 in which we aim to demonstrate a path to profitability, and we have an early-stage opportunity that may lead to the world's first disease-modifying drugs for ALS and schizophrenia in partnership with the U.S. National Institutes of Health and the governments of France and Switzerland. A recurring theme that we hear from shareholders is the feeling that they've been diluted over the past 2 years as we built a new, hopefully durable and potentially near-term profitable company.

In reality, management believes that the owners of approximately 11 million shares that were outstanding in September 2024 today own about 65% more value 2 years later based on their proportionate share in our current enterprise. Over the same period, the S&P 500 increased half that amount, 31%. While today's equity market is challenging for all biotechnology stocks, we hope that going forward, it will be less challenging for companies like ours that are actively booking revenue and earning profits than for companies that are still years away from a first drug approval. Over the 2 years since we changed our management team and became a working board building a working company, we've undergone extraordinary change in structure and focus.

The quarterly report that we filed yesterday is far longer than usual, and we hope you will read the business description carefully to better understand who we have become. We anticipate that the business structure we've laid out will be the structure by which we operate NRx for the foreseeable future. As outlined in the business description, we now have 4 divisions, each intended to be financed through mechanisms that are potentially nondilutive to NRXP shareholders and more importantly, each of which has near-term opportunity to become a profitable enterprise in its own right. We believe each of these has potential to return considerable value to those who own NRXP stock.

In brief, those divisions are: 1, our core NRx Pharmaceuticals company, which has expanded its focus from drugs that affect the central nervous system in depression and suicidality to encompass a promising sterile injectable products initiative; 2, our HOPE Therapeutics clinical division in which we treat patients with those CNS conditions; 3, NRx Defense Systems, which just signed its first prime contract with the Department of War; and 4, GeNeuro Incorporated, which has the potential to deliver the world's first disease-modifying drugs for ALS and schizophrenia.

NRx Pharmaceuticals was the original basis of -- sorry, NeuroRx Pharmaceuticals was the original basis of NRx Pharmaceuticals, focused on the development of an innovative drug to treat bipolar depression, the drug we call NRX-101. NeuroRx has now expanded to encompass not only its foundation drug, but a new sterile injectable products division that has just been granted its first drug approval. So the aim of NeuroRx sterile products is to deliver sterile injectable products at margins that are consistent with the margins for innovative drugs.

A key focus of our plan was to concentrate on immediately revenue-generating drugs such as preservative-free ketamine that could provide a solid financial foundation to our company as we seek to bring even more valuable innovative drugs to the market. As you know, Chaim Hurvitz, former President of Teva International, is one of our founding investors and Board members. Chaim and I learned a great deal from his father, Eli Hurvitz and later from Dr. Phillip Frost and the manner in which Teva built a solid foundation in immediately profitable generic drugs and then supported the extraordinary success of COPAXONE and successor innovative drugs. When we founded the company, we did not set out to sell sterile injectable drugs.

It was a byproduct of the FDA advising us in January 2023 that if we expected to use ketamine in conjunction with NRX-101, we would need to add psychiatry claims to generic ketamine. In working to satisfy that requirement, we discovered that the entire ketamine drug supply chain in the United States was broken. It had moved overseas and Americans were threatened by chronic shortage of ketamine and other sterile injectable products. We realized the critical need for sterile injectable drugs that could be manufactured in the United States at low cost and with minimal regulatory risk.

We estimate the current United States demand for sterile injectable ketamine alone at approximately $400 million a year and to be growing at more than 17% a year as ketamine is increasingly used in hospitals for pain control as well as anesthesia. This estimate does not fully incorporate the potential of ketamine to be used in treatment of depression and PTSD under our NRX-100 program. If we add a few similar sterile products, NRx can double or triple its currently addressable market in early 2027. The entire U.S. generic sterile products market is estimated at $23 billion according to IMARC. That's just generic drugs. It doesn't count the branded drugs.

Congressional and executive branch leaders have recognized the urgent national security need to bring the manufacture of strategic drugs back within the borders of the U.S. We're in active discussions with those leaders on both sides of the political aisle. In the post-COVID years, while nobody was looking, our sterile injectable supply chain became unstable to the point where 10% to 20% of those drugs are now supplied by compounding pharmacies for lack of an FDA-approved drug. FDA is actively engaged in enforcement actions that highlight the risks of compounding and FDA is forcing many compounders out of business. Moreover, 503B compounded drugs may not be legally sold when an FDA-approved drug is available and not in drug shortage.

This creates an urgent need and a growing opportunity for NRx's sterile injectable solutions. The real problem with these drugs is not the sterile drug, it's the glass bottle. During our COVID experience with ZYESAMI, we learned that the cost of bottling a drug in glass is about $3.25 a unit. The cost is driven not only by the cost of the glass, but also by the relatively low volume and high labor intensity of a sterile glass bottling line. Ask yourself, when is the last time you saw a glass milk bottle in the grocery store unless it was a boutique product.

Until now, injectable drugs could not be manufactured in more economical blow-fill-seal packaging because there was no FDA-approved mechanism to transfer the medication from the BFS container to a sterile syringe in a manner that medication could be withdrawn from a glass vial. We worked with our partner, Nephron Pharmaceuticals and our German equipment manufacturer to solve that problem using a Luer-Lock drug device combination now approved as part of NRx's abbreviated new drug application by the FDA on October 29, 2026, for preservative-free ketamine product. Although the Luer-Lock was previously incorporated in a grandfathered water for injection product, this was the first drug approval in which a blow-fill-seal vial was approved by FDA as a drug device combination.

This innovation, which required hundreds of pages of regulatory documentation and engineering testing will provide NRx with a market-leading platform for this and future sterile injectable drugs. Competitors will surely follow, but we predict it will take them considerable engineering time to stand up the manufacturing lines and then years of stability testing to get to the point where they can compete with us in the market. This manufacturing breakthrough has led to a cost of goods or COGS that's a fraction of the former cost of glass vial packaged drugs. For instance, 900,000 blow-fill-seal units can be manufactured on a BFS manufacturing line in the same time as 50,000 glass bottles can be filled, stoppered, crimp-capped, and packaged.

Compared with the roughly $3.25 per unit we saw with glass, we anticipate our COGS with BFS is approximately $0.75 a unit. The cost of buying and managing the glass generally exceeds the cost of the active pharmaceutical ingredient. This high COGS may help explain the diminished supply of sterile injectable products from overseas. It's at the point where the glass bottle manufacturers just have no margin left in their products. The innovative packaging of our first approved products also benefits the hospital personnel who handle it.

When pharmacists, nurses and doctors draw injectable products from a traditional glass vial, they first have to mount the needle on a syringe, pierce a rubber stopper with that needle and safely dispose of the needle. CDC estimates that hospital-based healthcare personnel in the United States report approximately 385,000 needle stick and other sharps injuries a year, a figure that is probably half of the true burden. In addition, the NRx Luer vial does not generate sharps medical waste, which is costly and complex to dispose of. Staff safety and staff time are at a premium in every U.S. hospitals and customers have applauded the value of the NRx BFS solution.

NRx human factor studies have demonstrated considerable time savings for medical staff with the Luer-Lock vial compared to traditional glass bottles and very high user satisfaction. The aim of our Innovative Pharmaceuticals division, on the other hand, is to develop NMDA antagonist drugs to treat depression and suicidality. As shareholders, you're well aware of our focus in obtaining FDA approval for ketamine to treat depression and suicidality. We plan to submit a new drug application for ketamine in the second quarter of this year when FDA granted us Fast Track designation. In the subsequent months, we've worked iteratively with FDA to solve several regulatory challenges and hope to submit a rolling NDA by the end of this year.

First of all, we had to solve the Luer-lock challenge that FDA raised in the context of our ANDA. As you know, it's now solved. Second, FDA asked us to document that the PHQ-9 depression scale used in most real-world evidence was comparable to the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression scale used in most clinical trials. We asked our partners at Yale University to address this challenge, and we've reproduced a sample of that comparative data in the 10-Q filed yesterday for you to read. Third, we decided to embark on a dual path to ketamine approval, seeking both regular approval and accelerated approval.

For regular approval, we will be submitting more than 500 patients of randomized clinical trial data and 65,000 patients of real-world evidence. Please familiarize yourself with the online guidance that FDA publishes under accelerated approval. Under that pathway, a sponsor can submit evidence that documents the effectiveness of a drug in achieving an intermediate clinical endpoint, such as short-term remission from depression and/or suicidality. In that pathway, the sponsor is able to obtain immediate approval to market a drug with the requirement that confirmatory evidence of long-term benefit will be delivered to FDA within 5 years.

That's why we're delighted to announce that we've now signed a collaboration agreement with Yale University and with the written approval of the PCORI or Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute, a government-funded initiative for NRx to join as the sponsor of a newly launched PCORI study that will compare IV ketamine to intranasal S-ketamine. We're confident that this 5-year study will provide the confirmatory data that the accelerated approval guidelines require and thus qualify us for accelerated approval. Whether by accelerated approval or regular approval, we believe NRX-100 can be approved in 2027. As you know, our company began with NRX-101, an oral fixed-dose combination of D-cycloserine and lurasidone to treat suicidal bipolar depression.

That drug was awarded breakthrough therapy designation by the FDA and was shown to reduce depression, suicidality and akathisia in 2 randomized controlled trials, where it demonstrated superiority to lurasidone, a standard of care drug for bipolar depression in relieving symptoms of akathisia and suicidality. Despite the effectiveness of NRX-101 in this indication, the future of twice-daily pills as a standard of care for treating depression is rapidly being challenged by interventional psychiatry advances in which our company is actively engaged. The unexpected positive development for NRX-101 was the discovery that the ingredients of NRX-101 could significantly augment the effectiveness of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, or TMS, and potentially enable a rapid 1-day treatment of depression with durable results.

In September 2026, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, awarded NRx Defense Systems, a prime contract to lead the SPARC-TMS trial, a Phase 2/3 clinical trial that has potential to support an FDA approval for NRX-101 in conjunction with rapid robotic Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation. The company is finalizing a cooperative research and development agreement with the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences to expand this trial to several leading military hospitals. Between the currently funded SPARC-TMS trial and the planned military hospital arm, more than 400 patients are expected to be enrolled and treated in 2027. The SPARC-TMS trial is scheduled to read out in early 2028.

A positive readout could support approval of NRX-101 with clinical trial costs funded by the Department of War as opposed to continued dilutive shareholder raises. We have a new pipeline product to announce today, NRX-200. Through our experience at HOPE Therapeutics, we've increasingly recognized the ergonomic challenges of administering IV ketamine to treat depression. IV infusion of ketamine, if it's done in compliance with laws found in most states, requires infusion nurses, nurse anesthetists, anesthesiologists who are similar highly trained personnel. Oral intramuscular and intranasal forms of ketamine are believed by many to be less efficacious in treating depression.

A steady state of low-dose ketamine is optimal to achieve the antidepressant effect, which cannot be achieved through any of the above routes. An ideal route of administration might be subcutaneous ketamine, which can be delivered by an insulin type pump with no IV needles or IV setup. The barrier to subcutaneous ketamine is that ketamine hydrochloride, the currently used form of the drug is highly acidic and barred from subcutaneous infusion. Any attempt to raise the pH of ketamine hydrochloride with standard buffers results in its precipitation from solution.

NRx has developed and demonstrated the feasibility of a proprietary formulation of ketamine based on an already FDA-approved cyclodextrin vehicle, which is exclusively licensed to NRx and for this purpose and which has a neutral pH. Should this subcutaneous approach prove successful, we believe that it could become the standard of care for administration of ketamine to treat depression and offer advantages over either intranasal or intravenous ketamine while providing NRx with long-term IP protection on this formulation because the vehicle itself is proprietary. NRX-200 will enter pharmacokinetic testing in early 2027. A first-in-human clinical trial is targeted for September 2027.

This trial will be conducted at HOPE Therapeutics, where our per patient costs are controlled and where we have direct quality oversight. In the first few years, there has been a sea change from traditional antidepressants to combined neuroplastic care. While SSRI and SNRI oral medications remain the most commonly used treatments, their complications are well known, including their risk of inducing suicidal ideation. NMDA antagonist drugs, psychedelic drugs and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation have advanced. We presented a comparison of the reported effects at the 2026 Cantor Fitzgerald Healthcare Conference, and that comparison is also included as an illustration in the 10-Q. I hope you look at it.

While we're far from a standard of care treatment that will replace traditional oral antidepressants, we believe the efficacy reported in the most successful clinical trials of psychedelic drugs does not exceed the efficacy of traditional antidepressants, although the psychedelic drugs are generally administered on one or several occasions rather than several times a day. Intravenous ketamine effectiveness has been reported in multiple clinical trials to exceed that of oral antidepressants, although the question of whether IV ketamine can be used as a chronic treatment because of its potential for addiction and neurotoxicity remains an open question.

These reported data underlie the enthusiasm for exploring a 1-day or short-term treatment with focused Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, especially among military personnel and first responders for whom traditional oral antidepressants and newer psychedelic medications are incompatible with continued military service. This recognition underlies DARPA's STRENGTHEN program and the SPARC-TMS clinical trial. We've put links to those programs in the 10-Q, and we hope you'll look at them. This also shapes our focus at HOPE Therapeutics. During 2025, we developed the operating model for HOPE and made initial clinic acquisitions with funding from the B Group.

HOPE generated its first clinical revenue in Q4 '25 and as of September 30, 2026, operates in 6 locations in Florida, including Dura Medical, Cohen and Associates and clinics founded by HOPE. We originally expected to incur additional debt and to lead a clinic roll-up. As we learn more, however, we saw roll-up failing all over the country and recognize the need for better technology HOPE is moving powerfully and deliberately to be at the forefront of that technology. We partnered with Zeta Surgical of Boston to implement the first robotic neuronavigated TMS and to treat the first patients with this technology advance.

In the preamble to the DARPA contract, the Department of War states that success in the SPARC-TMS project has potential to set standard of care for treating depression in the military and first responders. During 2026, NRx founded NRx Defense Systems, which we call NRXd as a fully qualified military contractor in response to DARPA's invitation to bid their broad agency announcement. NRXd focuses on military and first responder uses of NRx [ Hope ] technology in partnership with DARPA, the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, the Henry M. Jackson Foundation and first responder organizations.

NRxD's $11.2 million initial prime contract from DARPA for the SPARC-TMS clinical trial is a lead component of the STRENGTHEN program focused on treating depression, PTSD and suicidality in the military. We're partnered with Harvard Medical School's McLean Hospital and Arizona State University in the conduct of this trial. More importantly for shareholders, however, you now own a fully qualified DARPA contractor that meets the security and cybersecurity of current and future defense contracts. NRxD has been advised by DARPA that it satisfied its initial milestones and the first 2 invoices are approved for payment in Q4 2026. We anticipate achieving other milestones and other funding during that same quarter.

NRxD is anticipated to be funded through nondilutive capital to make a profit and to yield a modest contribution margin to the NRx parent company. We aim to have NRxD become an increasingly profitable component of NRx as additional opportunities arise to deploy our technology to serve patients in the military and in other governmental avenues who have depression, PTSD and suicidality. Finally, let's talk for a few moments about GeNeuro, whose aim is to develop the first disease-modifying drugs for ALS and schizophrenia. The 10-Q explains how human endogenous retroviruses entered the human genome more than 100,000 years ago.

Because this is such a new area of science and because it's something that most people have never heard of, we hope you'll take time to familiarize yourself with what's going on. The viral DNA that entered our genome through those endogenous retroviruses or HERVs has remained with us as part of the dark genome. When I got my biochemistry degree in 1978, they taught me that 8% of the human genome was junk DNA. We now know that, that 8% is actually the remnants of these old HERVs that entered the genome and stayed in our genome.

However, when parts of those ancient viruses are activated by various stimuli, could be environmental stimuli, could be a viral infection, could be trauma, neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS and schizophrenia may result. The GeNeuro assets were purchased in a Swiss bankruptcy auction after the failure of a Swiss biotechnology company that suffered from decisions to focus on clinical trial targets such as Long COVID rather than the core targets that we've described. That company never had the chance to develop its extraordinary discovery together with the U.S.

National Institutes of Health the discovery that HERV-K envelope protein may cause ALS and that an antibody to this toxic protein, which we call GNK-301 may enable patients with ALS to survive and even thrive. Please read the detail in our 10-Q and watch the keynote talk I recently gave at the Sachs Biotechnology Forum in Basel, if you want to understand this breakthrough. Not only does GeNeuro have a potentially disease-modifying drug for ALS, it has an antibody that has already been tested in multiple human trials called Temelimab, which we now intend to test for schizophrenia. We plan to hold a Science Day to explain GeNeuro's science during the first week in December.

Funds for GeNeuro are anticipated to come from government and private investors. NRx will own enough of GeNeuro that if GeNeuro succeeds, the value of this component to NRx's balance sheet might eclipse the rest of NRx. At the same time, we expect NRx to become profitable from the products I've described above, and GeNeuro is expected to be largely financed through mechanisms that do not dilute NRxP shareholders. There's far more going on with GeNeuro that can be addressed in this quarterly conference call, and we look forward to continuing to share our progress and to tell you about future opportunities to invest in GeNeuro. With that, I'll turn the call over to Michael Abrams, our Chief Financial Officer.

Michael Abrams: Thank you, Jonathan. For the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, NRx reported net patient revenue of $1.2 million compared with $0.2 million for the third quarter of 2025. Loss from operations was $8.1 million compared with $4 million from the prior quarter and a net loss of $2.2 million or $0.05 per share compared with a net loss of $5.9 million or $0.27 per share for the prior comparable quarter. For the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, NRx reported a net loss of $20.1 million versus a net loss of $29 million during the comparable period of 2025.

The change is primarily related to the impact of certain fair value accounting measurements and other nonrecurring charges related to the conversion and restructuring of previously issued convertible notes incurred during the 9 months ended September 30, 2025, which were partially offset by an increase in operating expense during the current period. For the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, NRx reported a loss from operations of $19.4 million versus a loss of operations of $11.6 million for the comparable period in 2025.

This change was driven by several factors, including: 1, an increase in cost of services from higher revenue generated at our HOPE clinics; 2, an increase in research and development expense related to the advancement of our various drug development initiatives; and 3, an increase in selling, general and administrative costs related to the commercial launch of our first approved drug for preservative-free IV ketamine. As of September 30, 2026, the company had approximately $19.8 million in cash and cash equivalents versus $7.8 million as of December 31, 2025. The increase is primarily related to the company's completion of a public offering of common stock with gross proceeds of more than $22 million.

Management believes current cash resources, revenue from the recent launch of the company's first approved drug, planned growth in clinic revenue at our HOPE clinics and opportunistic utilization of the company's active at-the-market offering facility will be sufficient to support operations for the foreseeable future. With that, I turn the call back over to Jonathan.

Jonathan Javitt: Thank you, Michael. It's been an extraordinary 2 years. To summarize, the third quarter and the weeks since have marked NRx's transition from a development stage company to a commercial pharmaceutical company. On October 29, FDA approved our abbreviated new drug application for preservative-free ketamine, our first drug approval and the first approval of a blow-fill-seal Luer-Lock vial as a drug device combination that will serve as a platform for a rapidly growing stable of sterile injectable products at a time when the United States desperately needs that capacity. Our 17-person veteran sales force is now in the field, and we received our first order yesterday.

We ended the quarter with approximately $20 million in cash and cash equivalents and no convertible debt on our balance sheet. Each of our 4 divisions is advancing. At NeuroRx, we aim to submit a rolling new drug application for NRX-100 by the end of this year and with our Yale collaboration supporting the accelerated approval pathway and NRX-200, our new subcutaneous ketamine formulation is expected to enter pharmacokinetic testing in early 2027. HOPE Therapeutics now operates 6 locations in Florida, is actively generating a growing amount of clinical revenue and is treating patients with robotic neuronavigated TMS.

NRx Defense Systems has just earned its first milestone payments from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and is leading the DARPA-funded SPARC-TMS trial of NRX-101. At GeNeuro, we plan to hold a Science Day during the first week of December to share with you the breakthrough importance of this technology. Our goal for 2027 is to build a commercially successful company that demonstrates profitability while funding our innovation for nondilutive sources whenever possible. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question comes from Elemer Piros from Lucid Capital Markets.

Elemer Piros: So several questions. The preservative-free ketamine, which you used to call KETAFREE, does that have a name, a new name or you stay with KETAFREE?

Jonathan Javitt: Right now, the label says ketamine preservative-free and customers are telling us that they like having a label that says exactly what the drug is. We continue to talk about adding a trade name. But right now, the customers like the clarity.

Elemer Piros: Okay. And with the newly announced NRX-200 program, the subcu formulation, when you go into a first-in-human trial other than the PK study, what is the plan there to show what sort of parameters for bioequivalence or what sort of trial are you envisioning there?

Jonathan Javitt: Well, we expect that NRX-200 delivered through a subcutaneous pump like an insulin pump will certainly be non-inferior to intranasal ketamine, will be equivalent to intravenous ketamine and will be superior to placebo. So we'll design a trial right around that. And it wouldn't surprise me if it mirrors what's going on in the PCORI study, where we're demonstrating non-inferiority of IV ketamine to SPRAVATO.

Elemer Piros: And so would NRX-100 and NRX-200 be complementary products on the market?

Jonathan Javitt: NRX-100 will have a period of data exclusivity that's measured in single-digit years because it's a new use for a generic drug, where NRX-200 will have almost an infinite period of exclusivity because the cyclodextrin vehicle has an ingredient composition that's about as secret as Coca-Cola. So how we'll dovetail those products is going to be a commercial decision, but I think you know us well enough to know that we'll do it cleverly.

Elemer Piros: Right. And the study with Yale, a 5-year study, is it 5 years to -- from start to finish or it's a 5-year observation of patients? If you could clarify that?

Jonathan Javitt: Well, the PCORI study is intended to have a readout within 5 years, which is well within the FDA requirement to submit confirmatory data of an accelerated approval within 5 years. So it basically gives us 2 ways to get NRX-100 approved, either FDA will decide that our real-world evidence is sufficient for regular approval or it's -- we believe it's certainly sufficient for accelerated approval with the PCORI data being submitted as the confirmatory information at the end of 5 years.

Elemer Piros: Okay. And my last question is, what is the order of magnitude of your first order for preservative-free ketamine?

Jonathan Javitt: We're going to announce something about what we've received over the course of the quarter as soon as the quarter ends.

Operator: The next question comes from Patrick Trucchio with H.C. Wainwright.

Patrick Trucchio: Congrats on all the progress. I was wondering how you envision ketamine sort of expanding in the market, if you envision sort of as the interventional psychiatry infrastructure continues to expand, should we expect sort of that rollout to expand with the infrastructure? And how much actual share do you think you could take from competing products in the market?

Jonathan Javitt: Well, if what you're talking about is preservative-free ketamine, the primary market for preservative-free ketamine is not psychiatry clinics. The primary market for preservative-free ketamine is hospitals and hospital outpatient departments where it's used for anesthesia and pain control in large quantities. That market is about $400 million a year, and it's growing -- seems to be growing by about 17% a year. We believe that customers like our product. They find the innovative packaging easier to use, safer for their staff, more efficient for their staff. And the real game changer will be how the preservative-free aspect is received. Customers like the idea of preservative-free. Consumers like it even better.

But if the government grants our citizen petition because we've shown the government that ketamine with benzethonium chloride is being used at toxic levels or at least at levels that exceed the government's toxicity threshold in hospitals every day, we have the potential for a market-clearing event. We're not saying that's going to happen. We'll be very happy if we take 20%, 30% of the market just by being better at what we do, having more innovative packaging, having a product that staff and patients like better.

But if we get that citizen petition, and it's certainly consistent with everything Secretary Kennedy has said about his determination to get toxic preservatives out of the food chain, out of the supply of drugs. If we get that, all of a sudden, we have a potential market-clearing event. What we really have to do is demonstrate that we can supply the whole U.S. market without a risk of a drug shortage. And given our ability to manufacture 900,000 doses per batch, that's basically an ability to make 4 million or 5 million units a month. That's enough to supply the whole United States. So obviously, we're going to shoot for the moon.

But if all we do is hit some singles and doubles, anybody who saw Moneyball knows that's a worthwhile objective.

Patrick Trucchio: That's really helpful. And understanding that we'll have more details on the ALS opportunity in December. I'm wondering how you ultimately envision GNK-301 as a treatment for a broad ALS population? Or would it be sort of more for a biologically defined subgroup? And how does that distinction -- how will that shape your development strategy ultimately?

Jonathan Javitt: Pat, that's a wonderful question, and I hope that you're going to be very involved in producing our Science Day. So the answer to your question is yes. It's targeted for a biologically defined subgroup. However, that biologically defined subgroup is the vast majority of people who have ALS. So all of this is work that's been done by GeNeuro in partnership with Professor Avi Nath, who is the Head of ALS at the U.S. National Institutes of Health. It's all in peer-reviewed publications, been reviewed by the nation's top scientists. And what we know -- and this is really brand-new science, but it's breathtaking science.

What we know is that 70% of people being seen at the National Institutes of Health with ALS have the envelope protein for endogenous retrovirus K in their cerebrospinal fluid in the fluid that surrounds the brain. And this envelope protein is highly neurotoxic. If you take the CSF from a patient with ALS and put it in a mouse, it gives ALS to the mouse. If you take that CSF and put it in human motor neuron cell culture, it kills the motor neuron cells in the same way that ALS does. And if you take our antibody, GNK-301 and add it to that system, you block the toxic effect.

So this is an area of science that I was involved in 25 years ago when we developed the first drugs for macular degeneration. To this day, nobody knows why VEGF, vascular endothelial growth factor is made in the retina of people with macular degeneration. And that toxic protein causes the retina to grow new blood vessels and make people go blind. To this day, nobody has ever been able to turn off VEGF production. But ever since 2004, we've had antibodies that soak up that VEGF. I was involved in Macugen. The most successful one in that early time was LUCENTIS or Avastin antibodies that soak up the toxic protein and prevent people from going blind. Same thing here.

Now that we've identified the toxic protein, which is the HERV-K envelope protein, we have an antibody that soaks it up just like a sponge soaks up spilled milk. And all of the animal work that's been done so far suggests that, that antibody can block the toxic effects of HERV-K envelope protein in people with ALS. So to go back to your question, does this work for a subgroup? Yes, it works for a subgroup. It works for a subgroup that we can identify just with a test for HERV-K envelope protein in the spinal tap or probably in the blood. And yes, that subgroup just happens to be almost everybody with ALS.

Operator: The next question comes from Tom Shrader with BTIG.

Thomas Shrader: I have some questions kind of clerical in nature. The 101 trial in TMS, is that going to be pure 101 or D-cycloserine? And just your thoughts on the lurasidone component? Is it -- just -- we know a lot about D-cycloserine in TMS. I don't think we know a lot about lurasidone. So maybe just an update on -- does that change anything in your mind? Or should we continue to look at D-cycloserine as the sort of comparator? And then I have a couple of follow-ups.

Jonathan Javitt: The trial that's funded by DARPA, the trial that is described in clinicaltrials.gov, the trial that's been approved by the FDA to proceed with patient enrollment uses NRX-101 exactly as you know it at a low dose. It's 175 milligrams of D-cycloserine, and I believe 7.5 milligrams of lurasidone, which is a pill that we already make. It's sitting in our warehouse. We have the matching placebo. It's ready to go into patients. There are data that have been developed over the last couple of months, suggesting that the lurasidone component does make a meaningful beneficial contribution in addition to the D-cycloserine. And you should expect those data to be published by our scientific colleagues at Harvard.

Thomas Shrader: Okay. And then the NRX-100, when you got Fast Track designation, at least you reported submitting data with that, which is something -- is that unusual for Fast Track? I usually think of data as being for breakthrough. And it sounds like you had -- how much have they looked at your trials? It sounds like from your comments that they have commented on the endpoint. I'm really getting at the NRX-100 NDA, is it partially reviewed as part of Fast Track? How much have they seen? And how much do you think is already accepted as the kind of package they're looking for?

Jonathan Javitt: Well, I wouldn't ever want to comment on what the FDA has already accepted, but you're asking a great question. So first of all, I don't know what other divisions of FDA do, but I can tell you that the psychiatry division is pretty rigorous about Fast Track, and they don't award Fast Track for a clinical-stage drug without looking at data. Yes, there are some Fast Track designations that get approved at preclinical stages without data, but those are for earlier-stage drugs. So yes, they looked at our data. They've looked at our data in a great amount of detail. They've looked at the clinical trials data.

And as we pointed out, they looked at it to the point where they said, "Oh, the clinical trials data are using MADRS, the real-world evidence that you're bringing in from Osmind is using PHQ-9. Now show us that there's equivalence between those scales." So people will say, "Oh, you haven't submitted the NDA yet." Well, okay, we're actively engaged in a scientific conversation with FDA, where we're not under the strict PDUFA clocks of an NDA, but we're looking at the data together. And they're identifying their issues about the data, just like they might do in an NDA process, except we're scientific collaborators in a sense, they don't have to issue a CRL when they have a question.

So in this case, they said, show us that the MADRS and the PHQ-9 are comparable scales, and there's a lot more science than we published in the 10-Q, but we showed you one of the bits of science that we're now submitting to FDA to show them that the PHQ-9 scale used in the 65,000 patients of real-world evidence yields comparable results to the MADRS scale that's used in the clinical trials. So we've been in a very active scientific dialogue with FDA. We don't feel a reason to talk about every stage of that scientific conversation because it doesn't serve anybody. Our objective is drug approval, and we're laser-focused on achieving that.

Thomas Shrader: And a final follow-up. You made a kind of an interesting comment. But for a ketamine-free competitor, they would need stability data to file. Just -- I thought it's an interesting hurdle. How much do they need? And I guess, how much do they need because it's potentially a key.

Jonathan Javitt: Well, under the regs, you're supposed to come in with 2 years of stability data. So if somebody wants to copy us, first of all, they've got to get their hands on a Rommelag blow-fill-seal machine. One of the things that's really turned this whole industry upside down is FDA decided that the competitor, the Weiler machines don't satisfy their sterility requirements. So all of a sudden, there's kind of one place in the world to get these state-of-the-art blow-fill-seal machines. We didn't say it in the conference call, but we've just bought 2 of them. So we've kind of bought out the manufacturing capacity for the short term.

Then they've got to get their hands on a set of molds to make the product that doesn't infringe on our intellectual property. And then they've got to install all of that, validate it at their manufacturing site, which takes half a year to a year. And once they've done all of that, they've got to fill some vials with their product, seal those vials and put them up for 2 years of stability. So sometimes people think patents are what protects you. Sometimes people think that data exclusivity under statute is what protects you. In this case, we estimate that we have a significant manufacturing head start on a lot of people.

Could there be some people out there who are as smart as we are? I sure hope there are because there's a $33 billion sterile injectable products market and clearly won't be us satisfying the whole thing. But is there an extraordinary opportunity to blow away glass, as I said, when's the last time you saw a glass milk bottle on the grocery store shelf.

Operator: The last question comes from Ed Woo with Ascendiant Capital.

Edward Woo: Yes, congratulations on all the progress. Following up your comment about the blow-fill-seal vials. You mentioned that you bought 2 machines. Do you have any exclusivity for those machines in the U.S.? Or is it more limited by the ability of manufacturer to make more machines in the near term?

Jonathan Javitt: Well, Rommelag blow-fill-seal machines get used for a lot of different things, everything from eyedrops that come in little 1 cc vials to IV bottles that are 0.5 liter or a liter. So we don't have any exclusivity on that. Don't expect ever to have exclusivity on that. But in terms of the design of our product, there's a lot about that, that's exclusive to us and our partners at Nephron.

The engineering work underlying this is something that would take somebody else more than a year in our estimate, just to do the engineering work, and they've got to turn that into machining and they've got to get the machine installed, then they've got to start filling and putting up for stability. So we've got a sustainable edge. My wife likes to say that unless you're at the front of the race pack, the view is always the same. So we think we're out front on this. And by the time other people catch up, we'll be upfront with something new. That's who we are.

Operator: There are no more questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Dr. Javitt for closing remarks. Please go ahead.

Jonathan Javitt: So thank you, operator, and thank all of you for joining us today and for your questions. We're grateful to our shareholders for their continued support, to our employees, our partners, our clinicians for the work that brought us to our first approval. And we're especially grateful to the patients and their families who've given us the real privilege of serving them, of making their lives better and for being part of their families. As always, please reach out to Brian Korb and our Investor Relations team with any further questions. We're available to you any time. Have a great day.

Operator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, this concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.

#2913. Is Anthropic Worth $1.4 Trillion? Here's What Investors Have to Believe

Anthropic is set for a splashy IPO. Is it worth buying?

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:10AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic, PBC ›

Anthropic's (ANT +0.00%) IPO is all set for Thursday, and the AI lab is going to make history.

While it won't top Space Exploration Technologies as the biggest IPO ever, which was valued at $1.75 trillion, it will come in at a close second at $1.4 trillion. What's more important is that it will mark a major milestone in the AI revolution.

Anthropic will be the first AI lab to go public, and by doing so, it will become the clearest representation of the success of AI itself. Up until this point, investors haven't had a good way to invest in companies like Anthropic and OpenAI that are making the products that have come to define AI.

Investors have been able to invest in stocks like Nvidia and other chipmakers that are known as AI stocks, but with Anthropic going public, the AI mantle will be passed.

So is Anthropic a good investment at an IPO valuation of $1.4 trillion? Here's what has to go right for it to work.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on stage at a conference. Image source: Anthropic.

Demand for AI compute continues to outstrip the available supply, but the long-term demand for generative AI capabilities isn't fully clear, though it's expected to grow. We're already seeing a backlash against the technology in the form of data center protests that shifted the midterm election results, fears of widespread job loss, and concerns that AI could become destructive, as Anthropic has called for a slowdown in AI development and stronger safety guardrails several times.

Right now, Anthropic is delivering blockbuster growth, but a number of factors could derail that, including political regulations, an AI infrastructure bubble bursting, or a rogue AI incident. While technological progress in AI is likely to move forward, it's not guaranteed that Anthropic and its chatbot peers will be widely embraced in the end.

Anthropic dialed down its target IPO valuation from $2 trillion to $1.4 trillion, in part because of concerns about its massive purchase commitments for chips, AI compute capabilities, and lease obligations.

Anthropic over the next several years owes about $900 billion in purchase commitments, many of which are non-cancelable.

In order for the stock to move higher, Anthropic will have to demonstrate that it is capable of meeting those obligations, ideally through positive cash flow, and that will require significant growth from the company.

CEO Dario Amodei has said before that one of his biggest challenges is knowing how much compute the company needs. We'll find out whether the company has overextended itself or hasn't secured enough compute capacity in the coming years.

The biggest competitive threat to Anthropic may be open-source and open-weight models, which have the potential to undercut Anthropic and siphon away its user base.

While open models aren't expected to match frontier models from Anthropic or others in terms of technological capabilities, they are already taking cheaper work, allowing organizations to avoid paying for expensive frontier tokens.

Dario Amodei has advocated for oversight on open models to ensure authoritarian governments don't achieve military superiority over the U.S., and said the U.S. should crack down on distillation, or open models essentially training themselves from established models.

As Anthropic grows in the coming years, investors should keep an eye on the open model development, as it has the potential to challenge Anthropic and upend the AI race.

Overall, while Anthropic faces a lot of risks in the coming years, the company is also growing rapidly and reasonably valued. It's a good bet to pop on Thursday.

#2909. Is Micron Next to Announce a Stock Split?

The memory chip maker has not split its shares since 2000.

By Will Healy – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›

Micron Technology's (MU -1.08%) market performance has investors thinking about something that has not occurred since the dot-com boom: a stock split. The company split its stock three times, with the last one occurring in May 2000.

Now, amid the AI boom and a price that was, until recently, above $1,000 per share, some investors are considering such a scenario again.

Indeed, one cannot dismiss the possibility of Micron's first stock split in more than 26 years. Nonetheless, I think it probably will not be the next stock to split, and here's why.

As of the time of this writing, Micron stock trades at around $735 per share. That makes it the 28th most expensive stock in terms of nominal price trading on U.S. markets today.

On the surface, that makes the chip stock an excellent candidate for a stock split, and investors should not be surprised to see such a move. Additionally, the 259% revenue growth in fiscal 2026 (ended Sept. 3) and the 107% increase forecast for fiscal 2027 suggest that the stock price could rise further.

However, given the state of its peers, it has no pressing need to make such a move. Some of the more prominent tech stock splits in recent years were Apple and Amazon. As components of the price-weighted Dow Jones Industrial Average, they face stock split pressure that Micron does not.

Furthermore, among tech stocks outside of the "Magnificent Seven," peers such as ASML Holding and Sandisk sell at higher nominal prices. Even though a stock can split at any time a company's board sees fit, the next stock split is more likely to come from one of these companies.

Another critical consideration is Micron's historical volatility. As previously mentioned, Micron split in May 2000. Soon after, Micron's pricing power disappeared when demand for its memory chips cratered, and the stock lost nearly all of its value.

This is concerning since analysts forecast that Micron's revenue growth will slow to just 16% in fiscal 2028. Investors tend to punish stocks with slowing revenue growth, and history suggests that could bode poorly for the stock.

Moreover, investors should not assume that the extreme cyclicality of the memory chip industry has disappeared. Indeed, Micron has locked its customers into long-term contracts, which should mitigate the effects of an industry slowdown.

However, given the historical risks of a falling stock price, investors should not expect Micron to rush to any stock split decision.

Under current conditions, Micron is more than likely not the next stock to split, and even if it does, it will likely do so cautiously.

Admittedly, Micron looks like an excellent stock split candidate on the surface, and that could lead to such a move. Its price has recently exceeded $1,000 per share, and larger, more prominent stocks have split their shares in recent years.

Nonetheless, 27 stocks are currently more expensive than Micron, and few of those are in the tech sector. Additionally, given its historical volatility, investors cannot rule out the possibility of a massive pullback. Such conditions probably mean it will approach the stock split issue carefully, if at all.

#2905. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2900. Pochettino's USMNT swan song signals change

From the moment Mauricio Pochettino was announced as United States men's national team head coach in September 2024, things felt different. It wasn't his experience or his personality - although, both were certainly noteworthy. Instead, it was his name. His stature. His reputation.

Suddenly, somehow, the United States - the perpetually overlooked, stigmatized name in the halls of global soccer - was dating the prom king.

It was unexpected. It was surreal. And it was bound to be fleeting.

Now, following a 2-0 victory against Haiti at TQL Stadium, in Cincinnati, the Mauricio Pochettino fairytale is officially over. After just two years in charge of the USMNT (and a whirlwind two years at that), Pochettino departs to take up the coveted / cursed position of Manchester United manager.

It's a change that's as disappointing as it is unsurprising. Despite the misty-eyed soundbites over the last week in which he described the decision as "one of the toughest" of his career, Pochettino's return to club football has felt inevitable.

He made no bones about his wandering eye, always quick to profess his love for the Premier League while maintaining his London residence throughout his time with the USMNT. Even when his contract extension was announced this summer, the conditions of that deal made it abundantly clear that should an attractive suitor come calling, he would answer. Now, after years apart, he'll get to rekindle that romance.

As Pochettino celebrated Christian Pulisic putting the U.S. ahead in the 25th minute with one of the most acrobatic goals of the attacker's career (a high-flying bicycle kick that cut the ball inside the far post), some of his personnel were already across the Atlantic, laying the groundwork for his upcoming rendezvous. Even if his couching staff was divided, Pochettino insisted that his focus was not. And with Julian Hall doubling the USMNT's lead in the 43rd minute, perhaps he wasn't lying.

It's rare that football managers exit on their own terms. Even rarer still when they finish out their tenure having already secured their next job. Likely rarest of all, is to go straight from a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final to the biggest derby in English football.

Then again, little about Pochettino's tenure has been normal.

To even appoint the Argentine, U.S. Soccer aimed higher, spent more, and was bolder than ever before. The mechanisms employed to secure his signature (including donations-as-salary from hedge-fund billionaire Ken Griffin) were as opportunistic as they were canny. Ultimately, they succeeded. But has Pochettino?

If this window is anything to go by then the answer is emphatically yes. Eight goals, zero conceded, across two competitive performances is beyond reproach. Exciting attacks, the promise of youth, undeniable tenacity - much of what fans hoped they would get from Pochettino's appointment was on display against Haiti. But stepping out of the moment, things become a little more complicated.

Pochettino's time as U.S. head coach saw no records broken and no trophies won. The USMNT's ranking is identical to when he took over while his win percentage is less than that of predecessor Gregg Berhalter. Meanwhile, his relationship with the players (Christian Pulisic, in particular) was at times tense, and his rapport with media and fans could even be patronizing. It was, however, also under his watch that 78 different players earned a cap, nine teenagers made debuts, and the USMNT put in one of their all-time great performances (Paraguay), World Cup or otherwise. Altogether, it's a portfolio that plays like a Rorschach test. Love him or hate him, you'll find stats to back you up.

But stats aren't really where Pochettino's legacy lies. Indeed, what Pochettino left the U.S. with - and perhaps even the wider soccer world - was a shift in perception.

The US can should think bigger. Our talent is plentiful. World Cups are winnable.

How true these notions actually are remains to be seen, but what isn't up for debate is who promoted them: Mauricio Pochettino. USMNT head coach Muaricio Pochettino. The sheer reality of that fact makes any future fantasies just a little more plausible. It's something that even Pochettino seemed to recognize. "Being head coach in USA now is prestigious," he said. Self-aggrandizing, sure, but also true - even if only symbolically.

And this, more than anything, is Pochettino's great success.

Two years ago, the thought of a top-tier, globally in-demand manager taking over the United States men's national team was unthinkable. International football simply wasn't a jewel in the managerial crown - let alone a program as disparaged as the U.S. But one Pochettino later, and the narrative has changed.

Now, some of the biggest names in soccer (Tuchel, Carlo, Klopp) find themselves helming national teams (England, Brazil, Germany, respectively) while arguably the biggest name is rumored to be intrigued by the prospect of taking over the USMNT.

The likelihood of Pep Guardiola becoming the next United States head coach is slim, at best. But what's remarkable is that it's no longer laughable.

This is a massive country, with tremendous resources, and enormous potential. The scale and scope of a USMNT "project", combined with the prospect of unleashing a sleeping giant, might actually entice a name as big as Pep (see Man City). Still, in the immediate context of Haiti and a Nation's League quarter final, it's a prospect that's hard to reconcile, and, ultimately, a reflection of the unique place that the U.S. now finds itself.

A place where B.J. Callaghan is mentioned alongside Julian Nagelsmann. Where the self-deprecating backwaters of USMNT fandom have turned a little less dark. Where the once overlooked now get second glances.

A place that was good enough for Mauricio Pochettino.

#2898. James reaches assists milestone, keeps seeing plays ‘before they actually happen'

James reaches assists milestone, keeps seeing plays 'before they actually happen' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Tyrese Maxey admitted that he wasn't entirely ready for LeBron James' first pass of the afternoon Sunday.

Maxey cut through the paint and James' bounce pass was perfect, but the Sixers' All-NBA guard missed his layup. He's not fully accustomed yet to James' precognitive gifts.

"There's still some times when you're surprised," Maxey said after the Sixers' win over the Pacers. "… I was cutting through just to cut and create space. The ball hit me in the chest and I missed the layup. I was like, 'Ah shoot, my bad.' He was like, 'Yeah, you weren't looking.'"

James has been trying to teach his teammates that he'll spot openings they may not notice.

"I just tell my guys, 'Always pay attention to me when I've got the ball,' because I definitely see plays develop before they happen," James said.

For the most part, James' teammates adhered to his request on the latest historic day in a milestone-filled career. By setting up VJ Edgecombe's layup with 1:19 left in the fourth quarter, James moved into third place on the NBA's all-time assists list, passing Jason Kidd.

The 22-time All-Star recorded 11 assists, his most so far as a Sixer, and now sits at 12,092 in his career. Chris Paul (12,552 assists) and John Stockton (15,806) are the only two players above James.

"It's obviously super humbling," James said. "It's something that I didn't foresee in my career, but I knew assists meant a lot to me. Just the movement of the ball, being able to find my teammates, putting the ball on time and on target.

"And also just being linked with some of the greats that have ever played this game and a dear friend of mine, J-Kidd. It's really special."

James is at or near the top of many all-time leaderboards. He's first in NBA history in points, games and minutes, sixth in steals and fifth in triple-doubles.

Passing has always been a core element of his game.

"First of all, he's got the vision and the awareness," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "He's got the size to see. I think he's got some anticipation. Just a half-second before a play happens, he knows how the defense is moving. … And he throws crisp passes. Some of those are cooking out to the corner three guys, so it doesn't let the close-out get there nearly as quickly."

Whether it's a long-range rocket, a drive-and-kick dish or a cross-court feed from the post that suggests he might have eyes in the back of his head, James has always enjoyed finding a wide range of ways to help his teammates.

"For someone that talented, he's very unselfish," Maxey said. "He really prides himself on getting guys open."

As James recalled Sunday, he had exceptional passing tools long before he entered the NBA 24 seasons ago.

"Since I was a kid, I've had the ability to see plays before they actually happen," he said. "Seeing movement, seeing cracks in the defense before they were even open … it's something that's been with me since I was a kid.

"I just had that vision and it just stuck with me throughout my playing days."

The Golden State Warriors are struggling amid the absence of superstar guard Stephen Curry, who is recovering from a right oblique abdominal tear.

Curry missed his second straight game on Monday as the Warriors suffered another blowout loss, this time against the New Orleans Pelicans.

The Warriors will be without Curry until Thanksgiving, though it's possible he could be sidelined for an even longer period, as per BasketNews.

GettySteph Curry #30 of the Golden State Warriors reacts after making a basket against the Los Angeles Lakers at Chase Center on October 30, 2026 in San Francisco, California.

Last season, Stephen Curry missed 39 games last season due to rest, minor issues and a major knee injury. Curry was out for 27 consecutive games after being diagnosed with patellofemoral pain syndrome in his right knee, more commonly known as runner's knee.

Speaking to ESPN's Anthony Slater, Curry shared how painful the injury was and the setbacks he suffered during his adjustment and recovery from what was described as a chronic issue the two-time MVP will have to play with for the rest of his career.

"Against Detroit, it took everything in me down there on the training table just to be like, 'Oh, I can go out here tonight and play,'" Curry said. "And I was just faking it for the first whatever (25 minutes)."

GettySteph Curry #30 of the Golden State Warriors warms up wearing a Golden State Valkyries before their preseason game at Chase Center on October 16, 2026 in San Francisco, California.

The Warriors superstar tried to return after the All-Star break and even worked out with Sabrina Ionescu. However, "there were certain directions of movement and stuff that just didn't work," so his return was pushed back.

Curry was supposed to scrimmage with the team in late March, but his right knee "felt worse than it had before." He called it a "true setback," though he managed to come back before the end of the regular season.

The Warriors labored to make the NBA play-in tournament. They shocked the LA Clippers to have a shot at the No. 8 spot, but they were blown out by the Phoenix Suns.

GettyStephen Curry #30 of the Golden State Warriors stands on the court during their game against the Los Angeles Lakers at Chase Center on October 30, 2026 in San Francisco, California.

In the same interview with ESPN's Anthony Slater, Stephen Curry admitted that the two-year, $115 million extension he signed in the offseason could be his last.

"I assumed that it would probably be one of, if not the last, contract I signed," Curry said. "I'm not afraid to say it. But maybe I'll surprise myself and want to keep going."

At the age of 38, Curry was playing at an MVP level before his oblique injury.

And with the way the Warriors lost their first two games since the injury, they still need their superstar more than ever.

#2892. Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return

Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

PG-13 was rated R in his return to Philadelphia.

The middle finger Paul George directed toward one baseline fan only reinforced that rating.

Tuesday night was expected to revolve around Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum sharing an NBA court as opponents for the first time. Instead, the other headliner in the summer's blockbuster trade stole the show.

George scored a game-high 36 points in Boston's 123-101 win over the Sixers. He shot 14 for 22 from the floor, made six of his 11 three-point attempts and scored 14 consecutive Boston points in the fourth quarter.

The game was tied at 79 with 3:19 remaining in the third quarter. Boston outscored Philadelphia 44-22 from that point forward.

The Celtics went nine minutes and 20 seconds without making a two-point field goal during the second half. Instead, they made nine consecutive field goals from three, the second-longest such streak by a Sixers opponent over the last 30 seasons.

Payton Pritchard opened the fourth with consecutive threes. George followed with eight straight points, helping the Celtics begin the quarter on a 14-0 run that turned a competitive game into a rout.

George's return carried a complicated history. His two seasons with the Sixers were repeatedly interrupted by injuries, but he also played a significant role in their most memorable playoff run in years.

Last spring, George helped the Sixers overcome a 3-1 deficit to eliminate Boston in seven games. He averaged 17.4 points and shot 55 percent from three during the series.

Tyrese Maxey was happy to see his former teammate Tuesday, even if he disliked what followed.

"It was good to see Paul," Maxey said. "I love him, love his family. … He gave us everything he had while he was here. We know what he did in the playoffs last year. Great person, great family, and we'll see him again."

Maxey then added one important qualifier.

George instead scored from nearly everywhere.

"He had some open threes. He had some pull-up threes. He had some middies," Maxey said. "He played within the game, too. That's what Paul does. He plays within the game. He takes what the defense gives him, and we gave him too many open looks tonight.

"PG, we know what PG does. We shouldn't even be allowing him to get up 11 threes, and that's on us."

Nick Nurse watched George attack the Sixers in several ways.

"He really had it going," Nurse said. "He'd post up, and-one, fallaways. He went down the lane, high archer off the glass, and-one. He scored in about every way he could tonight."

George heard boos during his return and said the arena carried the atmosphere, though not quite the intensity, of a playoff game.

"This building can be very electric as well," George said. "It was fun. It was fun to play in this environment."

One interaction extended beyond the usual reception for a returning player.

During a stoppage, the ball rolled toward a fan seated along the baseline. George said the fan looked directly at him before dropping the ball instead of returning it.

"There was a fan being an a–," George said. "The ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes, dropped the ball on the ground as if I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it, instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do.

"And so, yeah, then I rolled him a middle finger in return."

#2890. Cincinnati schedules home-and-home with Missouri for 2027 and 2032

While the 2026 regular season is in its twilight stages, some teams are already looking ahead to 2027.

On Tuesday, Cincinnati and Missouri announced a home-and-home non-conference series. Missouri will host the Bearcats at Faurot Field on Sept. 18, 2027, while Cincinnati welcomes the Tigers to Nippert Stadium on Sept. 11, 2032.

Although the campuses are separated by fewer than 500 miles, the 2027 matchup will mark the first-ever meeting between the Big 12 and SEC opponents.

Cincinnati has now finalized its non-conference schedule for the 2027 season. The Bearcats will host Central Connecticut of the FCS on Aug. 28, remain at home against Missouri State on Sept. 4, and complete their non-conference slate at Missouri on Sept. 18. Cincinnati does not have a game scheduled for the weekend of Sept. 11, when it will either play its Big 12 opener or take a bye.

Both Missouri and Cincinnati experienced recent cancelations in their 2027 non-conference slates, making them a perfect match for each other. The Tigers saw their 2027 home contest against Illinois get axed, while Cincinnati's looming road trip to Boston College was also removed from the schedule.

The Bearcats have won five consecutive regular season non-conference matchups, sweeping all three opponents during the 2026 season. The 2027 trip to Missouri will mark the program's first true road non-conference game since Sept. 14, 2024 when it traveled to crosstown rival Miami (OH). Also, it will be the Bearcats' first out-of-state non-conference road game since Sept. 9, 2023 at Pittsburgh and first SEC matchup since Sept. 3, 2022 at Arkansas.

Cincinnati traditionally had one non-conference vacancy reserved for Miami, as the two competed in one of the longest running series in college football. The rivals played their 129th and final scheduled meeting this past September, making it the fourth-most played FBS matchup behind Minnesota-Wisconsin, Auburn-Georgia, and North Carolina-Virginia.

Although an iconic rivalry has been shelved, the Bearcats can look forward to securing their first victory over SEC competition on Sept. 18, 2027 in Columbia.

#2889. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.
